# pymmcore-plus

> Control microscopes with Python: Micro-Manager's core, acquisition engine, widgets, and apps.

Python tools for controlling microscopes with Micro-Manager: pymmcore-plus (core + acquisition engine), useq-schema (experiment schema), pymmcore-widgets (Qt widgets), pymmcore-gui and napari-micromanager (applications).

# Getting started

# pymmcore-plus

These docs cover `pymmcore-plus` and the packages built around it, which let you control a microscope from Python by talking directly to [Micro-Manager](<https://micro-manager.org>)'s C++ core and device adapters (with no Java process involved). You can use them to script your hardware and run multi-dimensional acquisitions, or to build your own GUI (or just use one of ours).

[Get started](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/which-package/index.md>) [User guide](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/index.md>)

```python
import useq
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # demo devices

sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
    time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 5},
)
core.mda.run(sequence, output="data.ome.zarr")
```

## Where to start

If you're new here, [Getting Started](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/which-package/index.md>) walks you through installing things, controlling Micro-Manager's demo devices from Python, running a first acquisition, and putting together a small GUI (no microscope required). If you already know Micro-Manager, have a look at [Coming from Micro-Manager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/from-micro-manager/index.md>), which maps what you know onto these packages.

If you'd rather not write any code, [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) is our (work in progress) desktop application, and [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>) controls a microscope from inside [napari](<https://napari.org>).

## How the pieces fit together

Each package builds on the ones below it. You only need to go as far up the stack as you want (`pymmcore-plus` on its own is enough to script a microscope).

Applications

[**pymmcore-gui**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) · [**napari-micromanager**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>)

Desktop applications for running a microscope.

Widgets

[**pymmcore-widgets**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>)

Qt widgets for devices, properties, configurations and acquisitions.

Control &amp; acquisition

[**pymmcore-plus**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/index.md>) · [**useq-schema**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/index.md>)

The core, extended with events and an acquisition engine, and a schema for describing experiments.

Micro-Manager

[**pymmcore**](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>) · [device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/index.md>)

The C++ core and drivers for hundreds of cameras, stages, shutters, lasers, etc...

Your microscope

Micro-Manager's demo devices, or your own hardware

## Getting help

If you have usage questions (*"How do I...?"*), please ask on the [image.sc forum](<https://forum.image.sc/tag/pymmcore-plus>) with the `pymmcore-plus` tag, or come chat with us on [Zulip](<https://imagesc.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/442785-pymmcore.5B-plus.5D>). Bug reports and feature requests are always welcome on [GitHub](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus>) (each package has its own repository; see [Contributing](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/contributing/index.md>) if you're not sure which one).

# Your First Acquisition

A multi-dimensional acquisition (MDA) is a series of images collected across time points, stage positions, channels, z-planes, etc... In pymmcore-plus, the experiment is *described* with [useq-schema](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/index.md>) and *run* by the [acquisition engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>).

We'll need a core with a configuration loaded:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()
```

## Describing the experiment

An `MDASequence` declares what to acquire. It doesn't know anything about your hardware (beyond the names of things like channel presets), and can be saved to (and loaded from) JSON or YAML.

```python
import useq

x, y = core.getXYPosition()
z = core.getZPosition()

sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI", {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 50}],  # (1)!
    time_plan={"interval": 0.5, "loops": 3},  # (2)!
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1},  # (3)!
    stage_positions=[(x, y, z), (x + 100, y, z)],  # (4)!
    axis_order="tpcz",  # (5)!
)

sequence.sizes       # {'t': 3, 'p': 2, 'c': 2, 'z': 5}
len(list(sequence))  # 60 events
```

1. Channels are presets in the `Channel` configuration group (the default group), with an optional exposure in milliseconds.
2. 3 time points, 0.5 seconds apart.
3. A 4 µm z-stack in 1 µm steps, centered on the `z` of each stage position.
4. Two `(x, y, z)` stage positions, in µm: the current position, and one 100 µm away in x. These are absolute stage coordinates, so on a real microscope, make sure they're somewhere safe!
5. The nesting order, outermost first: for each **t**ime point, visit each **p**osition, and there, for each **c**hannel, take a **z**-stack.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Where is the z-stack?**
>
> A z-stack described with `range` (or `above` and `below`) is *relative* to the `z` of each stage position. If a position has no `z`, or the sequence has no stage positions at all, it is currently relative to z = 0, *not* to wherever your focus is. On a real microscope that could drive the objective a long way, which is why we pass the current `z` explicitly above.

Iterating over the sequence yields one `MDAEvent` per image, each describing what the hardware should do for that image (any field that is left unset means "leave it as it is"). See the [`MDASequence` reference](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/index.md>) for more of what a sequence can express (grids, well plates, autofocus, per-position sub-sequences, etc...).

## Running it

```python
@core.mda.events.frameReady.connect  # (1)!
def on_frame(image, event, metadata):
    print(event.index, image.shape)

core.mda.run(sequence, output="experiment.ome.zarr", overwrite=True)  # (2)!
```

1. Connect to events to process data as it arrives. `frameReady` is called with the image (a numpy array), the `MDAEvent` and a dict of metadata.
2. `mda.run` blocks until the acquisition is done. (Use `core.run_mda(sequence)` to run it on a background thread instead.) `overwrite=True` replaces `experiment.ome.zarr` if it already exists; without it, running the script a second time raises a `FileExistsError`.

... prints a line for each of the 60 images:

```text
{'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} (512, 512)
{'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} (512, 512)
{'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} (512, 512)
...
{'t': 2, 'p': 1, 'c': 1, 'z': 4} (512, 512)
```

## Where did the data go?

The `output` argument writes the images to disk as they arrive, and the extension picks the format. An `.ome.zarr` "file" is actually a folder. Each stage position is stored as a separate image inside it (`experiment.ome.zarr/0`, `experiment.ome.zarr/1`), as an array with dimensions `(t, c, z, y, x)`. You can read it back with [zarr](<https://zarr.readthedocs.io>) (`pip install zarr`):

```python
import zarr

data = zarr.open_array("experiment.ome.zarr/0/0", mode="r")
data.shape  # (3, 2, 5, 512, 512)
```

If you'd rather have files that you can drag into Fiji, use `output="experiment.ome.tiff"` (this needs the `io` extra: `pip install "pymmcore-plus[io]"`). With more than one stage position, you get one file per position, in a folder named after your output (`experiment/experiment_p000.ome.tiff`, `experiment/experiment_p001.ome.tiff`).

See [Saving data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>) for more on formats and options.

## Beyond sequences

`MDASequence` is just one way to make events. The engine will run *any* iterable of `MDAEvent` objects, so a plain list works too:

```python
events = [
    useq.MDAEvent(channel="DAPI", exposure=10),
    useq.MDAEvent(channel="FITC", x_pos=x + 50, y_pos=y),
]
core.mda.run(events)
```

The iterable needn't even be of known length. A generator or a `Queue` can decide on the next event based on previous images (see [Event-driven acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/event_driven_acquisition/index.md>)).

## Next steps

[The acquisition engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>) covers running acquisitions in more depth (pausing and cancelling, hardware triggering, etc...), and [Building sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>) shows more of what you can describe with an `MDASequence`. When you're ready for a graphical interface, have a look at [your first GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-gui/index.md>).

# Your First GUI

You can either use one of the existing applications ([pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) or [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>)), or build your own from [pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>), a library of Qt widgets for controlling a `CMMCorePlus`.

## Using an application

Once it's [installed](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/install/index.md>) (from GitHub, or as a bundled app for Windows and macOS), start it with the demo devices:

```sh
mmgui run --demo-config
```

Without `--demo-config`, the app starts with no devices loaded. You can load a configuration from the **Devices** menu, or start with `mmgui -c path/to/config.cfg`. See [Using pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/usage/index.md>) for more.

Once it's [installed](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/getting_started/index.md>), start it with:

```sh
napari-micromanager
```

Then pick a configuration file at the top left of the window (or start it with `napari-micromanager -c path/to/config.cfg`).

## Building your own

Widgets in `pymmcore-widgets` use the global `CMMCorePlus.instance()` by default (see the tip in [First steps](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-steps/#connecting-to-events>)), and they listen to the core's [events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>), so if you change something from a script (or from another widget), they'll update to match. (A few widgets don't use a core at all. The sequence editors, like `ChannelTable` and `MDASequenceWidget`, just edit `useq` objects.)

You'll need `pymmcore-widgets` and a Qt backend, PyQt6 or PySide6 (see [Installation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/install/#installing-the-packages>), and [PyQt6 or PySide6?](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/#installing-a-qt-backend>) if you're not sure which). The examples here import Qt from [`qtpy`](<https://github.com/spyder-ide/qtpy>), so they run with either one.

Then combine widgets like any other Qt widgets:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QHBoxLayout, QVBoxLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import (
    ChannelWidget,
    ExposureWidget,
    ImagePreview,
    LiveButton,
    SnapButton,
)

app = QApplication([])

core = CMMCorePlus.instance()  # (1)!
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

window = QWidget()
controls = QHBoxLayout()
controls.addWidget(ChannelWidget())
controls.addWidget(ExposureWidget())
controls.addWidget(SnapButton())
controls.addWidget(LiveButton())

layout = QVBoxLayout(window)
layout.addLayout(controls)
layout.addWidget(ImagePreview())
window.show()

app.exec()
```

1. This is the core the widgets below will use, so loading the configuration here is enough for all of them. Pass `mmcore=...` to a widget to use a different core (the `ConfigWizard` calls it `core=`).

A slightly larger version of this example ([`custom_gui.py`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/index.md>), which adds a configuration loader and a few more controls) looks like this:

## Next steps

The [widget gallery](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) is the best place to find widgets for your own GUI (each one has a screenshot and a runnable example). [Building a custom GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/index.md>) walks through the larger example above, and [Qt integration](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/integration-with-qt/index.md>) explains how to keep the GUI responsive while the hardware is busy.

# First Steps

At the heart of Micro-Manager is its *core* (`CMMCore`): a C++ library that loads your hardware configuration, talks to each device through its device adapter, and hands you images. Micro-Manager's Java application (MMStudio) is built on top of it, and [`pymmcore`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>) makes it available in Python.

The main object in `pymmcore-plus` is `CMMCorePlus`, an enhanced subclass of `pymmcore.CMMCore`. It aims to be a drop-in replacement, so if you've used `pymmcore` (or the `mmc` object in Micro-Manager's script panel), the methods you know are all still there. `CMMCorePlus` adds a number of things on top, and we'll look at a few of them here.

These examples use Micro-Manager's demo devices, so you don't need any hardware. You can paste them into a Python session (`python`, `ipython` or a Jupyter notebook) started in the environment where you [installed](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/install/index.md>) `pymmcore-plus`, or put them in a script.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Is Micro-Manager open?**
>
> `CMMCorePlus` doesn't connect to a running copy of Micro-Manager; it opens the devices itself. Most hardware can only be opened by one program at a time, so close Micro-Manager (MMStudio) before you load the same configuration here. (The demo devices don't mind.) See [Coming from Micro-Manager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/from-micro-manager/index.md>) for more.

## Loading a configuration

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # (1)!

print(core.getLoadedDevices())
# ('DHub', 'Camera', 'Dichroic', 'Emission', 'Excitation', 'Objective', 'Z', ...)
```

1. With no argument, this loads the demo configuration (`MMConfig_demo.cfg`). Pass the path to your own `.cfg` file to use your hardware (see [Using your own microscope](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/own-microscope/index.md>)).

## Snapping an image

```python
core.setExposure(25)  # milliseconds
image = core.snap()  # (1)!
print(image.shape, image.dtype)  # (512, 512) uint16
```

1. `snap` is a `CMMCorePlus` convenience that calls `snapImage()` and returns `getImage()` as a numpy array.

`image` is just a numpy array, so you can look at it or save it with whatever tools you like. For example, to save it as a TIFF (that you can open in Fiji), use [tifffile](<https://github.com/cgohlke/tifffile>), which comes with the `io` extra (or `pip install tifffile`):

```python
import tifffile

tifffile.imwrite("snap.tif", image)
```

(In a Jupyter notebook, `matplotlib.pyplot.imshow(image)` is a quick way to have a look at it.)

## Reading and setting properties

Each device has a number of *properties*. You can use the classic string-based API:

```python
core.getProperty("Camera", "Binning")      # '1'
core.setProperty("Camera", "Binning", "2")
core.getImageWidth()                       # 256
```

...or the object-oriented `Device` and `DeviceProperty` views:

```python
camera = core.getDeviceObject("Camera")
gain = camera.getPropertyObject("Gain")
gain.value = 1
gain.range()  # (-5.0, 8.0)
```

See [Devices &amp; properties](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/devices/index.md>) for more.

## Configuration groups and presets

A *configuration group* (such as "Channel") holds a number of *presets* (such as "DAPI" or "FITC"), each of which sets several properties at once. These are the same groups and presets you'd see in Micro-Manager's main window:

```python
core.getAvailableConfigs("Channel")   # ('Cy5', 'DAPI', 'FITC', 'Rhodamine')
core.setConfig("Channel", "FITC")
core.getCurrentConfig("Channel")      # 'FITC'
```

See [Configuration groups](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/configuration/index.md>) for more.

## Moving stages

Positions are in microns:

```python
core.setXYPosition(100, 200)
core.setZPosition(10)
core.waitForSystem()  # (1)!
core.getXYPosition()  # [100.005, 199.995]
```

1. Stage movements may return before the hardware has finished moving. `waitForSystem` blocks until all devices are done.

## Connecting to events

`CMMCorePlus` emits [events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>) as the state of the microscope changes, and you can connect your own callbacks to them. (This is how the widgets in `pymmcore-widgets` stay in sync with the core.)

```python
@core.events.propertyChanged.connect  # (1)!
def on_change(device: str, prop: str, value: str) -> None:
    print(f"{device}.{prop} changed to {value}")

core.setProperty("Camera", "Gain", "2")  # prints "Camera.Gain changed to 2"
```

1. Using `connect` as a decorator registers the function below it as a callback. `core.events.propertyChanged.connect(on_change)` does the same thing.

> [!TIP]
>
> **`CMMCorePlus.instance`**
>
> Creating/accessing a `CMMCorePlus` object using `CMMCorePlus.instance()` is a convenient way to access the same core instance from multiple places in your code. The widgets in [`pymmcore-widgets`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) also use `CMMCorePlus.instance()` by default, so any widgets you use will automatically connect to the same core instance without any additional configuration.
>
> Attempts *are* made to make it thread-safe. But please open an issue if you find any problems.

## Next steps

From here, you'll probably want to run [your first acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-acquisition/index.md>). When you're ready to use a real microscope, see [Using your own microscope](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/own-microscope/index.md>). The [User Guide](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/index.md>) covers each topic in more depth, and the `CMMCorePlus` reference lists all of the core's methods, marking what `pymmcore-plus` adds or changes.

# Coming from Micro-Manager

If you've used Micro-Manager's Java application (MMStudio), much of what you know carries over. `pymmcore-plus` uses the same C++ core (`MMCore`) and the same device adapters as MMStudio, and it reads the same configuration files. What's different is everything above the core. In place of MMStudio's Java GUI and acquisition engine, you get a Python object (`CMMCorePlus`), an acquisition engine written in Python, and (if you want a GUI) widgets and applications written in Python.

## One program at a time

`pymmcore-plus` doesn't connect to a running copy of Micro-Manager; it *replaces* it. Each program loads its own copy of the core, and the core opens your devices itself (serial ports, camera drivers, etc...). Most devices can only be opened by one program at a time, so if MMStudio has your configuration loaded, loading it again from Python will usually fail (and if it doesn't, the two programs will be fighting over the same hardware). So please close MMStudio before you load your configuration in Python, and vice versa. (The demo devices don't mind, so it's fine to have both open while you're trying things out.)

If you want to keep using MMStudio *and* control it from Python at the same time, that's what Pycro-Manager is for (see [below](<#how-is-this-different-from-pycro-manager>)).

## Where things went

| In MMStudio | Here |
| --- | --- |
| Hardware Configuration Wizard and `.cfg` files | The same files: `core.loadSystemConfiguration("MyScope.cfg")`. See [Using your own microscope](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/own-microscope/index.md>). |
| Device Property Browser | `core.getProperty()` and `core.setProperty()`, or the `PropertyBrowser` widget |
| Groups and presets (main window) | `core.setConfig("Channel", "FITC")`, or `GroupPresetTableWidget` |
| Snap and Live | `core.snap()` and `core.startContinuousSequenceAcquisition()`, or `SnapButton` and `LiveButton` |
| Multi-D Acquisition window | Describe the experiment with a `useq.MDASequence` and run it with `core.mda.run()` (see [Your first acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-acquisition/index.md>)), or use the `MDAWidget` |
| Stage Position List | `stage_positions` in an `MDASequence` |
| Saving acquisitions | `core.mda.run(sequence, output="data.ome.zarr")` (or `.ome.tiff`). See [Saving data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>). |
| Pixel Size Calibration | The same pixel size presets in your `.cfg` file (`core.getPixelSizeUm()`), or the `PixelConfigurationWidget` |
| Script panel (Beanshell) | Python (see [below](<#scripts>)) |
| Device adapters (the `mmgr_dal_*` files) | The very same files. `mmcore install` downloads them for you. |

If you'd rather have all of this in one window, [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) is our (work in progress) pure-Python replacement for MMStudio.

## Scripts

`CMMCorePlus` has the same methods as the core object (`mmc`) in MMStudio's script panel, so Beanshell scripts translate to Python almost line by line:

```java
mmc.setConfig("Channel", "FITC");
mmc.setExposure(50);
mmc.snapImage();
img = mmc.getImage();
```

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()  # (1)!
mmc.setConfig("Channel", "FITC")
mmc.setExposure(50)
mmc.snapImage()
img = mmc.getImage()  # a numpy array
```

1. MMStudio had already done this for you. Pass the path to your own `.cfg` file (with no argument, this loads the demo devices).

A few things are different: images come back as numpy arrays (rather than Java arrays), lists of strings come back as Python tuples (rather than `StrVector`s), and `CMMCorePlus` adds a number of conveniences on top (like `snap()`, which does the last two lines in one go). The `mm` object (MMStudio's own API for displays, data stores, the acquisition manager, etc...) is part of the Java GUI, so it has no equivalent here.

If you're working inside one of our applications, the core is already there for you. In [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>)'s console it's called `mmc` (just like in MMStudio), and in [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>)'s console it's `mmcore`.

## How is this different from Pycro-Manager?

A common question about `pymmcore-plus` and related libraries is how they differ from [Pycro-Manager](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pycro-manager>), another Python library written by Henry Pinkard for working with Micro-Manager.

The two projects are not mutually exclusive! They aim to support different use cases.

The primary difference is that Pycro-Manager (with its default Java backend) controls Micro-Manager via a ZMQ-based connection to a remote Java process in which the Micro-Manager GUI is running (or a headless Java process if the GUI is not running). The Java process in turn communicates with the C++ core driving the hardware.

`pymmcore-plus` aims to remove the need for a Java process by communicating directly with the C++ core (via the [`pymmcore`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>) library), and re-implementing any necessary event-based or GUI-based functionality in pure Python or C.

A major advantage of Pycro-Manager is that you get the entire Java-based Micro-Manager ecosystem, including the GUI and plugins. A potential disadvantage (depending on your needs) is that it requires a Java runtime environment and cross-process communication.

(Pycro-Manager has since added a [Python backend](<https://pycro-manager.readthedocs.io/en/latest/backends.html>) for its headless mode, which also runs the core inside the Python process via `pymmcore`, along with a Python version of its acquisition engine. It's a separate project from `pymmcore-plus`, with its own API.)

If you are looking to control a microscope via Python without any need for Java or interprocess communication, `pymmcore-plus` may help. Note, however, that you will be sacrificing the MMStudio GUI! See [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>), [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>) and [pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) for our ongoing efforts to implement a complete Python-based GUI for Micro-Manager.

If you've been using Pycro-Manager and like its API, see [A Pycro-Manager-style API](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/pycro-manager-api/index.md>) for an example of what that could look like on top of `pymmcore-plus`.

# Installation

There are two things to install: the Python package(s) you want, and Micro-Manager's device adapters (the C++ drivers for your hardware). The device adapters include a set of demo devices, so you can try out the examples in these docs without a microscope.

You'll need Python 3.11 or newer.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Where do I type these commands?**
>
> In a terminal (on Windows, PowerShell or the Anaconda Prompt). We recommend installing into a fresh environment rather than into your system Python. For example, with [conda](<https://conda-forge.org/download/>):
>
> ```sh
> conda create -n pymm python=3.12
> conda activate pymm
> ```
>
> ... or with [uv](<https://docs.astral.sh/uv/>), in the folder you'll be working in:
>
> ```sh
> uv venv  # creates a .venv folder here
> ```
>
> The `uv add` command in the uv tab below adds a dependency to a uv *project* (a folder with a `pyproject.toml`, which `uv init` creates). If you just made an environment with `uv venv`, use `uv pip install` in place of `uv add`. Either way, `uv run <command>` runs a command in that environment (e.g. `uv run python my_script.py`).

## Installing the packages

Pick what you need, and copy the commands:

```sh
pip install "pymmcore-plus[cli]"
```

```sh
uv add "pymmcore-plus[cli]"
```

The parts in square brackets are optional *extras*. `cli` makes sure you get the `mmcore` command line tool (it's currently included anyway), and `io` adds support for saving OME-TIFF files. (Saving to OME-Zarr works without it.)

> [!NOTE]
>
> **All install options**
>
> | You want | Command |
> | --- | --- |
> | The core library and the `mmcore` CLI | `pip install "pymmcore-plus[cli]"` |
> | … plus OME-TIFF writing (and `tifffile`) | `pip install "pymmcore-plus[cli,io]"` |
> | Qt widgets (choose a Qt backend) | `pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]"` or `"pymmcore-widgets[PySide6]"` |
> | The pymmcore-gui application (needs `git`) | `pip install git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui` |
> | The napari plugin | `pip install "napari-micromanager[PyQt6]"` |
>
> Each package brings in everything it builds on, so you only need the top-most one: `pymmcore-gui` already includes `pymmcore-widgets`, `pymmcore-plus[cli,io]` and PyQt6; `napari-micromanager` and `pymmcore-widgets` include `pymmcore-plus[cli]`.
>
> All of these are on [PyPI](<https://pypi.org/user/tlambert03/>). (Some are on conda-forge too, but those packages are currently out of date, so please use `pip` inside your conda environment.)

## Installing the device adapters

The `mmcore` command downloads the latest compatible Micro-Manager device adapters for your platform:

```sh
mmcore install
```

(If you used `uv venv`, that's `uv run mmcore install`.)

They go into a folder in your user data directory, where `pymmcore-plus` will find them automatically. For more details (choosing a version, using an existing Micro-Manager installation, and what the "device interface version" is), see [Micro-Manager device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/index.md>).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Apple Silicon and Linux**
>
> On Apple Silicon Macs and on Linux, `mmcore install` currently downloads only Micro-Manager's test adapters (the demo camera and a few others). That's all you need for the examples in these docs. For real hardware on those platforms, see [Using your own microscope](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/own-microscope/#getting-the-device-adapters>).

## Checking your setup

`mmcore info` prints the versions of the relevant packages, and the folder that the device adapters will be loaded from:

```console
$ mmcore info
python            : 3.14.2 (main, Dec  9 2025, 19:29:30) [Clang 21.1.4 ]
platform          : macOS-27.0.1-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O
pymmcore-plus     : 0.18.1
pymmcore          : 12.5.1.75.0
pymmcore-nano     :
core-version-info : MMCore version 12.5.1
api-version-info  : Device API version 75, Module API version 10
adapter-path      : ~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm/Micro-Manager-75.20260226
useq-schema       : 0.9.2
```

If `adapter-path` says `not found`, `pymmcore-plus` can't find any device adapters (did `mmcore install` work?). If something else went wrong, have a look at [Troubleshooting](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/troubleshooting/index.md>), and please let us know on [image.sc](<https://forum.image.sc/tag/pymmcore-plus>) if that doesn't help.

## Next steps

Once that's done, head to [First steps](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-steps/index.md>) to start controlling the demo devices from Python, or jump straight to [your first acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-acquisition/index.md>) or [your first GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-gui/index.md>).

# Which Package Do I Need?

There are five packages here, each building on the ones below it (see the [stack on the home page](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/#how-the-pieces-fit-together>)). Most people only need one of them:

| If you want to… | Use | Start here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control a microscope with a point-and-click app | pymmcore-gui | [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) |
| Control a microscope from inside [napari](<https://napari.org>) | napari-micromanager | [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>) |
| Script your microscope from Python or Jupyter | pymmcore-plus | [First steps](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-steps/index.md>) |
| Run multi-dimensional acquisitions from code | pymmcore-plus (includes useq-schema) | [Your first acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-acquisition/index.md>) |
| Describe experiments independently of any hardware | useq-schema | [Describing experiments](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/index.md>) |
| Build your own Qt GUI for a microscope | pymmcore-widgets | [Your first GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-gui/index.md>) |

(A *multi-dimensional acquisition*, or MDA, is a series of images across time points, stage positions, channels, z-planes, etc... It's what Micro-Manager's Multi-D Acquisition window does.)

Installing a package also installs the ones it builds on (`pip install pymmcore-widgets` gets you `pymmcore-plus`, `useq-schema` and `pymmcore` too). The Micro-Manager device adapters (the drivers for your hardware) are *not* Python packages, though, and always need to be installed separately. [Installation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/install/index.md>) covers both, so whichever package you pick, start there.

If you've used Micro-Manager before, you may also want to read [Coming from Micro-Manager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/from-micro-manager/index.md>).

## What each package does

**[pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/index.md>)**

Extends [`pymmcore`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>), the Python bindings for Micro-Manager's C++ core. `CMMCorePlus` aims to be a drop-in replacement for `CMMCore`, adding an event system, an acquisition engine written in Python, and a number of convenience methods. It also provides the `mmcore` command line tool.

**[useq-schema](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/index.md>)**

A schema for describing multi-dimensional acquisitions (`MDASequence`, `MDAEvent`). It *tries* to stay agnostic to the acquisition engine (though it was designed around what Micro-Manager can do).

**[pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>)**

Qt widgets for a `CMMCorePlus`: property browsers, device controls, configuration editors, MDA editors, image previews, etc...

**[pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>)**

A desktop application built from all of the above (plus the [ndv](<https://github.com/pyapp-kit/ndv>) viewer). The goal is a pure-Python replacement for Micro-Manager's Java GUI. It's still early days, so expect some rough edges.

**[napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>)**

A napari plugin for controlling a microscope from the napari viewer. It's still maintained, but current development is focused on pymmcore-gui.

# User guide

# User Guide

The User Guide is organized by topic, roughly following the stack from the hardware up. Each page belongs to one package's docs (the badge at the top says which), and names of classes and functions link to the [API reference](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/api/index.md>). If you're new here, [Getting Started](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/which-package/index.md>) is probably a better place to begin.

- **Controlling hardware**

  ---

  [Installing device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/index.md>), [using your own microscope](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/own-microscope/index.md>), [devices and properties](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/devices/index.md>), [configuration groups](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/configuration/index.md>), and [events and callbacks](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>) (which are how GUIs, and your own code, stay in sync with the core).
- **Describing experiments**

  ---

  How [useq-schema](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/index.md>) describes an acquisition as a sequence of events, and [building sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>) with time points, z-stacks, channels, positions, grids, etc...
- **Running acquisitions**

  ---

  [The acquisition engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>), [saving data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>), [event-driven acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/event_driven_acquisition/index.md>), and [writing your own engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/custom_engine/index.md>).
- **Building GUIs**

  ---

  The [widget gallery](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>), [building a custom GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/index.md>) from those widgets, and [keeping it responsive](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/integration-with-qt/index.md>).
- **Applications**

  ---

  [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>), our desktop application, and [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>), which controls a microscope from inside napari.
- **Advanced topics**

  ---

  [Device adapters written in Python](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/unicore/index.md>) (`UniMMCore`), a preview of [useq-schema v2](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/v2-migration/index.md>), and a [Pycro-Manager-style API](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/pycro-manager-api/index.md>).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Something not working?**
>
> The troubleshooting pages cover [the core and device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/troubleshooting/index.md>) and [Qt and widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/troubleshooting/index.md>). Turning up the [logging](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/logging/index.md>) (or [profiling](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/profiling/index.md>), if things are slow) can also help you work out what's going on. If you're still stuck, please ask on the [image.sc forum](<https://forum.image.sc/tag/pymmcore-plus>).

# Using Your Own Microscope

[Getting Started](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/which-package/index.md>) uses Micro-Manager's demo devices throughout. To control real hardware, you need two more things: the device adapters for your hardware, and a configuration file that says which devices you have and how they're set up.

(If Micro-Manager is running and connected to the same hardware, close it first. See [One program at a time](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/from-micro-manager/#one-program-at-a-time>).)

## What's a configuration file?

A Micro-Manager configuration file (`.cfg`) is a plain text file listing the devices to load (and which device adapter each one comes from), their initial property values, which device plays which role (camera, shutter, focus stage), and the configuration groups, presets and pixel sizes you've defined. Here are a few lines from the demo configuration, `MMConfig_demo.cfg`:

```text
# Devices
Device,Camera,DemoCamera,DCam
Device,Z,DemoCamera,DStage
Device,XY,DemoCamera,DXYStage
...
# Roles
Property,Core,Camera,Camera
Property,Core,Focus,Z
...
# Group: Channel
# Preset: FITC
ConfigGroup,Channel,FITC,Dichroic,Label,Q505LP
ConfigGroup,Channel,FITC,Emission,Label,Chroma-HQ535
...
PixelSize_um,Res10x,1.0
```

You rarely need to edit one by hand. If you already have a configuration file from Micro-Manager, you can use it as it is (both use the same core, so they read the same files). Micro-Manager's [configuration guide](<https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager_Configuration_Guide>) describes the format in detail.

## Making a configuration file

The Hardware Configuration Wizard walks you through adding your devices, setting their properties, assigning roles and saving the file. There are three versions of it, and you can use whichever is handiest:

- In [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>): **Devices \> Hardware Config Wizard...**
- As a widget in your own Python code, `ConfigWizard`:

  ```python
  from pymmcore_widgets import ConfigWizard
  from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

  app = QApplication([])
  wizard = ConfigWizard()  # (1)!
  wizard.show()
  app.exec()
  ```

  1. Pass `config_file="MyScope.cfg"` to start from an existing file. Like most widgets, it uses `CMMCorePlus.instance()` unless you pass a core (here, the argument is called `core=`).
- In Micro-Manager itself: **Devices \> Hardware Configuration Wizard...**. If `mmcore install` downloaded a full Micro-Manager for you (on Windows and Intel Macs), `mmcore mmstudio` will start it.

## Getting the device adapters

On Windows and Intel Macs, `mmcore install` downloads a complete Micro-Manager nightly build, which includes the device adapters for most supported hardware. On Apple Silicon Macs and on Linux, it currently downloads only the test adapters (`DemoCamera`, `Utilities` and a few others), so for real hardware on those platforms you'll need to build the adapters you need from [source](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mmCoreAndDevices>).

If you already have Micro-Manager installed (with the adapters you need), `pymmcore-plus` can use it, as long as its *device interface version* matches the one your `pymmcore` expects. `mmcore list` shows the installations it found (and which of them are compatible), and `mmcore use <path>` picks one. See [Micro-Manager device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/index.md>) for more on all of this.

Some devices also need the manufacturer's own drivers or SDK installed (many cameras do, for example). Micro-Manager's [device support pages](<https://micro-manager.org/Device_Support>) say what each adapter needs.

## Loading it

In Python, pass the path to `loadSystemConfiguration`:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration("path/to/MyScope.cfg")  # (1)!
```

1. Relative paths are looked for in the current directory first, then in the device adapter folder.

Both applications can load a configuration at startup:

```sh
mmgui -c path/to/MyScope.cfg                # pymmcore-gui
napari-micromanager -c path/to/MyScope.cfg  # napari-micromanager
```

... and `mmcore bench -c path/to/MyScope.cfg` times a few basic operations on each of your devices, which is a quick way to check that they load.

If loading fails, the error message usually names the device that couldn't be initialized. `mmcore logs` shows the end of the log file (which has more detail), and [Troubleshooting](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/troubleshooting/index.md>) covers the most common problems.

If you change the configuration from Python (for example, by defining new presets), `core.saveSystemConfiguration("MyScope.cfg")` writes it back out.

## Groups, channels and pixel sizes

Once the devices are loaded, most day-to-day settings live in configuration groups and their presets (see [Configuration groups](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/configuration/index.md>)). When you list `channels` in an `MDASequence`, they're looked up in a group named `Channel` by default. If your channel group has a different name, say so:

```python
import useq

useq.MDASequence(channels=[{"config": "DAPI", "group": "Filters"}])
```

Pixel sizes are stored in the configuration file too, as presets tied to your objectives, and the core picks the right one as the objective changes. With the demo configuration:

```python
core.getAvailablePixelSizeConfigs()  # ('Res10x', 'Res20x', 'Res40x')
core.setConfig("Objective", "20X")
core.getPixelSizeUm()                # 0.5
```

You can set these up with the `PixelConfigurationWidget` (in pymmcore-gui, **Window \> Pixel Size Configuration**), and then save the configuration.

# Micro-Manager Device Adapters

Just like the underlying [`pymmcore`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>) library, `pymmcore-plus` relies on the device adapters and C++ core provided by [mmCoreAndDevices](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mmCoreAndDevices#mmcoreanddevices>). (The Python packages themselves are covered on the [Installation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/install/index.md>) page.)

## Installing Micro-Manager device adapters

The device adapters can be installed in two ways:

1. **Use the `mmcore` command line tool**

   `pymmcore-plus` provides a quick way to install the latest compatible version of Micro-Manager:

   ```bash
   mmcore install
   ```

   This will download the most recent nightly build of Micro-Manager that matches your version of `pymmcore` and, by default, place it in a `pymmcore-plus/mm` folder in the user's data directory:

   | OS | Path |
   | --- | --- |
   | Windows | `C:\Users\UserName\AppData\Local\pymmcore-plus\pymmcore-plus\mm` |
   | macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm` |
   | Linux | `~/.local/share/pymmcore-plus/mm` |

   If you would like to modify the location of the installation, or the release of Micro-Manager to install, you can use the `--dest` and `--release` flags respectively.

   For more information on the `install` command, run:

   ```bash
   mmcore install --help
   ```

   To explore all the `mmcore` command line tool functionalities, run `mmcore --help` (or see the [CLI reference](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/cli/index.md>)).
2. **Download manually from micro-manager.org**

   Go to the [Micro-Manager nightly builds](<https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager_Nightly_Builds>) page and download a build for your operating system whose device interface version matches your `pymmcore` (see [below](<#understanding-device-interface-versions>)). This is *not* necessarily the latest release.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Apple Silicon and Linux**
>
> Micro-Manager only publishes nightly builds for Windows and Intel macOS. On Linux, and on macOS with an Apple Silicon (M1, M2, ...) processor, `mmcore install` prints `Unsupported platform/architecture for nightly build` and installs just the *test* adapters (`DemoCamera`, `Utilities`, `SequenceTester` and `NotificationTester`) from [mm-test-adapters](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mm-test-adapters>). That's enough for the demo configuration used throughout these docs, but to control real hardware you will need to build the adapters you need (see [Building device adapters](<#building-device-adapters>) below).

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Critical**
>
> The *device interface version* MUST match between `pymmcore` and the Micro-Manager device adapters. See [below](<#understanding-device-interface-versions>).

## Showing the current installation

To see which Micro-Manager installations `pymmcore-plus` has found, and which one it is using, run:

```shell
mmcore list
```

The output looks something like this (the active installation is marked with ➤):

```console
Required pymmcore device interface version: 75

📁 ~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm
   ➤ Micro-Manager-75.20260226 (DIV 75) (active)
   • Micro-Manager-74.20260129 (DIV 74) (incompatible)
```

From Python, you can use `find_micromanager`:

```shell
python -c "from pymmcore_plus import find_micromanager; print(find_micromanager())"
```

## Setting the active installation

When you create a `CMMCorePlus`, `pymmcore-plus` looks for device adapters in the following places, and uses the first one whose device interface version matches `pymmcore`:

1. The `MICROMANAGER_PATH` environment variable (always used, if set).
2. A path previously selected with `mmcore use` (see below). If it's no longer compatible, it is forgotten (with a warning).
3. The `mmcore install` folder in the user data directory (see the table above). If there are several compatible installations there, the last one in alphabetical order is used.
4. The [`mm-test-adapters`](<https://pypi.org/project/mm-test-adapters/>) Python package, if it is installed.
5. A `Micro-Manager*` folder in the default Micro-Manager install location: `C:\Program Files\` on Windows, `/Applications/` on macOS, and `/usr/local/lib/` on Linux.

So if you already have Micro-Manager installed in the default location, and `mmcore list` says that it is compatible, it will be found automatically (unless one of the earlier locations also has a compatible installation). If `mmcore list` says that it's incompatible, run `mmcore install` to get a compatible set of adapters.

> [!TIP]
>
> **Using the Micro-Manager app too?**
>
> That's fine, but `pymmcore-plus` doesn't connect to a running Micro-Manager (it loads the device adapters itself). Most devices can only be opened by one program at a time, so close Micro-Manager before you load the same hardware configuration in Python (and vice versa).

To override the device adapter search path for a single session (or script), set the `MICROMANAGER_PATH` environment variable:

```shell
export MICROMANAGER_PATH=/path/to/installation
```

(For a single core object, you can also pass the folder directly: `CMMCorePlus(mm_path="/path/to/installation")`.)

If you want to permanently set the Micro-Manager installation path that `pymmcore-plus` uses, you can use the `mmcore use` command:

```shell
mmcore use <some path or pattern>
```

... where `<some path or pattern>` is either a path to an existing directory (containing Micro-Manager device adapters) or a pattern to match against directories returned by `find_micromanager`.

Alternatively, you can use the `use_micromanager` function, passing *either* a path to an existing directory, or a pattern to match against directories returned by `find_micromanager`:

```shell
python -c "from pymmcore_plus import use_micromanager; use_micromanager(path=..., pattern=...)"
```

## Building device adapters

On Linux and Apple Silicon there are no pre-built Micro-Manager adapters beyond the test devices, so you will need to build the C++ core and device adapters yourself from [mmCoreAndDevices](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mmCoreAndDevices#mmcoreanddevices>). To do that, follow the [build instructions](<https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager/blob/main/doc/how-to-build.md#building-on-unix>) in the micro-manager repo, then point `pymmcore-plus` at the folder with `mmcore use`.

On macOS and Linux, `mmcore build-dev` can also clone the repository and build a few adapters for you (`DemoCamera`, `Utilities` and `SequenceTester` by default, or the names you pass it). Not all adapters will build this way, and you'll need the build tools described in the instructions above. Run `mmcore build-dev --help` for the options.

## Understanding device interface versions

Micro-Manager's C++ layer (called MMCore) controls devices via adapters that are compiled into platform-specific shared libraries. These libraries are always compiled to work with a *specific* "device interface version" expected by the MMCore object itself. If you try to load a device adapter with a device interface version that does not match the version expected by the core, then you will get an error.

[pymmcore](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>) is a library that wraps the C++ code and makes it available to Python. It has a 5-number version string that looks something like `12.5.1.75.0`. The first three parts (here: `12.5.1`) represent the version of the MMCore library. The next number (here: `75`) *is the device interface version that pymmcore expects*. (The last number is a pymmcore-specific build number). To query version information of your installed libraries you can run:

```bash
mmcore --version
```

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Critical**
>
> **You *must* use device adapter libraries that were compiled for the same device interface version as your version of pymmcore.**
>
> By default, when you run `mmcore install`, it will pick the latest compatible version to install. However, you can also do this explicitly. For example, with an older pymmcore that expects device interface version `74`, you could explicitly install the last compatible device adapters listed on the table below with `mmcore install` as follows:
>
> ```sh
> mmcore install -r 20260225
> ```

Here is a list of the latest device interface numbers, the date of the first nightly build where they were available, the last nightly build date to support that version, and the commit in [mmCoreAndDevices](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mmCoreAndDevices>) that bumped the version.

| Version | Release Date | Last Release | Commit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 75 | 20260226 |  | [3c6312ac5](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mmCoreAndDevices/commit/3c6312ac5>) |
| 74 | 20250815 | 20260225 | [7e9f2f214](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mmCoreAndDevices/commit/7e9f2f214>) |

# Configuration and Groups

Configuring a microscope with Micro-Manager entails storing and retrieving a number of device settings. In general, a single setting comprises a device name, a property name, and a value. A **Configuration** object (a *preset*, in the Micro-Manager app) represents a *collection* of individual settings; that is, it represents a number of device parameters all in a specific state, such as would be used to prepare the microscope to image a specific channel, like "DAPI", or "FITC".

A **Configuration Group** is, in turn, a *collection* of `Configuration` objects; for example, all of the `Configuration` objects that represent different "Channel" settings.

Conceptually, Configurations and Groups are organized like this:

```YAML
ConfigGroupA:
    Configuration1:
        deviceA:
            propertyA: 'value_a'
            propertyB: 'value_b'
        deviceB:
            propertyC: 'value_c'
        ...
    Configuration2:
        deviceA:
            propertyA: 'value_d'
            propertyB: 'value_e'
        deviceB:
            propertyC: 'value_f'
        ...
    ...
ConfigGroupB:
    Configuration1:
        deviceC:
            propertyA: 'value_g'
        ...
    ...
```

## Using groups and presets

Groups and presets are usually defined in your configuration (`.cfg`) file. The demo configuration has a few of them:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # demo config

core.getAvailableConfigGroups()
# ('Camera', 'Channel', 'Channel-Multiband', 'LightPath', 'Objective', 'System')
core.getAvailableConfigs("Channel")
# ('Cy5', 'DAPI', 'FITC', 'Rhodamine')

core.setConfig("Channel", "FITC")  # (1)!
core.getCurrentConfig("Channel")  # 'FITC'
```

1. This sets all of the properties in the `FITC` preset (and emits the `configSet` event).

To see what a preset actually does, use `getConfigData`. It returns a `Configuration` that can be indexed with `(device, property)` keys, and iterated over as `(device, property, value)` tuples:

```python
cfg = core.getConfigData("Channel", "DAPI")
cfg["Dichroic", "Label"]  # '400DCLP'
list(cfg)
# [('Dichroic', 'Label', '400DCLP'), ('Emission', 'Label', 'Chroma-HQ620'),
#  ('Excitation', 'Label', 'Chroma-D360'), ('Core', 'Shutter', 'White Light Shutter')]
```

## Defining presets

New presets are defined one setting at a time with `defineConfig` (the group is created if it doesn't exist yet), or all at once with a [`ConfigGroup`](<#pymmcore-plus-objects>) object:

```python
core.defineConfig("Channel", "Brightfield", "Dichroic", "Label", "400DCLP")

# or, equivalently, with a ConfigGroup:
channel = core.getConfigGroupObject("Channel")
channel["Brightfield"] = {
    ("Dichroic", "Label"): "400DCLP",
    ("Emission", "Label"): "Chroma-HQ700",
}
channel.setConfig("Brightfield")
```

These changes only live in memory. To keep them, save the whole system configuration to a new file (which you can load next time with `loadSystemConfiguration`):

```python
core.saveSystemConfiguration("my_config.cfg")
```

Pixel size presets work much the same way, with their own methods (`definePixelSizeConfig`, `getPixelSizeConfigData`, etc...), except that you don't set them yourself. The core picks the one that matches the current state of the microscope. With the demo config, for example, `core.setConfig("Objective", "20X")` changes `getCurrentPixelSizeConfig()` to `'Res20x'` and `getPixelSizeUm()` to `0.5`.

## `pymmcore-plus` objects

MMCore and pymmcore's [configuration](<https://micro-manager.org/apidoc/MMCore/latest/class_configuration.html>) object implements a basic container interface, but with custom method names like `addSetting`, `getSetting`, and `deleteSetting`.

`pymmcore-plus` provides a `Configuration` subclass that supports mapping-style indexing, where the keys are 2-tuples of `(deviceLabel, propertyLabel)` and the values are the property values: `cfg["Camera", "Exposure"]`, `cfg["Camera", "Exposure"] = "10"` and `del cfg["Camera", "Exposure"]` all work. (Note, however, that iterating over a `Configuration` object behaves like iterating over a list of 3-tuples `(deviceLabel, propertyLabel, value)`, not a dict, and there are no `keys()` or `items()` methods. Use `cfg.dict()` if you want a nested dict.) All of the `CMMCorePlus` methods that return a configuration return this subclass, unless you pass `native=True`.

`pymmcore-plus` also offers a `ConfigGroup` object (returned by `getConfigGroupObject`), which is a `MutableMapping` where the keys are [Configuration Preset](<https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager_Configuration_Guide#configuration-presets>) names and the values are `Configuration` objects.

See `Configuration` and `ConfigGroup` for the full API. The related core methods are in the *Config groups &amp; presets* section of the `CMMCorePlus` method summary.

# Constants

All of the constants in the `pymmcore` library are in the top level `pymmcore` namespace, making it a bit difficult to know what type or enumeration they refer to.

All of these constants are reimplemented in the `pymmcore_plus` library as enums (`enum.IntEnum` or `enum.StrEnum`) and are available in the `pymmcore_plus` namespace (and are listed below).

For example, the integer corresponding to the `AfterLoadSequence` action type could be accessed as `pymmcore.AfterLoadSequence` or `pymmcore_plus.ActionType.AfterLoadSequence`.

```python
In [1]: import pymmcore

In [2]: pymmcore.AfterLoadSequence
Out[2]: 4

In [3]: from pymmcore_plus import ActionType

In [4]: ActionType.AfterLoadSequence
Out[4]: <ActionType.AfterLoadSequence: 4>

In [5]: int(ActionType.AfterLoadSequence)
Out[5]: 4
```

Additionally, it becomes easier to see what constants are available for each type or enumeration.

```python
In [6]: list(ActionType)
Out[6]:
[
    <ActionType.NoAction: 0>,
    <ActionType.BeforeGet: 1>,
    <ActionType.AfterSet: 2>,
    <ActionType.IsSequenceable: 3>,
    <ActionType.AfterLoadSequence: 4>,
    <ActionType.StartSequence: 5>,
    <ActionType.StopSequence: 6>
]
```

Lastly, many of the methods that return integers in `pymmcore.CMMCore` have been re-implemented in `pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus` to return the appropriate enumeration.

```python
import pymmcore

core = pymmcore.CMMCore()
# ...  load config and devices
core.getDeviceType("Camera")  # 2


import pymmcore_plus

core = pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus()
# ...  load config and devices
core.getDeviceType("Camera")  # <DeviceType.CameraDevice: 2>
```

There is as yet no mechanism to programmatically detect the device.

Communication attributes are valid, but the device does not respond.

Communication verified, parameters have been set to valid values.

## PixelFormat

Bases: `StrEnum`

Subset of GeniCam Pixel Format names used by pymmcore-plus.

(This is similar to PixelType, but follows GeniCam standards.)

See [https://docs.baslerweb.com/pixel-format\#unpacked-and-packed-pixel-formats](<https://docs.baslerweb.com/pixel-format#unpacked-and-packed-pixel-formats>) for helpful clarifications. Note that **unpacked** pixel formats (like Mono8, Mono12, Mono16) are always 8-bit aligned. Meaning Mono12 is actually a 16-bit buffer.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MONO8` | `str` | 8-bit (unpacked) monochrome pixel format. |
| `MONO10` | `str` | 10-bit (unpacked) monochrome pixel format. (16-bit buffer) |
| `MONO12` | `str` | 12-bit (unpacked) monochrome pixel format. (16-bit buffer) |
| `MONO14` | `str` | 14-bit (unpacked) monochrome pixel format. (16-bit buffer) |
| `MONO16` | `str` | 16-bit (unpacked) monochrome pixel format |
| `MONO32` | `str` | 32-bit (unpacked) monochrome pixel format |
| `RGB8` | `str` | 8-bit RGB pixel format. (24-bit buffer) |
| `RGB10` | `str` | 10-bit RGB pixel format. (48-bit buffer) |
| `RGB12` | `str` | 12-bit RGB pixel format. (48-bit buffer) |
| `RGB14` | `str` | 14-bit RGB pixel format. (48-bit buffer) |
| `RGB16` | `str` | 16-bit RGB pixel format. (48-bit buffer) |

### MONO8

```python
MONO8 = 'Mono8'
```

### MONO10

```python
MONO10 = 'Mono10'
```

### MONO12

```python
MONO12 = 'Mono12'
```

### MONO14

```python
MONO14 = 'Mono14'
```

```python

```

# Custom Acquisition Engines

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Important**
>
> This page assumes you have a basic understanding of how the default MDA acquisition engine works to execute a sequence of `useq.MDAEvent` objects. If you haven't already done so, please read the [Acquisition Engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>) guide first.

While the default MDA acquisition engine is sufficient for many common use cases, you may find that you need to customize it to accomplish your goals, for example when:

- driving hardware for which a [Micro-Manager device adapter](<https://micro-manager.org/Device_Support>) does not exist,
- conditionally executing arbitrary python code before, during, or after each acquisition event,
- using an alternate [high-performance camera driver](<https://github.com/acquire-project/acquire-python>),
- handling user-specific `MDAEvent.metadata` values,
- intercepting and modifying the event sequence<sup>*</sup>.

  > **<sup>*</sup>Note**
  >
  > If all you want is to modify the event sequence (e.g. to add additional events in a non-deterministic way) but you don't need to modify the behavior of the acquisition engine itself, you likely don't need to customize the acquisition engine. See the guide on [Event-Driven Acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/event_driven_acquisition/index.md>) for details.

## The `MDARunner` and `MDAEngine`

Let's start by taking a quick look at how the acquisition logic in pymmcore-plus is structured. There are two key classes involved:

1. An **`MDARunner`** instance is responsible for receiving a sequence of `useq.MDAEvent` objects and driving an `MDAEngine` to execute them. The `MDARunner` is the object that has the actual `run()` method. It also emits all the events, such as `frameReady`, and sends the images to the `output` (if any). Users shouldn't need to subclass or modify `MDARunner` directly.
2. An `MDAEngine` instance (anything that implements the [**`PMDAEngine`** protocol](<#the-mdaengine-protocol>)) is responsible for actually setting up and executing each event in the sequence. The default implementation of the `PMDAEngine` protocol is the **`MDAEngine`** class, but you can register your own custom engine, using either a subclass of the default engine, or any other object that implements the `PMDAEngine` protocol.

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()

core.mda  # <- The MDARunner instance
core.mda.engine  # <- The MDAEngine instance
```

## The `MDAEngine` protocol

`pymmcore-plus` defines a protocol (a.k.a. "interface" in the Java world) that all acquisition engines must implement. The API reference has the formal details, but let's discuss the three key methods here.

1. `setup_sequence()` - Setup state of system before an MDA is run.
2. `setup_event()` - Prepare state of system for an event.
3. `exec_event()` - Execute the event.

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> **The `PMDAEngine` Protocol**
>
> ```python
> class MyEngine:
>     def setup_sequence(self, sequence: MDASequence) -> SummaryMetaV1 | None:
>         """Setup state of system (hardware, etc.) before an MDA is run.
>
>         This method is called once at the beginning of a sequence.
>         (The sequence object needn't be used here if not necessary)
>         """
>
>     def setup_event(self, event: MDAEvent) -> None:
>         """Prepare state of system (hardware, etc.) for `event`.
>
>         This method is called before each event in the sequence. It is
>         responsible for preparing the state of the system for the event.
>         The engine should be in a state where it can call `exec_event`
>         without any additional preparation.  It may raise `SkipEvent`
>         to skip this event.
>         """
>
>     def exec_event(
>         self, event: MDAEvent
>     ) -> Iterable[tuple[NDArray, MDAEvent, FrameMetaV1] | None]:
>         """Execute `event`.
>
>         This method is called after `setup_event` and is responsible for
>         executing the event. The default assumption is to acquire an image,
>         but more elaborate events will be possible.  Returns (or yields)
>         an `(image, event, metadata)` tuple for each acquired frame.
>         """
> ```

Your engine doesn't need to inherit from anything, but if you subclass `PMDAEngine` itself, Python will refuse to create it until these three methods are implemented.

The return value of `exec_event` is what the runner turns into data:

- It must be an iterable (a list, a tuple, or a generator that `yield`s) of `(image, event, metadata)` tuples, one per acquired frame. For each tuple, the runner emits `frameReady(image, event, metadata)` and sends the frame to the `output`.
- Return an empty iterable (or `None`) if the event didn't produce an image.
- A `None` *inside* the iterable stands for a frame that should have been acquired, but wasn't (e.g. a camera that dropped a frame); the runner tells the data sink to leave a gap for it.

The following methods are optional, but will be used if they are defined:

1. `event_iterator()` - Optional wrapper on the event iterator. To customize the event sequence. (This is how the default engine merges events for [hardware triggering](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/#hardware-triggered-sequences>). It isn't called when an *iterator*, such as a generator, is passed to the runner.)
2. `teardown_event()` - Called after `exec_event()`. To clean up after an event.
3. `teardown_sequence()` - Called after the sequence is complete. To clean up after an MDA.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Saving data from your own engine**
>
> The data sink behind `output=` (see [Saving Data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>)) uses the summary metadata returned by `setup_sequence` to learn the image size and dtype, and it reads `exposure_ms` from each frame's metadata. Subclasses of `MDAEngine` get both for free. If you yield your own frames, build their metadata with `self.get_frame_metadata(event)` (or, in an engine that doesn't subclass `MDAEngine`, with `pymmcore_plus.metadata.frame_metadata` and `summary_metadata`). An empty dict works for `frameReady`, but fails with `KeyError: 'exposure_ms'` when saving.

## The built-in `MDAEngine`

The default implementation of the `PMDAEngine` protocol is the **`MDAEngine`** class. It can handle microscope setup and image acquisition for a standard `MDAEvent` (see [what the engine does](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/#what-the-engine-does>)), and opportunistically queues [hardware-triggered sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/#hardware-triggered-sequences>). It also serves as a good base class for custom engines if you want to extend the default behavior. (You may also find the [source code](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/blob/main/src/pymmcore_plus/mda/_engine.py>) for the `MDAEngine` class helpful as a reference when writing a custom engine.) Its `setup_event` and `exec_event` hand off to `setup_single_event` / `exec_single_event` for regular events, and to `setup_sequenced_event` / `exec_sequenced_event` for hardware-triggered ones, so you can override just the part you need.

## Customizing the `MDAEngine`

If you want to customize *how* the instrument sets up or executes each event, the easiest approach is to subclass the default `MDAEngine` class and override or extend the methods you need to customize, then register your custom engine with `core.register_mda_engine()`.

```python
from collections.abc import Iterator

import numpy as np
import useq
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from pymmcore_plus.mda import MDAEngine


class MyEngine(MDAEngine):  # (1)!
    def setup_event(self, event: useq.MDAEvent) -> None:
        """Prepare state of system (hardware, etc.) for `event`."""
        # do some custom pre-setup
        super().setup_event(event)  # (2)!
        # do some custom post-setup

    def exec_event(
        self, event: useq.MDAEvent
    ) -> Iterator[tuple[np.ndarray, useq.MDAEvent, dict] | None]:
        """Execute `event`."""
        # do some custom pre-execution
        yield from super().exec_event(event)  # (3)!
        # do some custom post-execution


core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

# Register the custom engine with the runner
core.register_mda_engine(MyEngine(core))  # (4)!

# Run an MDA
core.mda.run([useq.MDAEvent()])
```

1. Create a custom engine by subclassing the default engine
2. Note that it's not required to call the `super()` methods here if you don't want to
3. The default `exec_event` is a *generator*: nothing is acquired until the runner iterates over it. Using `yield from` keeps it that way, and makes your "post-execution" code run *after* the image has been acquired (and emitted). (If you wrote `return super().exec_event(event)` instead, any code between that call and the `return` would run *before* the image is acquired.)
4. Note that `MDAEngine.__init__` accepts a `CMMCorePlus` instance as its first argument, so you'll need to pass that in when instantiating your custom engine.

`register_mda_engine` sets `core.mda`'s engine (with `core.mda.set_engine()`, which you may also call directly), and then emits the `mdaEngineRegistered` signal, which you can use to be alerted when someone swaps out the engine:

```python
@core.events.mdaEngineRegistered.connect
def on_new_engine(new_engine, old_engine):
    print("new engine registered!")
```

The engine can't be changed while an acquisition is running.

## Skipping an event

If `setup_event` finds that an event can't be done (a device didn't respond, a position is out of reach, etc...), it may raise `SkipEvent`. The runner then skips `exec_event` for that event (but still calls `teardown_event`), and tells the data sink to leave a gap, so the rest of the data still lands in the right place:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.mda import MDAEngine, SkipEvent


class CarefulEngine(MDAEngine):
    def setup_event(self, event: useq.MDAEvent) -> None:
        if event.index.get("p") == 1:  # (1)!
            raise SkipEvent(reason="position 1 is out of reach")
        super().setup_event(event)
```

1. Any check you like. For a hardware-triggered `SequencedEvent`, which stands for several frames, pass the number of frames to skip: `SkipEvent(num_frames=len(event.events))`.

## Utilizing `MDAEvent` metadata

More often than not, if you are customizing the acquisition engine, it will be because you'd like to do something *other* than drive the Micro-Manager core to set up and acquire an image. Perhaps you need to control a micro-fluidic device, or control a DAQ card, or communicate with a remote server, etc.

In all of these cases, you will likely need additional parameters (beyond the fields defined in the `MDAEvent` class) to pass to your control code. For this, the `MDAEvent` class has a `metadata` attribute that is explicitly provided for user-defined data.

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from pymmcore_plus.mda import MDAEngine
import useq


class MyEngine(MDAEngine):
    def setup_event(self, event: useq.MDAEvent) -> None:
        if "my_key" in event.metadata:  # (1)!
            self._my_custom_setup(event.metadata["my_key"])
        else:
            super().setup_event(event)

    def _my_custom_setup(self, params: dict) -> None:
        print(f"Setting up my custom device with {params}")

    def exec_event(self, event: useq.MDAEvent):
        if "my_key" in event.metadata:
            return self._my_custom_exec(event.metadata["my_key"])  # (2)!
        return super().exec_event(event)

    def _my_custom_exec(self, params: dict) -> tuple:
        print(f"Executing my custom stuff with {params}")
        return ()  # no images from this event


core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

core.register_mda_engine(MyEngine(core))
core.mda.engine.use_hardware_sequencing = False  # (3)!

experiment = [
    useq.MDAEvent(),
    useq.MDAEvent(metadata={"my_key": {"param1": "val1"}}),  # (4)!
    useq.MDAEvent(),
    useq.MDAEvent(metadata={"my_key": {"param1": "val2"}}),
]

core.mda.run(experiment)
```

1. You can use any characteristics of the `MDAEvent`, such as the `index`, or the presence of a special key in the `metadata` attribute, to determine whether you want to do something special for that event.
2. You don't *have* to return here. If you also want to do the default image acquisition, you can call `super().exec_event(event)` as well.
3. **Don't skip this.** With hardware sequencing on (the default), the engine merges consecutive events that it can run as one hardware-triggered sequence, and it doesn't compare their `metadata` when deciding. The four events above would be merged into a single `SequencedEvent` (with empty `metadata`), and neither of our custom branches would ever run.
4. Add metadata to the event. You can do this either by constructing your own sequence of `MDAEvent` objects, or by using [`MDASequence`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>) to build the sequence for you, then editing the `metadata` attributes as needed.

... which prints:

```text
Setting up my custom device with {'param1': 'val1'}
Executing my custom stuff with {'param1': 'val1'}
Setting up my custom device with {'param1': 'val2'}
Executing my custom stuff with {'param1': 'val2'}
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Example**
>
> For a real-world example of an `MDAEngine` subclass that uses `MDAEvent.metadata` to drive hardware for Raman spectroscopy, see Ian Hunt-Isaak's [raman-mda-engine](<https://github.com/ianhi/raman-mda-engine>). (engine subclass [here](<https://github.com/ianhi/raman-mda-engine/blob/main/raman_mda_engine/_engine.py>))

# Devices and Properties

`pymmcore-plus` offers two classes that provide a more *object-oriented* interface to common operations and queries performed on devices and their properties.

In the original `CMMCore` API, there are a lot of methods that accept a `deviceLabel` string as the first argument (and perhaps additional arguments) and query something about that device (e.g. `getDeviceLibrary`, `getDeviceType`, `waitForDevice`, etc...). In `pymmcore-plus`, the `Device` class acts as a "view" onto a specific device. You pass the `deviceLabel` once (to the constructor), and these become methods that no longer need it.

Similarly, there are many methods in the `CMMCore` API that require both a device label and a device property name, and query or modify that property (e.g. `isPropertySequenceable`, `getProperty`, `isPropertyReadOnly`, etc...). Here, the `DeviceProperty` class acts as a "view" onto a specific device property, with an object-oriented interface to these methods.

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # demo config

camera = core.getDeviceObject("Camera")
print(camera.type(), camera.library())  # Camera DemoCamera

exposure = camera.getPropertyObject("Exposure")
exposure.value = 42
print(exposure.value, exposure.isReadOnly(), exposure.range())  # 42.0 False (0.0, 10000.0)
```

To loop over the loaded devices or properties (optionally filtered by type, label, etc...), use `iterDevices` and `iterProperties`, which yield these same objects:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import DeviceType

[dev.label for dev in core.iterDevices(DeviceType.Stage)]  # ['Z']
[prop.name for prop in core.iterProperties(device_label="Camera", has_limits=True)]
```

See `Device`, `DeviceProperty` and `DeviceAdapter` (the same idea, for a device adapter library) for the full API.

## Property info

`DeviceProperty.dict()` returns everything about a property at once. Continuing the example above:

```python
>>> exposure.dict()
{'valid': True,
 'value': 42.0,
 'type': 'number',
 'device_type': 'CameraDevice',
 'read_only': False,
 'sequenceable': False,
 'sequence_max_length': None,
 'pre_init': False,
 'range': (0.0, 10000.0),
 'allowed_values': ()}
```

(`range` is `None` for properties without limits, and `allowed_values` lists the choices for properties that have them, like the camera's `Binning`.)

## Temporarily changing settings

You may want to temporarily set something on the core (for example `core.setAutoShutter(False)` when writing an [MDA engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/custom_engine/index.md>)) and put it back afterwards. For this case you can use the convenience method `CMMCorePlus.setContext`:

```python
with core.setContext(exposure=100, autoShutter=False):
    print(core.getExposure(), core.getAutoShutter())  # 100.0 False
    core.snapImage()

print(core.getExposure(), core.getAutoShutter())  # back to the original values
```

This works for any name that has matching `get<Name>` and `set<Name>` methods on the core (e.g. `exposure`, `autoShutter`, `shutterOpen`, `channelGroup`, etc...). The original values are restored when the `with` block exits, even if an exception was raised inside it.

# Event-Driven Acquisition

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Important**
>
> This page assumes you have a basic understanding of how the default MDA acquisition engine works to execute a sequence of `useq.MDAEvent` objects. If you haven't already done so, please read the [Acquisition Engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>) guide first.

You may not always know the exact sequence of events that you want to execute ahead of time. For example, you may want to start acquiring images at a certain frequency, but then take a burst of images at a faster frame rate or in a specific region of interest when a specific (possibly rare) event occurs. This is sometimes referred to as **event-driven acquisition**, or "smart-microscopy".

> [!NOTE]
>
> **In publications**
>
> For two compelling examples of this type of event-driven microscopy, see:
>
> 1. Mahecic D, Stepp WL, Zhang C, Griffié J, Weigert M, Manley S. *Event-driven acquisition for content-enriched microscopy.* Nat Methods 19, 1262–1267 (2022). [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-022-01589-x](<https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-022-01589-x>)
> 2. Shi Y, Tabet JS, Milkie DE, Daugird TA, Yang CQ, Ritter AT, Giovannucci A, Legant WR. *Smart lattice light-sheet microscopy for imaging rare and complex cellular events.* Nat Methods 21, 301–310 (2024). [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-023-02126-0](<https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-023-02126-0>)

Obviously, in this case, you can't just create a list of `useq.MDAEvent` objects and pass them to the acquisition engine, since that list needs to change based on the results of previous events.

Fortunately, the `MDARunner.run()` method is designed to handle this case.

## `Iterable[MDAEvent]`

The key thing to observe here is the signature of the `MDARunner.run()` method:

```python
from typing import Iterable
import useq


class MDARunner:
    def run(self, events: Iterable[useq.MDAEvent], **kwargs) -> None: ...
```

> [!TIP]
>
> The `run` method expects an *iterable* of `useq.MDAEvent` objects.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Iterable**
>
> An `Iterable` is any object that implements an `__iter__()` method that returns an [iterator object](<https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#iterator-types>). This includes sequences of known length, like `list`, `tuple`, but also many other types of objects, such as [generators](<https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#generator-types>), `deque`, and more.
