Other types such as `Queue` can easily be converted to an iterator as well, as we'll see below.

## Useful iterables

Many python objects are iterable. Let's look at a few types of iterables that can be used to implement event-driven acquisition in pymmcore-plus.

### Generators

[Generators](<https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generator>) are functions that contain `yield` statements. When called, they return a [generator iterator](<https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generator-iterator>) that can be used to iterate over the values yielded by the generator function.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Say what?**
>
> That may sound a bit confusing, but it's actually quite simple. It just means that you can use the output of a generator function in a for loop:
>
> ```python
> from typing import Iterator
>
>
> # a generator function, which contains "yield" statements
> def my_generator_func() -> Iterator[int]:
>     yield 1
>     yield 2
>
>
> # calling the function returns an iterator
> gen_iterator = my_generator_func()
>
> # which we can iterate over (e.g. in a for loop)
> for value in gen_iterator:
>     print(value)  # prints 1, then 2
> ```

Let's create a generator that yields `useq.MDAEvent` objects, but simulate a "burst" of events when a certain condition is met:

```python
import random
import time
from typing import Iterator

import useq


def some_condition_is_met() -> bool:
    # Return True 20% of the time ...
    # Just an example of some probabilistic condition
    # This could be anything, the results of analysis, etc.
    return random.random() < 0.2


# generator function that yields events
def my_events() -> Iterator[useq.MDAEvent]:
    i = 0
    while True:
        if some_condition_is_met():
            # yield a burst of events
            for _ in range(5):
                yield useq.MDAEvent(metadata={"bursting": True})
        elif i > 5:
            # stop after a few rounds
            # (just an example of some stop condition)
            return
        else:
            # yield a regular single event
            yield useq.MDAEvent()

        # wait a bit before yielding the next event (1)
        time.sleep(0.1)
        i += 1
```

1. Note, we could also take advantage of the `min_start_time` field in MDAEvent, but this demonstrates that the generator can also control the timing of events.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **example output of `list(my_events())`**
>
> We can use the `list()` function to iterate over the generator and collect the yielded events:
>
> ```python
> list(my_events())
> ```
>
> Because of the random condition, the output will be different each time, but it might look something like this:
>
> ```python
> [
>     MDAEvent(),
>     MDAEvent(metadata={"bursting": True}),  # (1)!
>     MDAEvent(metadata={"bursting": True}),
>     MDAEvent(metadata={"bursting": True}),
>     MDAEvent(metadata={"bursting": True}),
>     MDAEvent(metadata={"bursting": True}),
>     MDAEvent(),
>     MDAEvent(),
>     MDAEvent(),
>     MDAEvent(),  # (2)!
> ]
> ```
>
> 1. `some_condition_is_met` returned `True` on the second iteration, so the generator yielded a burst of events.
> 2. Our "stop condition" of `i > 5` was met, so the generator returned and stopped yielding events.

To run this "experiment" using pymmcore-plus, we can pass the output of the generator to the `MDARunner.run()` method:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

core.run_mda(my_events())
```

### Queues

Python's `Queue` class is a thread-safe way to pass data between threads. Generally, a Queue is shared between threads, and one thread [puts](<https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html#queue.Queue.put>) data (such as an `MDAEvent` to execute) into the queue, while another thread [gets](<https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html#queue.Queue.get>) data out of the queue.

A `Queue` instance itself is not an iterable...

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **👎**
>
> ```python
> >>> from queue import Queue
> >>> list(Queue())
> Traceback (most recent call last):
> File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
> TypeError: 'Queue' object is not iterable
> ```

however, a `Queue` can be easily converted to an iterator using the two-argument version of the builtin `iter()` function:

> [!TIP]
>
> **👍**
>
> ```python
> >>> from queue import Queue
> >>> q = Queue()
> >>> q.put(1)
> >>> q.put(2)
> >>> q.put('STOP')
> >>> iterable_queue = iter(q.get, 'STOP') # !! (1)
> >>> list(iterable_queue)
> [1, 2]
> ```
>
> 1. 🎩 Thanks [Kyle Douglass](<https://github.com/kmdouglass>) for discovering this handy, if obscure, second argument to `iter()`!

We can use this `iter(queue.get, sentinel)` pattern to create a queue-backed iterable that can be passed to the `run_mda()` method. The acquisition engine will then execute events as they get `put` into the queue, until the stop sentinel is encountered.

```python
from queue import Queue
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from useq import MDAEvent

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

q = Queue()  # create the queue
STOP = object()  # any object can serve as the sentinel
q_iterator = iter(q.get, STOP)  # create the queue-backed iterable


# (optional) connect some callback to the frameReady signal
@core.mda.events.frameReady.connect
def on_frame(img, event):
    print(f"Frame {event.index} received: {img.shape}")


# start the acquisition in a separate thread
core.run_mda(q_iterator)

# now we can put events into the queue
# according to whatever logic we want:
q.put(MDAEvent(index={"t": 0}, exposure=20))
q.put(MDAEvent(index={"t": 1}, exposure=40))

# ... and eventually stop the acquisition
q.put(STOP)
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> **More complete event-driven acquisition example**
>
> The following example is modified from [this gist](<https://gist.github.com/kmdouglass/d15a0410d54d6b12df8614b404d9b751>) by [Kyle Douglass](<https://gist.github.com/kmdouglass>).
>
> It simulates a typical event-driven acquisition, where an Analyzer object analyzes the results of each image and provides a dict of results. The Controller object then decides whether to continue or stop the acquisition (by placing the `STOP_EVENT` sentinel in the queue).
>
> event\_driven\_acquisition.py
>
> ```python
> """Simple simulator demonstrating event-driven acquisitions with pymmcore-plus."""
>
> import random
> from queue import Queue
>
> import numpy as np
> from useq import MDAEvent
>
> from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
>
>
> class Analyzer:
>     """Analyzes images and returns a dict of results."""
>
>     def run(self, data) -> dict:
>         # Fake analysis; randomly return a "STOP" result 10% of the time
>         if random.random() < 0.1:
>             return {"result": "STOP"}
>         else:
>             return {"result": random.random()}
>
>
> class Controller:
>     STOP_EVENT = object()
>
>     def __init__(self, analyzer: Analyzer, mmc: CMMCorePlus, queue: Queue):
>         self._analyzer = analyzer  # analyzer of images
>         self._queue = queue  # queue of MDAEvents
>         self._images: Queue[np.ndarray] = Queue()  # images waiting to be analyzed
>
>         self._mmc = mmc
>         mmc.mda.events.frameReady.connect(self._on_frame_ready)
>
>     def _on_frame_ready(self, img: np.ndarray, event: MDAEvent) -> None:
>         # This is called in the acquisition thread: just hand the image over
>         self._images.put(img)
>
>     def run(self) -> None:
>         # convert the queue to an iterable
>         queue_sequence = iter(self._queue.get, self.STOP_EVENT)
>
>         # Start the acquisition (run_mda is non-blocking)
>         self._mmc.run_mda(queue_sequence)
>
>         # Queue the first image acquisition
>         self._queue.put(MDAEvent(exposure=10))
>
>         # loop until the analyzer returns "STOP"
>         while True:
>             # wait for the next image, and analyze it (in this thread)
>             result = self._analyzer.run(self._images.get())["result"]
>
>             # Decide what to do. This is the key part of the reactive loop.
>             if result == "STOP":
>                 print("Analyzer says stop. Stopping...")
>                 self._queue.put(self.STOP_EVENT)
>                 break
>             else:
>                 # Adjust the exposure time based on the results and continue
>                 print("Analyzer returned results. Continuing...")
>                 next_event = MDAEvent(exposure=10 * result)
>                 self._queue.put(next_event)
>
>
> def main():
>     # Setup the MM Core
>     mmc = CMMCorePlus()
>     mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()
>
>     # create the Queue that will hold the MDAEvents
>     q = Queue()
>
>     # Setup the controller and analyzer
>     analyzer = Analyzer()
>     controller = Controller(analyzer, mmc, q)
>
>     # Start the acquisition
>     controller.run()
>
>
> if __name__ == "__main__":
>     main()
> ```

### MDASequence

It's worth noting that the `MDASequence` class is itself an `Iterable[MDAEvent]`. It implements an `__iter__` method that yields the events in the sequence, and it can be passed directly to the `run_mda()` method as we saw in the [Acquisition engine guide](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/#running-an-mda-sequence>). It is a *deterministic* sequence, so it wouldn't be used on its own to implement conditional event sequences; it can, however, be used in conjunction with other iterables to implement more complex sequences.

Take this simple sequence as an example:

```python
my_sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    time_plan={"loops": 5, "interval": 0.1}, channels=["DAPI", "FITC"]
)
```

In the generator example above, we could yield the events in this sequence when the condition is met (saving us from constructing the events manually)

```python
# in the generator example above:
def my_events() -> Iterator[useq.MDAEvent]:
    while True:
        if some_condition_is_met():
            yield from my_sequence  # yield the events in the sequence
        else:
            ...
```

In the `Queue` example above, we could `put` the events in the sequence into the queue:

```python
# ... we can put events into the queue
# according to whatever logic we want:
for event in my_sequence:
    q.put(event)
```

## Things to keep in mind

A few things to keep in mind when you pass the runner an *iterator* (a generator, or `iter(queue.get, STOP)`) instead of a list or an `MDASequence`:

- The engine can't look ahead, so events are never merged into [hardware-triggered sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/#hardware-triggered-sequences>).
- The shape of the data isn't known in advance, so if you pass `output=`, the frames are written into one flat `(t, y, x)` stack, in the order they were acquired (see [Saving Data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/#lists-and-generators-are-saved-as-a-flat-stack>)).
- `min_start_time` is measured from the start of the run, or from the last event that had `reset_event_timer=True`. So to start an event "5 seconds after *this* one started", set `reset_event_timer=True` on this event, and `min_start_time=5` on the next.
- `frameReady` callbacks run in the acquisition thread (with the default psygnal backend), and the next event waits for them. If deciding on the next event takes a while, do that work in another thread (the `Controller` in the example above only stores the image in its callback, and analyzes it in the main thread). See [Threads](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/#threads>).

# Events and Callbacks

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Terminology confusion!**
>
> A quick warning on terminology: the name "event" may refer to two different things in pymmcore-plus, which are not to be confused.
>
> This page discusses the "events" that are emitted by the `CMMCorePlus` and `MDARunner` objects. These are occurrences that your program can react to by registering callback functions. These are also known as "**signals**" in the context of the Qt framework or psygnal.
>
> The term "event" may also be used to refer to the **`useq.MDAEvent`** objects that are consumed by the [Acquisition Engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>). These are *not* the same as the "events" discussed on this page.

Both the `CMMCorePlus` object and the `CMMCorePlus.mda` (`MDARunner`) objects have `events` attributes that can be used to register callbacks for events that occur as the state of the microscope changes, or as an acquisition sequence progresses.

## Event backends

`pymmcore-plus` supports both **Qt**-based and [**psygnal**](<https://github.com/pyapp-kit/psygnal>)-based event signaling.

**The default behavior is to use Qt-backed signals when a global `QApplication` instance exists at the time the `CMMCorePlus` object is created, and `psygnal` otherwise.** The backend is chosen once, when the core is created, so if you're building a Qt application, create the `QApplication` *before* the `CMMCorePlus`. (The difference matters mostly for [threads](<#threads>), see below.)

If you would like to force a specific event backend, you can do so by setting the `PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND` environment variable to `qt`, `psygnal`, or `auto` (for the default behavior).

```bash
export PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND=psygnal
```

```text
set PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND=psygnal
```

```python
# before instantiating CMMCorePlus
import os

os.environ["PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND"] = "psygnal"
```

```powershell
$env:PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND = "psygnal"
```

## Connecting callbacks to events

To connect a callback to an event, use the `connect` method of the specific event emitter that you would like to listen to. (All event backends support the same connection/disconnection API.)

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Example: Connecting callbacks**
>
> Given a `CMMCorePlus` object `core`:
>
> ```python
> import numpy as np
> import useq
>
> from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
>
> core = CMMCorePlus()
> ```
>
> Register a callback to listen to property changes on the `CMMCorePlus`:
>
> ```python
> @core.events.propertyChanged.connect
> def on_property_changed(dev: str, prop: str, value: str):
>     print(f"Property {prop!r} on device {dev!r} changed to {value}")
> ```
>
> Register a callback to process data during an acquisition sequence:
>
> ```python
> @core.mda.events.frameReady.connect
> def on_image_captured(data: np.ndarray, event: useq.MDAEvent, metadata: dict):
>     print(f"Event index {event.index} captured with shape {data.shape}")
> ```

The signature of the callback function should match the signature of the event emitter's signal (although it may accept *fewer* arguments than the signal emits, in which case the extra ones are dropped). The available events and their signatures are listed in the [events reference](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/reference/events/index.md>), and are defined by two protocols:

- `PCoreSignaler`: events emitted at `CMMCorePlus.events` when the state of the microscope changes.
- `PMDASignaler`: events emitted at `CMMCorePlus.mda.events` as an acquisition sequence progresses.

You may **disconnect** a callback from an event by calling the `disconnect` method of the event emitter with the callback function as the argument.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Example: Disconnecting callbacks**
>
> ```python
> core.events.propertyChanged.disconnect(on_property_changed)
> ```

### Listening to a single device or property

`propertyChanged` fires for every property on every device. If you only care about one device (or one property on one device), use `devicePropertyChanged`. Note that the callback then receives fewer arguments:

```python
def on_gain_changed(value: str):
    print(f"Gain is now {value}")


def on_camera_changed(prop: str, value: str):
    print(f"Camera {prop} is now {value}")


# called with (value) when the camera's Gain changes
core.events.devicePropertyChanged("Camera", "Gain").connect(on_gain_changed)

# called with (property_name, value) when any camera property changes
core.events.devicePropertyChanged("Camera").connect(on_camera_changed)
```

## Threads

`run_mda` runs the acquisition on a new thread, and all of the `core.mda.events` signals are emitted from that thread. (`core.mda.run()` blocks and runs the acquisition in the thread you called it from, so the signals are emitted there.) What happens next depends on the event backend:

- With **psygnal**, callbacks are called synchronously, *in the acquisition thread*. A slow `frameReady` callback will delay the next event, so do heavy processing elsewhere (handler objects passed to `output=` are called from a separate thread, so they don't hold up the acquisition). Don't touch Qt widgets from these callbacks.
- With **Qt**, callbacks connected from the main thread are delivered on the main thread (through Qt's event loop), which is what you want for updating a GUI.

The same goes for `core.events`: with psygnal, callbacks run in whichever thread made the change (usually yours, but some device adapters notify the core from their own threads).

See [processing frames yourself](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/#processing-frames-yourself>) for handing frames off to another thread.

## Following changes in the core

Here's a small script that reacts to a change in the microscope's state (the same pattern you'd use to keep a GUI in sync with the hardware):

properties\_and\_state\_events.py

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()


@core.events.propertyChanged.connect
def _on_prop_changed(dev, prop, value):
    # Note that when state devices change either the state or the label
    # TWO propertyChanged events will be emitted, one for prop 'State'
    # and one for prop 'Label'. Probably, best to check the property
    # name and only respond to one of them
    if dev == "Objective" and prop == "Label":
        print("new objective is", value)


core.setState("Objective", 3)
```

... which prints `new objective is Nikon 20X Plan Fluor ELWD`.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **State devices emit two events**
>
> When a state device (like a filter wheel or objective turret) changes, *two* `propertyChanged` events are emitted: one for the `State` property and one for the `Label` property.
>
> ```text
> propertyChanged: Objective State 3
> propertyChanged: Objective Label Nikon 20X Plan Fluor ELWD
> ```
>
> So it's usually best to check the property name and only respond to one of them, as the example above does.

# IPython Tab Completion

`pymmcore-plus` provides an IPython completer that allows you to use tab-completion for methods on the `CMMCorePlus` object. If you hit `<Tab>` after the parenthesis of a core method that expects the name of an existing device, you will be presented with suggestions for the names of loaded devices (of the appropriate type). The same works for property names (e.g. the second argument of `getProperty`), config group and preset names, and device adapter names.

The completer is installed automatically when you import `pymmcore_plus` in an IPython session (including Jupyter notebooks). You may disable this feature by setting the [environment variable](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/env_var/index.md>) `PYMM_DISABLE_IPYTHON_COMPLETIONS` to `1` before importing `pymmcore_plus`.

# Logging

By default, pymmcore-plus logs to the console at the `WARNING` level and to a logfile in the pymmcore-plus application data directory at the `DEBUG` level. The logfile is named `pymmcore-plus.log` and is rotated at 40MB, with a maximum retention of 20 logfiles.

## Customizing logging

The `pymmcore_plus.configure_logging` function allows you to customize the log level, logfile name, and logfile rotation settings. For example, to see everything that pymmcore-plus is doing in the console:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import configure_logging

configure_logging(stderr_level="DEBUG")
```

You may also configure logging using the following environment variables (set them before importing `pymmcore_plus`):

| Variable | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PYMM\_LOG\_LEVEL | `WARNING` | The console log level (e.g. `INFO` or `DEBUG`). |
| PYMM\_LOG\_FILE | `pymmcore-plus.log` in the pymmcore-plus log directory | The logfile location. Set to `0`, `false`, `no`, or `none` to disable logging to a file. |
| PYMM\_LOG\_RICH | `0` (disabled) | Use [rich](<https://rich.readthedocs.io/>) for stderr logging. Set to `1`, `true`, or `yes` to enable. Note: adds some formatting overhead ([\#449](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/issues/449>)). |

(See [environment variables](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/env_var/index.md>) for the full list.)

> [!TIP]
>
> **pymmcore-plus log directory**
>
> The application data directory is platform-dependent. Here are the log folders for each supported platform:
>
> | OS | Path |
> | --- | --- |
> | macOS | \~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/logs |
> | Linux | \~/.local/share/pymmcore-plus/logs |
> | Win | C:\\Users\\username\\AppData\\Local\\pymmcore-plus\\pymmcore-plus\\logs |
>
> You can also use `mmcore logs --reveal` to open the log directory in your file manager.

Note that both pymmcore-plus and the underlying CMMCore object will write to the log file. By default, CMMCorePlus will call `setPrimaryLogFile()` with the location of the pymmcore-plus logfile upon instantiation. The C++ core's own logging can be controlled with the methods in the *Logging &amp; errors* section of `CMMCorePlus` (e.g. `enableDebugLog` and `setPrimaryLogLevel`).

## Managing logs with the CLI

The `mmcore` CLI provides a `logs` subcommand for managing logs.

```console
$ mmcore logs --help

 Usage: mmcore logs [OPTIONS]                                                   

 Display recent output from pymmcore-plus log.                                  

╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --num     -n      <int>  Number of lines to display.                         │
│ --tail    -t             Continually stream logs.                            │
│ --clear   -c             Delete all log files.                               │
│ --reveal                 Reveal log file in Explorer/Finder.                 │
│ --help                   Show this message and exit.                         │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

A particularly useful command is `mmcore logs --tail`, which will continually stream the current logfile to the console. This can be started in another process and left running to monitor an experiment in progress.

To delete all logfiles, use `mmcore logs --clear`.

# The Acquisition Engine

One of the key features of pymmcore-plus is the acquisition engine. This allows you to define and execute a sequence of events. The sequence may be a typical multi-dimensional acquisition (MDA), such as a z-stack across multiple channels, stage positions, and time points; or it can be any custom sequence of events that you define. It needn't even be a sequence of known length: you can define an iterable or a `queue.Queue` of events that reacts to the results of previous events, for event-driven "smart" microscopy.

The built-in acquisition engine will support many standard use-cases, but you can also subclass and customize it, allowing arbitrary python code to be executed at each step of the acquisition. This makes it possible to incorporate custom hardware control (e.g. to control devices for which Micro-Manager has no adapters), data analysis, or other logic into the experiment.

There are two objects involved, and you'll see both names in these docs. The **runner**, `core.mda` (an `MDARunner`), is what you call. It walks through the events (waiting until each one is due, and handling pause and cancel), emits signals such as `frameReady`, and sends the images to wherever you asked it to save them. The **engine**, `core.mda.engine` (an `MDAEngine`, unless you've replaced it), is what actually drives the hardware for each event (moving the stages, setting the channel and exposure, and snapping the image).

## Running a very simple sequence

To execute a sequence, you must:

1. Create a `CMMCorePlus` instance (and probably load a configuration file)
2. Pass an iterable of `useq.MDAEvent` objects to the `run_mda()` method.

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from useq import MDAEvent

# Create the core instance.
mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()  # (1)!
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()  # (2)!

# Create a super-simple sequence, with one event
mda_sequence = [MDAEvent()]  # (3)!

# Run it!
mmc.run_mda(mda_sequence)
```

1. Here, we use the global `CMMCorePlus.instance` singleton.
2. This loads the demo configuration by default. Pass the path to your own config file to load that instead (see `CMMCorePlus.loadSystemConfiguration`).
3. An experiment is just an iterable of `useq.MDAEvent` objects.

> [!TIP]
>
> `CMMCorePlus.run_mda` is a convenience method that runs the experiment in a separate thread, and returns that `Thread` right away (call `.join()` on it, or pass `block=True`, to wait for the acquisition to finish). If you want to run it in the current thread, use `CMMCorePlus.mda.run` directly, which blocks until the acquisition is done:
>
> ```py
> mmc.mda.run(mda_sequence)
> ```

The code above will execute a single, very boring event! It will snap one image (the default action of an `MDAEvent`) with the current exposure time, channel, stage position, etc... and then stop.

Let's make it a little more interesting.

## The `MDAEvent` object

The `useq.MDAEvent` object is the basic building block of an experiment. It is a relatively simple dataclass that defines a single action to be performed. For complete details, see the [useq-schema documentation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/event/index.md>), but some key attributes you might want to set are:

- **exposure** (`float`): The exposure time (in milliseconds) to use for this event.
- **channel** (`Channel`): The configuration preset to use. May be given as a `str` (the name of a preset in the `Channel` group), or as a `dict` with two keys: `config` and `group` (the preset and configuration group, respectively).
- **x\_pos**, **y\_pos**, **z\_pos** (`float`): An `x`, `y`, and `z` stage position to use for this event.
- **min\_start\_time** (`float`): The minimum time to wait before starting this event, in seconds, relative to the start of the sequence (or to the last event that had `reset_event_timer=True`).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Example**
>
> ```python
> snap_a_dapi = MDAEvent(channel="DAPI", exposure=100, x_pos=1100, y_pos=1240)
> ```
>
> **NOTE:** The name `"DAPI"` here must be a name of a [preset](<https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager_Configuration_Guide#configuration-presets>) in your Micro-Manager "Channel" configuration group.

For any missing keys, the implied meaning is "use the current setting". For example, an `MDAEvent` without an `x_pos` or a `y_pos` will use the current stage position.

The implied "action" of an `MDAEvent` is to snap an image. Events can carry other actions too (see [what the engine does](<#what-the-engine-does>)).

## A multi-event sequence

With our understanding of `MDAEvent` objects, we can now create a slightly more interesting experiment. This one will snap four images: two channels at two different stage positions.

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from useq import MDAEvent

# Create the core instance.
mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()

# Snap two channels at two positions
mda_sequence = [
    MDAEvent(channel={"config": "DAPI"}, x_pos=1100, y_pos=1240),
    MDAEvent(channel={"config": "FITC"}, x_pos=1100, y_pos=1240),
    MDAEvent(channel={"config": "DAPI"}, x_pos=1442, y_pos=1099),
    MDAEvent(channel={"config": "FITC"}, x_pos=1442, y_pos=1099),
]

# Run it!
mmc.run_mda(mda_sequence)
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Logs**
>
> By default, only warnings and errors are printed to the console. If you set the environment variable `PYMM_LOG_LEVEL=INFO` before running the code above, you will also see each event as it is executed:
>
> ```text
> 2026-10-27 00:20:41,785 - pymmcore-plus - INFO - (_runner.py:677) MDA Started: GeneratorMDASequence()
> 2026-10-27 00:20:41,785 - pymmcore-plus - INFO - (_runner.py:553) channel=Channel(config='DAPI') x_pos=1100.0 y_pos=1240.0
> 2026-10-27 00:20:41,972 - pymmcore-plus - INFO - (_runner.py:553) channel=Channel(config='FITC') x_pos=1100.0 y_pos=1240.0
> 2026-10-27 00:20:41,997 - pymmcore-plus - INFO - (_runner.py:553) channel=Channel(config='DAPI') x_pos=1442.0 y_pos=1099.0
> 2026-10-27 00:20:42,052 - pymmcore-plus - INFO - (_runner.py:553) channel=Channel(config='FITC') x_pos=1442.0 y_pos=1099.0
> 2026-10-27 00:20:42,077 - pymmcore-plus - INFO - (_runner.py:762) MDA Finished: GeneratorMDASequence()
> ```
>
> See [logging](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/logging/index.md>) for more details on how to configure and review logs.

At this point, you might be thinking that constructing a sequence by hand is a little tedious. And you'd be right! That's why we have the `MDASequence` class.

## Building sequences with `MDASequence`

For most standard multi-dimensional experiments, you will want to use `useq.MDASequence` to construct your sequence of events. It allows you to declare a "plan" for each axis in your experiment (channels, time, z, etc...) along with the order in which the axes should be iterated:

```python
import useq

mda_sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 6},  # 6 time points, 2 seconds apart
    channels=[
        {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50},
        {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 80},
    ],
)
```

`MDASequence` comes from useq-schema, which has its own guide: [Building Sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>) walks through z-stacks, grids, skipping channels at some time points, per-position settings, and saving sequences to (and loading them from) YAML or JSON files.

## Running an MDA sequence

Calling `list()` on an instance of `MDASequence` gives you a list of `MDAEvent` objects. This means that `MDASequence` ***is*** an [iterable](<https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-iterable>) of `MDAEvent`... which is exactly what we need to pass to the `run_mda()` method.

So, you can directly pass an instance of `MDASequence` to `run_mda`:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
import useq

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()

# create a sequence
mda_sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[{"z": mmc.getZPosition()}],  # (1)!
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 10},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    channels=[
        {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50},
        {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 20},
    ],
)

# Run it!
mmc.run_mda(mda_sequence)
```

1. A `range` z plan is *relative* to the `z` of each stage position, so here we use the current focus position. Without a position, the stack would be centered on z = 0, *not* on the current focus (see [Relative to what?](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/#a-z-stack-at-three-positions>)).

## Handling acquired data

You will almost certainly want to *do* something with the data that is collected during an MDA 😂.

To save it to disk, pass `output=` with a path ending in `.ome.zarr` or `.ome.tiff`:

```python
mmc.mda.run(mda_sequence, output="experiment.ome.zarr")
```

[Saving Data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>) explains the formats, what you get on disk, how to read it back, and how to control the details.

You will also want to know how to connect callbacks to the `frameReady` event, so that you can handle incoming data as it is acquired:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
import numpy as np
import useq

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()


@mmc.mda.events.frameReady.connect  # (1)!
def on_frame(image: np.ndarray, event: useq.MDAEvent, metadata: dict):
    # do what you want with the data
    print(
        f"received frame: {image.shape}, {image.dtype} "
        f"@ index {event.index}, z={event.z_pos}"
    )


mda_sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[{"z": mmc.getZPosition()}],
    time_plan={"interval": 0.5, "loops": 10},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
)

mmc.run_mda(mda_sequence)
```

1. The `frameReady` signal accepts a callback with up to three arguments: the image data as a numpy array, the `MDAEvent` that triggered the callback, and a dict of frame metadata (see `FrameMetaV1`).

This callback is called in the acquisition thread, so the next event waits for it to finish (see [Threads and callbacks](<#threads-and-callbacks>) below). See also [additional events you may wish to connect to](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/reference/events/index.md>).

## Cancelling or pausing

You can pause or cancel the acquisition with the `CMMCorePlus.mda.set_paused` or `CMMCorePlus.mda.cancel` methods.

```python
mmc.mda.set_paused(True)   # pauses the mda
mmc.mda.set_paused(False)  # resumes the mda

mmc.mda.cancel()  # cancels the mda
```

Both take effect between events. (A hardware-triggered sequence, described below, can be cancelled while it runs, but not paused.)

## What the engine does

When a run starts, the default engine's `setup_sequence` stops live mode (if it's running), applies the sequence's `setup` event (if any), and fills in the field of view of grid plans that don't specify one, from the camera ROI and pixel size.

Then, for each event, the runner waits until the event's `min_start_time` and emits `eventStarted`, and the engine's `setup_event`:

1. moves the XY stage to `x_pos`/`y_pos`, then the focus stage to `z_pos` (plus any correction found by an earlier hardware autofocus event at that position),
2. sets the SLM image, if there is one,
3. sets the channel preset (skipped if it's the same preset as last time),
4. sets the exposure, any `properties`, and the camera ROI,
5. turns off autoshutter and opens the shutter, if the event asks to `keep_shutter_open`,

and then calls `waitForSystem()`. Anything that is `None` on the event is left as it is. `exec_event` then calls `snapImage()`, and `getImage()` for each camera channel (more than one with a Multi Camera device), and the runner emits `frameReady` for each image. A `HardwareAutofocus` action runs `fullFocus()` instead of acquiring an image, and the default engine doesn't acquire anything for other actions (such as a `CustomAction`).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **The engine puts things back**
>
> At the end of a run, the default engine returns the XY stage, focus, exposure, configuration presets, autoshutter and camera ROI to where they were when the run started (moving Z and XY in whichever order keeps the objective away from the sample). This is only done automatically when the focus direction of your focus stage is known (`FocusDirection` in your config file, or "Stage Focus Direction" in the Hardware Configuration Wizard). To choose for yourself, set `restore_initial_state`:
>
> ```python
> mmc.mda.engine.restore_initial_state = False  # leave everything where the MDA put it
> ```

## Hardware-triggered sequences

Having the computer "in-the-loop" for every event in an MDA sequence can add unwanted overhead that limits performance in rapid acquisition sequences. Because of this, some devices support *hardware triggering*. This means that the computer can tell the device to queue up and start a sequence of events, and the device will take care of executing the sequence without further input from the computer.

Just like [Micro-Manager's acquisition engine](<https://micro-manager.org/Hardware-based_Synchronization_in_Micro-Manager>), the default acquisition engine in `pymmcore-plus` can opportunistically use hardware triggering whenever possible. Consecutive events are merged into a single `SequencedEvent` when the things that change between them (exposure, XY position, Z position, SLM image, or any property in the channel preset or in the event's `properties`) can be sequenced by your hardware, and the sequence fits within each device's maximum sequence length. The camera then runs a sequence acquisition, and the frames are read from the buffer as they arrive.

A few things always end a hardware-triggered sequence:

- a new time point with a different `min_start_time`. So time-lapses with an interval are never merged across time points (only `"interval": 0` bursts are);
- a change of camera ROI;
- an event with an action other than acquiring an image (e.g. hardware autofocus);
- a change of a stage `Position` set through the event's `properties`.

Events are also *never* merged when you pass an *iterator* to the runner (a generator, or a queue-backed iterator as in [event-driven acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/event_driven_acquisition/index.md>)), rather than a list or an `MDASequence`. In that case, the engine doesn't get to look ahead.

This behavior is on by default, but you can disable it by setting `CMMCorePlus.mda.engine.use_hardware_sequencing = False`, which may be useful for various debugging or testing purposes (or when your events carry `metadata` that a [custom engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/custom_engine/#utilizing-mdaevent-metadata>) needs to see one event at a time):

```python
mmc.mda.engine.use_hardware_sequencing = False  # default is True
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> **How does pymmcore-plus know if my device supports hardware triggering?**
>
> The low-level `CMMCore` object itself has a number of methods that query whether certain devices are capable of hardware triggering, such as
>
> - `pymmcore.CMMCore.isStageSequenceable`
> - `pymmcore.CMMCore.isPropertySequenceable`
> - `pymmcore.CMMCore.isXYStageSequenceable`
> - `pymmcore.CMMCore.isExposureSequenceable`
>
> Hint: Many devices that support sequencing have a property (often named `Sequence` or similar) that can be used to toggle their responses to the above queries, thereby enabling or disabling sequencing.
>
> To see how the engine will group your events, pass them (with your configuration loaded) to `iter_sequenced_events`, which is what the engine uses:
>
> ```python
> from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
> from pymmcore_plus.core import iter_sequenced_events
> import useq
>
> mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
> mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()
>
> z_stack = useq.MDASequence(z_plan={"range": 2, "step": 1}, stage_positions=[{"z": 0}])
> print(list(iter_sequenced_events(mmc, z_stack)))
> # [MDAEvent(index={'p': 0, 'z': 0}, z_pos=-1.0), MDAEvent(...), MDAEvent(...)]
>
> mmc.setProperty("Z", "UseSequences", "Yes")  # the demo Z stage can be sequenced
> print(list(iter_sequenced_events(mmc, z_stack)))
> # [SequencedEvent(z_pos=-1.0, properties=[], z_sequence='(3 items)')]
> ```

## Threads and callbacks

The `mmc.mda.events` signals are emitted from the acquisition thread, and (with the default psygnal backend) the next event waits for your `frameReady` callbacks to return. So keep them quick, or pass a handler object to `output=` instead, which runs on its own thread (see [Saving Data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/#processing-frames-yourself>)). [Threads](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/#threads>) explains which thread your callbacks run in, and how the Qt backend changes that.

## A complete example

Here is a script that puts most of the above together. Run it with `--zarr` or `--tiff` to also save the data:

run\_mda.py

```python
import itertools
import sys

import numpy as np
from useq import MDAEvent, MDASequence

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()  # (1)!
mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()  #  load demo configuration (2)

# describe the experiment (3)
sequence = MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[{"z": mmc.getZPosition()}],  # (4)!
    channels=[{"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 10}, {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 50}],
    time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 5},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    axis_order="tpcz",
)
counter = itertools.count(1)


# connect callback using a decorator (5)
@mmc.mda.events.frameReady.connect
def new_frame(img: np.ndarray, event: MDAEvent):
    print(f"Frame {next(counter):>3}, shape", img.shape, event.index)


# or connect callback using a function
def on_start(sequence: MDASequence):
    print(f"now starting sequence {sequence.uid}!")


mmc.mda.events.sequenceStarted.connect(on_start)

# parse command line arguments to determine output format, default is no output.
output = None
if "--tiff" in sys.argv:
    output = "example_mda.ome.tiff"
elif "--zarr" in sys.argv:
    output = "example_mda.ome.zarr"

# run the sequence (6)
mmc.mda.run(sequence, output=output, overwrite=True)
```

1. Access the global singleton: `CMMCorePlus.instance`
2. See `CMMCorePlus.loadSystemConfiguration`
3. See [Building Sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>) for the many ways to describe an experiment with `useq.MDASequence`.
4. The z plan is relative to this position's `z`, so the stack is centered on the current focus position.
5. For info on all of the signals available to connect to, see [Events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/reference/events/index.md>).
6. `mda.run` blocks until the acquisition is done. Use `mmc.run_mda(sequence)` to run it on a new thread instead.

## Next steps

Now that you have a basic understanding of how to create and run multi-dimensional acquisition sequences in pymmcore-plus, you may want to take a look at some more advanced features:

- [saving data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>) to OME-Zarr or OME-TIFF
- [creating non-deterministic sequences for event-driven acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/event_driven_acquisition/index.md>)
- [customizing the acquisition engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/custom_engine/index.md>)

# Saving Data

To save the images from an acquisition, pass `output=` to `core.mda.run()` (or `core.run_mda()`). Frames are written to disk as they arrive, by [ome-writers](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/ome-writers/>), and the extension of the path picks the format:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
import useq

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()

sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[(0, 0, 0), (100, 100, 0)],
    channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
    time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 3},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1},
)

core.mda.run(sequence, output="experiment.ome.zarr")  # (1)!
```

1. Or `output="experiment.ome.tiff"`. Note that `mda.run` blocks until the acquisition is done, while `run_mda` runs it on another thread (see [The Acquisition Engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/#running-a-very-simple-sequence>)).

There are two formats to choose from:

- **`.ome.zarr`** writes an [OME-Zarr](<https://ngff.openmicroscopy.org/>) (v0.5, which is built on Zarr v3). This works with the default install.
- **`.ome.tiff`** writes OME-TIFF. This needs [tifffile](<https://github.com/cgohlke/tifffile>), which is what the `io` extra adds:

  ```bash
  pip install "pymmcore-plus[io]"
  ```

  (Without it, you'll get `ValueError: No available backends found for format 'ome-tiff'`.) OME-TIFF is a good choice if you want to open the files in tools like Fiji (via Bio-Formats).

The shape of the data comes from the sequence. In the example above, each position gets a `(t, c, z, y, x)` array of shape `(3, 2, 5, 512, 512)`. The dimensions are stored in the order OME expects (time, channel, z, y, x), whatever `axis_order` you acquired them in.

## Where did the data go?

The path you pass isn't always a single file:

| output | one position | several positions (or a grid plan) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `experiment.ome.zarr` | a zarr folder holding one image | a zarr folder with one image per position, named after the position if it has a `name` (`A1/`, ...), or numbered (`0/`, `1/`, ...). With a grid plan, each tile is its own image (`0_0_0/`, `0_1_0/`, ...: position, row, column) |
| `experiment.ome.tiff` | a single file | a folder, `experiment/`, with one file per position (or grid tile): `experiment_p000.ome.tiff`, `experiment_p001.ome.tiff`, ... |

## Running it again (`overwrite`)

If the output already exists, the run fails right away:

```text
FileExistsError: Zarr group already exists at .../experiment.ome.zarr. Use overwrite=True to replace it.
```

Pass `overwrite=True` to replace it:

```python
core.mda.run(sequence, output="experiment.ome.zarr", overwrite=True)
```

`run_mda` doesn't take an `overwrite` argument (yet). To overwrite from `run_mda`, put it in an [`AcquisitionSettings`](<#more-control-with-acquisitionsettings>) object instead: `output=AcquisitionSettings(root_path="experiment.ome.zarr", overwrite=True)`.

## Opening the data in Python

An OME-TIFF reads straight into a numpy array with tifffile:

```python
import tifffile

data = tifffile.imread("experiment/experiment_p000.ome.tiff")
print(data.shape)  # (3, 2, 5, 512, 512), i.e. (t, c, z, y, x)
```

An OME-Zarr can be read with any reader that supports Zarr v3, for example [zarr-python](<https://zarr.readthedocs.io/>) (`pip install zarr`):

```python
import zarr

root = zarr.open_group("experiment.ome.zarr", mode="r")
data = root["0/0"][:]  # (1)!
print(data.shape)  # (3, 2, 5, 512, 512), i.e. (t, c, z, y, x)
```

1. With several positions, `root["0"]` is the image for the first position (or `root["A1"]`, if you named it), and `"0"` inside it is the full-resolution array. With a single position there's no position level, so the array is just `root["0"]`. (`list(root)` shows what's there.)

Some metadata is saved along with the pixels:

- The summary metadata (devices, properties, pixel size, the `MDASequence` itself, etc...; see `SummaryMetaV1`) is stored under a `"pymmcore_plus"` key, in the attributes of the root zarr group (`root.attrs["pymmcore_plus"]["summary_metadata"]`) or as an OME-XML annotation in the TIFF.
- For each frame, the time (`delta_t`), exposure time, and stage position are written into the OME metadata. The rest of the per-frame metadata that `frameReady` emits (`FrameMetaV1`) is *not* saved. If you need it, connect to `frameReady` and store it yourself (see [below](<#processing-frames-yourself>)).

## More control with `AcquisitionSettings`

Instead of a path, `output` also accepts an `ome_writers.AcquisitionSettings` object, which lets you choose things like compression, the backend, and whether to overwrite:

```python
from ome_writers import AcquisitionSettings

settings = AcquisitionSettings(
    root_path="experiment.ome.zarr",
    compression="blosc-zstd",
    overwrite=True,
)
core.run_mda(sequence, output=settings)
```

The dimensions (and well-plate layout, if any) are always filled in from the sequence, so you don't need to (and can't) set them here. To change the chunking, use the `dimension_overrides` argument of `mda.run` / `run_mda`, keyed by dimension name:

```python
core.mda.run(
    sequence,
    output="experiment.ome.zarr",
    dimension_overrides={"y": {"chunk_size": 256}, "x": {"chunk_size": 256}},
)
```

See the [ome-writers documentation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/ome-writers/usage/>) for the rest of the `AcquisitionSettings` options.

While an acquisition is running, `core.mda.get_view()` returns an array-like view of the data written so far. (`output="memory"` keeps the data in memory instead of writing a file, which is handy for viewers and tests.)

## Lists and generators are saved as a flat stack

The array shape is taken from the `MDASequence`. If you pass anything else (a list of `MDAEvent`s, a generator, a queue iterator as in [Event-Driven Acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/event_driven_acquisition/index.md>), or a `useq.v2.MDASequence`), there's no shape to go on, so the frames are written in the order they arrive into one `(t, y, x)` array of unknown length:

```python
core.mda.run(list(sequence), output="flat.ome.zarr")  # shape (60, 512, 512)
```

The same happens (with a warning in the log) for an `MDASequence` whose positions have their own sub-sequence with anything other than a `grid_plan` (for example, [a different z-stack at one position](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/#different-plans-at-different-positions>)), since the positions then don't share one shape.

Each frame's `MDAEvent` (and its `index`) is still available in the `frameReady` signal, if you need to sort the frames out later.

## Processing frames yourself

To do something else with the images (analysis, a different file format, sending them somewhere, etc...), connect a callback to the `frameReady` signal. It receives up to three arguments: the image (a numpy array), the `MDAEvent`, and the frame metadata dict:

```python
import numpy as np


@core.mda.events.frameReady.connect
def on_frame(image: np.ndarray, event: useq.MDAEvent, metadata: dict) -> None:
    print(f"received frame {event.index}: {image.shape}, {image.dtype}")
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Keep it quick**
>
> With the default (psygnal) event backend, a `frameReady` callback runs in the acquisition thread, so the next event waits until your callback returns. See [Threads](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/#threads>) for details.

If the processing is slow, write a *handler* object instead, and pass it in `output=`. A handler is any object with a `frameReady` method (it may also have `sequenceStarted` and `sequenceFinished` methods). Handlers are called from a separate thread, so they don't hold up the acquisition (`mda.run` waits for them to catch up before it returns). Here we make a maximum-intensity projection of each z-stack, while also saving the raw data:

```python
class MaxProjector:
    """Keep a maximum-intensity projection of each z-stack."""

    def sequenceStarted(self, sequence: useq.MDASequence, metadata: dict) -> None:
        self.projections: dict[tuple, np.ndarray] = {}

    def frameReady(
        self, image: np.ndarray, event: useq.MDAEvent, metadata: dict
    ) -> None:
        idx = event.index
        key = (idx.get("p", 0), idx.get("t", 0), idx.get("c", 0))
        if key in self.projections:
            np.maximum(self.projections[key], image, out=self.projections[key])
        else:
            self.projections[key] = image.copy()

    def sequenceFinished(self, sequence: useq.MDASequence) -> None:
        print(f"made {len(self.projections)} projections")


projector = MaxProjector()  # (1)!
core.mda.run(sequence, output=["experiment.ome.zarr", projector], overwrite=True)
```

1. Keep a reference to the handler, so that you can use `projector.projections` after the run.

`output` may be a list holding any number of handlers, plus *at most one* path (or `AcquisitionSettings`).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Deprecated: `pymmcore_plus.mda.handlers`**
>
> Older versions of pymmcore-plus wrote data with the handler classes in `pymmcore_plus.mda.handlers` (`OMEZarrWriter`, `OMETiffWriter`, `TensorStoreHandler` and `ImageSequenceWriter`). These are deprecated in favor of `output=` with a path, as described above, and importing the module emits a `FutureWarning`. They will be removed in a future version; if you rely on one, please copy it into your own code.

## Next steps

- [Events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/reference/events/index.md>) lists every signal emitted during an acquisition.
- [Event-Driven Acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/event_driven_acquisition/index.md>) builds the sequence on the fly, based on the data.
- The `pymmcore_plus.metadata` reference describes the summary and frame metadata.

# UniMMCore

> [!TIP]
>
> **Experimental**
>
> This is an experimental feature, and the API may change in future releases.

## A unified controller of C++ and pure-Python devices

The `UniMMCore` class is a subclass of `CMMCorePlus` that can control both "classic" C++ devices (via the CMMCore) as well as pure-Python device adapters. This simplifies the task of controlling new devices using pure-Python code, without the need to write and compile a C++ device adapter.

The Python devices work alongside the existing C++ device adapters, and you use them through the same `CMMCorePlus` API. When you call methods like `core.setXYPosition()` or `core.snapImage()`, UniMMCore routes the call to the appropriate device implementation (C++ or Python) based on which device is currently active. Properties and hardware sequencing are supported for Python devices too.

## Getting started

To use UniMMCore, replace `CMMCorePlus` with `UniMMCore`:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import UniMMCore

# Instead of: core = CMMCorePlus()
core = UniMMCore()

# Load traditional C++ devices defined in a config file (optional)
core.loadSystemConfiguration(...)

# Load Python devices (we'll discuss creating these below)
from my_custom_devices import MyCamera

core.loadPyDevice("MyCamera", MyCamera())
core.initializeDevice("MyCamera")

# Set as the current camera device
core.setCameraDevice("MyCamera")

# Use the same API, UniMMCore routes to Python device automatically
core.setExposure(100)
img = core.snap()  # or core.snapImage(), followed by core.getImage()
```

## Supported device types

UniMMCore currently supports the following device types for Python implementation (all of them share the [common methods](<#common-methods>)):

- [`CameraDevice`](<#camera-devices-cameradevice>) (and `SimpleCameraDevice`)
- [`StageDevice`](<#stage-devices-stagedevice>) (single axis, e.g. focus)
- [`XYStageDevice`](<#xy-stage-devices-xystagedevice>) (and `XYStepperStageDevice`)
- [`StateDevice`](<#state-devices-statedevice>)
- [`ShutterDevice`](<#shutter-devices-shutterdevice>)
- [`SLMDevice`](<#slm-devices-slmdevice>)
- [`HubDevice`](<#hub-devices-hubdevice>)
- [`GenericDevice`](<#generic-devices-genericdevice>)

### Common methods

All device base classes inherit from `Device`, and may re-implement any of the following methods:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import Device


class MyDevice(Device):
    def initialize(self) -> None:
        """Initialize the device.

        Note: Communication with and initialization of the device should be
        done here, *not* in `__init__`.
        """

    def shutdown(self) -> None:
        """Called when device is unloaded."""

    def busy(self) -> bool:
        """Return `True` if the device is busy. (Returns False by default)."""

    @classmethod
    def name(cls) -> str:
        """Return the name of the device.

        By default, the class name is used.  (This is *not* the same as
        the user-defined label)
        """

    def description(self) -> str:
        """Return a description of the device.

        By default, the class docstring is used.
        """
```

### Camera devices (`CameraDevice`)

For image acquisition devices. Implement the following abstract methods:

```python
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterator, Sequence

import numpy as np

from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import CameraDevice


class MyCamera(CameraDevice):
    def get_exposure(self) -> float:
        """Return current exposure time in milliseconds."""
        pass

    def set_exposure(self, exposure: float) -> None:
        """Set exposure time in milliseconds."""
        pass

    def shape(self) -> tuple[int, ...]:
        """Return (height, width, [channels]) of current image."""
        pass

    def dtype(self) -> np.dtype:
        """Return NumPy dtype of camera images."""
        pass

    def start_sequence(
        self, n: int | None, get_buffer: Callable[[Sequence[int], np.dtype], np.ndarray]
    ) -> Iterator[dict]:
        """Acquire `n` images (or until stopped, if `n` is None).

        For each image, call `get_buffer(shape, dtype)`, fill the returned array
        in place, and then yield a metadata dict for that image.
        """
        pass
```

`start_sequence` is used for sequence acquisitions *and* for `snapImage` (which is a sequence of one), so it's the only acquisition method you need to write.

For simple or simulated cameras, you can use `SimpleCameraDevice` instead. In place of `shape()` and `start_sequence()`, it only needs `sensor_shape()` and `snap()`, and it provides software ROI for you:

```python
import numpy as np

from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import SimpleCameraDevice


class MySimpleCamera(SimpleCameraDevice):
    def get_exposure(self) -> float: ...
    def set_exposure(self, exposure: float) -> None: ...

    def sensor_shape(self) -> tuple[int, ...]:
        """Return (height, width) of the full sensor."""
        ...

    def dtype(self) -> np.dtype: ...

    def snap(self, buffer: np.ndarray) -> dict:
        """Fill the full-frame buffer with image data."""
        ...
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> `SimpleCameraDevice` is *not* recommended for real hardware cameras: a per-frame `snap()` prevents SDK-level optimizations like ring buffers and DMA transfers. Use `CameraDevice` with `start_sequence()` instead.

### Stage devices (`StageDevice`)

For single-axis stages, like a focus drive (set it as the focus device with `core.setFocusDevice(label)`):

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import StageDevice


class MyZStage(StageDevice):
    def set_position_um(self, val: float) -> None:
        """Set stage position in micrometers."""

    def get_position_um(self) -> float:
        """Get current stage position in micrometers."""

    def set_origin(self) -> None:
        """Set the current position as the origin."""

    def home(self) -> None:
        """Move stage to home position."""

    def stop(self) -> None:
        """Stop stage movement."""
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> If you plan to save your configuration to a file (see [Python devices in config files](<#python-devices-in-config-files>)), also implement `set_focus_direction(self, sign: int)` (it may do nothing). The saved file includes a `FocusDirection` line for each stage, and the default implementation raises an error when that line is loaded again.

### XY stage devices (`XYStageDevice`)

For controlling 2-axis positioning stages:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import XYStageDevice


class MyStage(XYStageDevice):
    def set_position_um(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
        """Set stage position in micrometers."""
        pass

    def get_position_um(self) -> tuple[float, float]:
        """Get current stage position in micrometers."""
        pass

    def set_origin_x(self) -> None:
        """Set current X position as origin."""
        pass

    def set_origin_y(self) -> None:
        """Set current Y position as origin."""
        pass

    def stop(self) -> None:
        """Stop stage movement."""
        pass

    def home(self) -> None:
        """Move stage to home position."""
        pass
```

For stepper motor stages with sequence support, use `XYStepperStageDevice`:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import XYStepperStageDevice


class MyStepperStage(XYStepperStageDevice):
    def get_position_steps(self) -> tuple[int, int]:
        """Get position in motor steps."""
        pass

    def set_position_steps(self, x: int, y: int) -> None:
        """Set position in motor steps."""
        pass

    def get_step_size_x_um(self) -> float:
        """Get X-axis step size in micrometers."""
        pass

    def get_step_size_y_um(self) -> float:
        """Get Y-axis step size in micrometers."""
        pass

    def home(self) -> None:
        """Move stage to home position."""
        pass

    def stop(self) -> None:
        """Stop stage movement."""
        pass

    # Additional methods for sequence support
    def get_sequence_max_length(self) -> int:
        """Maximum length of position sequences."""
        pass

    def send_sequence(self, sequence: tuple[tuple[float, float], ...]) -> None:
        """Load sequence of (x, y) positions."""
        pass
```

### State devices (`StateDevice`)

For devices with discrete states (filter wheels, objective turrets, etc.):

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import StateDevice


class MyFilterWheel(StateDevice):
    def set_state(self, pos: int) -> None:
        """Set device to specified state/position."""
        pass

    def get_state(self) -> int:
        """Get current state/position."""
        pass
```

### Shutter devices (`ShutterDevice`)

For controlling shutters or any binary open/close devices:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import ShutterDevice


class MyShutter(ShutterDevice):
    def get_open(self) -> bool:
        """Return True if shutter is open."""
        pass

    def set_open(self, open: bool) -> None:
        """Open (True) or close (False) the shutter."""
        pass
```

### SLM devices (`SLMDevice`)

For Spatial Light Modulators:

```python
import numpy as np

from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import SLMDevice


class MySLM(SLMDevice):
    def shape(self) -> tuple[int, ...]:
        """Return (height, width) of the SLM, or (height, width, 3) for RGB."""
        pass

    def dtype(self) -> np.dtype:
        """Return NumPy dtype of the SLM image (e.g. uint8)."""
        pass

    def set_image(self, pixels: np.ndarray) -> None:
        """Load an image into the SLM (without displaying it yet)."""
        pass

    def display_image(self) -> None:
        """Display the currently loaded image."""
        pass

    def get_exposure(self) -> float:
        """Get exposure time in milliseconds."""
        pass

    def set_exposure(self, interval_ms: float) -> None:
        """Set exposure time in milliseconds."""
        pass
```

The core derives `getSLMWidth`, `getSLMHeight`, `getSLMNumberOfComponents` and `getSLMBytesPerPixel` from `shape()` and `dtype()`. To support SLM sequences, also override `get_sequence_max_length`, `send_sequence`, `start_sequence` and `stop_sequence`.

### Hub devices (`HubDevice`)

For a controller that has other devices attached to it. Override `get_installed_peripherals()` to return `(name, description)` pairs, where each `name` is the name of a device class importable from the same module as the hub:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import HubDevice


class MyHub(HubDevice):
    def get_installed_peripherals(self) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
        return [("MyZStage", "Focus drive"), ("MyShutter", "Shutter")]
```

### Generic devices (`GenericDevice`)

For devices that don't fit other categories but need property control:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import GenericDevice


class MyGenericDevice(GenericDevice):
    # Only basic Device methods needed - mainly for property-only devices
    pass
```

## Device properties

Properties are defined either on the class using the `@pymm_property` decorator, or dynamically at runtime using `Device.register_property`.

These two methods may be freely mixed, and accept largely the same arguments.

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import GenericDevice, pymm_property


class MyDevice(GenericDevice):
    _my_prop = 42

    @pymm_property(name="MyProp", default_value=42, limits=(0, 100))
    def my_prop(self) -> int:
        """MyProp property with limits 0-100 and default 42."""
        return self._my_prop

    @my_prop.setter
    def my_prop(self, value: int) -> None:
        self._my_prop = value
```

In many cases, you may not know ahead of device initialization which properties are supported. In this case, you can register properties at runtime in `initialize()`:

```python
from pymmcore_plus.experimental.unicore import GenericDevice


class MyDevice(GenericDevice):
    def initialize(self) -> None:
        cls = type(self)
        self.register_property(
            name="MyProp",
            getter=cls._get_my_prop,
            setter=cls._set_my_prop,
            default_value=42,
            limits=(0, 100),
        )

    def _set_my_prop(self, value: int) -> None: ...

    def _get_my_prop(self) -> int: ...
```

### Properties with constraints

Properties may have value constraints such as numerical limits or (categorical) allowed values:

```python
class MyStage(XYStageDevice):
    @pymm_property(limits=(0.0, 100.0))
    def speed(self) -> float:
        """Stage speed (0-100%)."""
        return self._speed

    @pymm_property(allowed_values=[1, 2, 4, 8])
    def step_size(self) -> int:
        """Step size multiplier."""
        return self._step_size
```

### Sequenceable properties

In order to declare a property as "sequenceable" (i.e. supporting hardware-synchronized parameter changes), you must:

1. Define a `sequence_max_length` of greater than zero.
2. Implement `sequence_loader` and `sequence_starter`, (and optionally `sequence_stopper`) methods.

```python
class MyDevice(GenericDevice):
    @pymm_property(sequence_max_length=100)
    def someprop(self) -> float:
        return self._someprop

    @someprop.setter
    def set_someprop(self, value: float) -> None:
        self._someprop = value

    @someprop.sequence_loader
    def load_someprop_sequence(self, sequence: list[float]) -> None:
        """Load a sequence of someprop values into hardware."""

    @someprop.sequence_starter
    def start_someprop_sequence(self) -> None:
        """Tell hardware to start the sequence."""

    @someprop.sequence_stopper  # optional
    def stop_someprop_sequence(self) -> None:
        """Tell hardware to stop the sequence."""
```

```python
class MyDevice(GenericDevice):
    def initialize(self) -> None:
        cls = type(self)
        self.register_property(
            name="someprop",
            getter=cls._get_someprop,
            setter=cls._set_someprop,
            sequence_loader=cls.load_someprop_sequence,
            sequence_starter=cls.start_someprop_sequence,
            sequence_stopper=cls.stop_someprop_sequence,
            sequence_max_length=100,
            default_value=10.0,
            limits=(0.1, 10000.0),
        )

    def _get_someprop(self) -> float:
        return self._someprop

    def _set_someprop(self, value: float) -> None:
        self._someprop = value

    def load_someprop_sequence(self, sequence: list[float]) -> None:
        """Load a sequence of someprop values into hardware."""

    def start_someprop_sequence(self) -> None:
        """Tell hardware to start the sequence."""

    def stop_someprop_sequence(self) -> None:
        """Tell hardware to stop the sequence."""
```

### Property types and validation

Properties are automatically typed based on their return annotations, but you can be explicit:

```python
class MyDevice(GenericDevice):
    @pymm_property(property_type=str)
    def serial_number(self) -> str:
        return "12345"

    @pymm_property(property_type=int, limits=(1, 1000))
    def gain(self) -> int:
        return self._gain
```

## Device lifecycle

All Python devices follow this lifecycle:

### 1\. Creation and loading

```python
# Create device instance
device = MyCamera()

# Load into core with a label
core.loadPyDevice("Camera1", device)
```

### 2\. Initialization

```python
# Initialize the device (calls device.initialize())
core.initializeDevice("Camera1")
```

Override `initialize()` for device-specific setup:

```python
class MyCamera(CameraDevice):
    def initialize(self) -> None:
        """Called when device is initialized."""
        # Setup hardware connections, configure device, etc.
        self.connect_to_hardware()
        super().initialize()  # Call parent if needed
```

### 3\. Usage

Once loaded and initialized, use the device through the standard CMMCore API:

```python
# Set as current device
core.setCameraDevice("Camera1")

# Use standard API
core.setExposure(50)
image = core.snap()
```

### 4\. Shutdown

```python
# Shutdown specific device
core.unloadDevice("Camera1")

# Or shutdown all devices
core.unloadAllDevices()
```

Override `shutdown()` for cleanup:

```python
class MyCamera(CameraDevice):
    def shutdown(self) -> None:
        """Called when device is unloaded."""
        self.disconnect_from_hardware()
        super().shutdown()
```

## Thread safety

When the core calls into a Python device, it does so with the device locked, so those calls don't run concurrently.

If you need manual locking:

```python
device = MyCamera()
core.loadPyDevice("Camera", device)

# Manual locking
with device:
    # Device is locked for this block
    device.some_internal_method()
```

## Events and metadata

You can connect to the [events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>) of a `UniMMCore` as usual, but note that it doesn't (yet) emit `propertyChanged` when you set a property on a Python device, or `exposureChanged` for a Python camera (state devices are the exception). Until it does, a device can emit events itself, through its `core` attribute:

```python
class MyDevice(GenericDevice):
    _level = 1

    @pymm_property(limits=(0, 10))
    def level(self) -> int:
        return self._level

    @level.setter
    def level(self, value: int) -> None:
        self._level = value
        self.core.events.propertyChanged.emit(self.get_label(), "level", str(value))
```

(Please open an issue if this matters for your device.)

Sequence acquisitions include metadata just as C++ camera adapters do:

```python
core.startSequenceAcquisition(10, 0, True)
while core.isSequenceRunning() or core.getRemainingImageCount():
    if core.getRemainingImageCount():
        img, metadata = core.popNextImageAndMD()
        print(f"Image {metadata['ImageNumber']}: {metadata['ElapsedTime-ms']} ms")
```

(The metadata contains the standard keys, like `ImageNumber`, `ElapsedTime-ms`, `Camera`, `Width` and `Height`, plus whatever your `start_sequence` yielded.)

## Error handling

Exceptions raised in Python devices propagate to the caller:

```python
class MyCamera(CameraDevice):
    def set_exposure(self, exposure: float) -> None:
        if exposure < 0:
            raise ValueError("Exposure must be positive")
        if exposure > 10000:
            raise ValueError("Exposure too long")
        self._exposure = exposure
```

```python
core.setExposure(-5)  # raises ValueError: Exposure must be positive
```

## Python devices in config files

`UniMMCore` can load and save Python devices in regular Micro-Manager `.cfg` files. Python device lines are prefixed with `#py`, so a regular `CMMCorePlus` (or Micro-Manager itself) reads them as comments and ignores them:

```text
# C++ devices
Device,Camera,DemoCamera,DCam

# Python devices: pyDevice,<label>,<module>,<class>
#py pyDevice,PyCamera,my_devices,MyCamera
#py Property,Core,Camera,PyCamera
```

The module must be importable (e.g. installed, or on `sys.path`) when the file is loaded with `core.loadSystemConfiguration("my.cfg")`. To write the current state (C++ and Python devices) to a file, use `core.saveSystemConfiguration("my.cfg")`. Pass `prefix_py_devices=False` to write the Python lines without the `#py` prefix (the file can then only be loaded by `UniMMCore`).

## Complete examples

For complete working examples, see these scripts in the [`examples/`](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/tree/main/examples>) folder of the repository:

- [`unicore_camera.py`](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/blob/main/examples/unicore_camera.py>): a synthetic camera with temporal patterns
- [`unicore_hamamatsu.py`](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/blob/main/examples/unicore_hamamatsu.py>): a real Hamamatsu camera
- [`unicore.py`](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/blob/main/examples/unicore.py>): a basic XY stage with properties

# Building Sequences

For most standard multi-dimensional experiments, you will want to use `useq.MDASequence` to construct your sequence of events. It allows you to declare a "plan" for each axis in your experiment (channels, time, z, etc...) along with the order in which the axes should be iterated. Iterating over the sequence yields `useq.MDAEvent` objects (usually one per image), so `list(sequence)` shows you which events an acquisition engine will be asked to run.

A sequence is just data, so you can build and inspect the examples on this page without a microscope. To *run* a sequence, see [The Acquisition Engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>).

## Axes and plans

Each axis has a field on `MDASequence`, and a one-letter key that is used in `axis_order` and in the `index` of each event:

| key | field | describes | reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `t` | `time_plan` | time points (interval, duration, number of loops, or several phases) | [time plans](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/#time-plans>) |
| `p` | `stage_positions` | a list of stage positions (or a well plate) | `Position`, [well plates](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/#well-plates>) |
| `g` | `grid_plan` | a grid (or random points) at each position | [grid plans](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/#grid-plans>) |
| `c` | `channels` | a list of channel presets, each with an optional exposure | `Channel` |
| `z` | `z_plan` | a z-stack | [z plans](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/#z-plans>) |

`axis_order` (default `"tpgcz"`) says how the axes are nested (the "fastest" axes come last). There are also a few fields that aren't axes, such as `autofocus_plan` ([hardware autofocus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/hardware_autofocus/index.md>)), `keep_shutter_open_across`, `setup`, and `metadata`. See the [`MDASequence` reference](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/index.md>) for all of them.

Let's look at how `MDASequence` can be used to create a few common experiments.

## A two-channel time series

```python
from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 6},  # (1)!
    channels=[
        {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50},
        {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 80},
    ],
)
```

1. 6 time points, 2 seconds apart. See also, [additional time plans](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/#time-plans>).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **output of `list(mda_sequence)`**
>
> `min_start_time` is the time (in seconds) at which the event should start. `reset_event_timer=True` on the first event tells the engine to (re)start the clock that `min_start_time` is measured from.
>
> ```python
> [
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="DAPI"),
>         exposure=50.0,
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>         reset_event_timer=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         exposure=80.0,
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 1, "c": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="DAPI"),
>         exposure=50.0,
>         min_start_time=2.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 1, "c": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         exposure=80.0,
>         min_start_time=2.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 2, "c": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="DAPI"),
>         exposure=50.0,
>         min_start_time=4.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 2, "c": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         exposure=80.0,
>         min_start_time=4.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 3, "c": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="DAPI"),
>         exposure=50.0,
>         min_start_time=6.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 3, "c": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         exposure=80.0,
>         min_start_time=6.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 4, "c": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="DAPI"),
>         exposure=50.0,
>         min_start_time=8.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 4, "c": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         exposure=80.0,
>         min_start_time=8.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 5, "c": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="DAPI"),
>         exposure=50.0,
>         min_start_time=10.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 5, "c": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         exposure=80.0,
>         min_start_time=10.0,
>     ),
> ]
> ```

## A z-stack at three positions

```python
from useq import MDASequence, Position

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},  # (1)!
    stage_positions=[  # (2)!
        (10, 10, 20),
        {"x": 30, "y": 40, "z": 50},
        Position(x=60, y=70, z=80),
    ],
)
```

1. A 4-micron z-stack with 0.5 micron steps, centered on each position's `z`. See also, [additional z plans](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/#z-plans>).
2. These are all valid ways to specify a stage position. None of `x`, `y`, or `z` are required.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **output of `list(mda_sequence)`**
>
> ```python
> [
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 0}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=18.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 1}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=18.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 2}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=19.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 3}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=19.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 4}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=20.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 5}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=20.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 6}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=21.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 7}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=21.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "z": 8}, x_pos=10.0, y_pos=10.0, z_pos=22.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 0}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=48.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 1}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=48.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 2}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=49.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 3}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=49.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 4}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=50.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 5}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=50.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 6}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=51.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 7}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=51.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 1, "z": 8}, x_pos=30.0, y_pos=40.0, z_pos=52.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 0}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=78.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 1}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=78.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 2}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=79.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 3}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=79.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 4}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=80.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 5}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=80.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 6}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=81.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 7}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=81.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 2, "z": 8}, x_pos=60.0, y_pos=70.0, z_pos=82.0),
> ]
> ```

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Relative to *what*?**
>
