> Most z plans (`range`, `above`/`below`, relative positions) and grid plans (`rows`/`columns`, `width`/`height`, random points) are *relative*: they are added to the `z` (or `x`/`y`) of each stage position. If a position doesn't specify `z`, or there are no `stage_positions` at all, a relative z plan is centered on **z = 0**, *not* on the current focus position:
>
> ```python
> >>> [e.z_pos for e in MDASequence(z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1})]
> [-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]
> ```
>
> (A relative grid with no `x`/`y` is likewise centered on x = y = 0.) On a real microscope, that may send the objective somewhere you didn't expect. So when you want a z-stack "around where I am now", put the current position in the sequence, e.g. with pymmcore-plus:
>
> ```python
> MDASequence(
>     z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1},
>     stage_positions=[Position(z=core.getZPosition())],
> )
> ```
>
> (Absolute plans, like `ZTopBottom` or `ZAbsolutePositions`, aren't affected.)

## A grid of z-stacks

Here we use `axis_order` to declare that we want the full z-stack to happen at each `(row, col)` before moving to the next position in the grid.

```python
from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[{"x": 100, "y": 200, "z": 300}],
    grid_plan={"fov_width": 20, "fov_height": 10, "rows": 2, "columns": 2},
    z_plan={"range": 10, "step": 2.5},
    axis_order="pgz",  # (1)!
)
```

1. The "fastest" axes come last. By putting `z` after `g` in the `axis_order`, we're saying "at each `g`, do a full `z` iteration".

> [!NOTE]
>
> **output of `list(mda_sequence)`**
>
> ```python
> [
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 0, "z": 0}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=295.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 0, "z": 1}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=297.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 0, "z": 2}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=300.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 0, "z": 3}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=302.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 0, "z": 4}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=305.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 1, "z": 0}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=295.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 1, "z": 1}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=297.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 1, "z": 2}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=300.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 1, "z": 3}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=302.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 1, "z": 4}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=205.0, z_pos=305.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 2, "z": 0}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=295.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 2, "z": 1}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=297.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 2, "z": 2}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=300.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 2, "z": 3}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=302.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 2, "z": 4}, x_pos=110.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=305.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 3, "z": 0}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=295.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 3, "z": 1}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=297.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 3, "z": 2}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=300.0),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 3, "z": 3}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=302.5),
>     MDAEvent(index={"p": 0, "g": 3, "z": 4}, x_pos=90.0, y_pos=195.0, z_pos=305.0),
> ]
> ```

> [!TIP]
>
> You can usually leave out `fov_width` and `fov_height`. pymmcore-plus fills them in from the camera ROI and pixel size when the acquisition starts.

## Skipping timepoints or z-stacks

The `Channel` field has a few tricks, such as skipping timepoints or z-stacks for specific channels. Here we take a fast z-stack (leaving the shutter open) in the `FITC` channel only, and a single image in the `DIC` channel every 3 timepoints:

```python
from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    z_plan={"range": 10, "step": 2.5},  # (1)!
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 6},
    channels=[
        "FITC",
        {"config": "DIC", "acquire_every": 3, "do_stack": False},
    ],
    keep_shutter_open_across=["z"],
)
```

1. There are no stage positions here, so the stack is centered on z = 0 (see [above](<#a-z-stack-at-three-positions>)).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **output of `list(mda_sequence)` (first two timepoints)**
>
> ```python
> [
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 0, "z": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>         z_pos=-5.0,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>         reset_event_timer=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 0, "z": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>         z_pos=-2.5,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 0, "z": 2},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>         z_pos=0.0,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 0, "z": 3},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>         z_pos=2.5,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 0, "z": 4},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>         z_pos=5.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 0, "c": 1, "z": 2},
>         channel=Channel(config="DIC"),
>         min_start_time=0.0,
>         z_pos=0.0,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 1, "c": 0, "z": 0},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=2.0,
>         z_pos=-5.0,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 1, "c": 0, "z": 1},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=2.0,
>         z_pos=-2.5,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 1, "c": 0, "z": 2},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=2.0,
>         z_pos=0.0,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 1, "c": 0, "z": 3},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=2.0,
>         z_pos=2.5,
>         keep_shutter_open=True,
>     ),
>     MDAEvent(
>         index={"t": 1, "c": 0, "z": 4},
>         channel=Channel(config="FITC"),
>         min_start_time=2.0,
>         z_pos=5.0,
>     ),
>     # ... t=2 is like t=1, then t=3 has DIC again (like t=0), etc...
> ]
> ```

## Different plans at different positions

A stage position may carry its own `sequence`, whose plans replace the global ones at that position (any plan it doesn't set comes from the main sequence). Here, the second position gets a different z-stack:

```python
from useq import MDASequence

mda_sequence = MDASequence(
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 1},
    stage_positions=[
        {"x": 0, "y": 0, "z": 10},
        {
            "name": "Cell 1",
            "x": 100,
            "y": 50,
            "z": 12,
            "sequence": {"z_plan": {"above": 2, "below": 0, "step": 0.5}},
        },
    ],
)

for event in mda_sequence:
    print(event.index, event.pos_name, event.z_pos)
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> **output**
>
> ```text
> {'p': 0, 'z': 0} None 8.0
> {'p': 0, 'z': 1} None 9.0
> {'p': 0, 'z': 2} None 10.0
> {'p': 0, 'z': 3} None 11.0
> {'p': 0, 'z': 4} None 12.0
> {'p': 1, 'z': 0} Cell 1 12.0
> {'p': 1, 'z': 1} Cell 1 12.5
> {'p': 1, 'z': 2} Cell 1 13.0
> {'p': 1, 'z': 3} Cell 1 13.5
> {'p': 1, 'z': 4} Cell 1 14.0
> ```

> [!NOTE]
>
> pymmcore-plus can't yet save a sequence like this one as a multi-dimensional array (the positions don't share one shape), so it writes the frames as a [flat stack](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/#lists-and-generators-are-saved-as-a-flat-stack>). A sub-sequence that only adds a `grid_plan` is fine.

## A note on syntax

If you prefer, you can use `useq` objects rather than `dicts` for all of these fields. This has the advantage of providing type-checking and auto-completion in your IDE.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Example**
>
> The following two sequences are equivalent:
>
> ```python
> import useq
>
> mda_sequence1 = useq.MDASequence(
>     time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 10},
>     z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
>     channels=[
>         {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50},
>         {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 80},
>     ],
> )
>
> mda_sequence2 = useq.MDASequence(
>     time_plan=useq.TIntervalLoops(interval=2, loops=10),
>     z_plan=useq.ZRangeAround(range=4, step=0.5),
>     channels=[
>         useq.Channel(config="DAPI", exposure=50),
>         useq.Channel(config="FITC", exposure=80),
>     ],
> )
>
> assert mda_sequence1 == mda_sequence2
> ```

## Saving and loading sequences

`MDASequence` objects can be serialized and deserialized to and from JSON or YAML, making it easy to save and load them from file:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import useq

mda_sequence = useq.MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[(100, 100, 30)],
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 10},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    channels=[
        {"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 50, "do_stack": False},
        {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 20},
    ],
    axis_order="tpcz",
)

Path("mda_sequence.yaml").write_text(mda_sequence.yaml())
```

... results in:

mda\_sequence.yaml

```yaml
axis_order:
- t
- p
- c
- z
channels:
- config: DAPI
  do_stack: false
  exposure: 50.0
- config: FITC
  exposure: 20.0
stage_positions:
- x: 100.0
  y: 100.0
  z: 30.0
time_plan:
  interval: 2.0
  loops: 10
z_plan:
  range: 4.0
  step: 0.5
```

... which can be loaded back into an `MDASequence` object:

```python
mda_sequence = useq.MDASequence.from_file("mda_sequence.yaml")
```

For JSON, use `mda_sequence.model_dump_json(exclude_unset=True)` to write and the same `from_file` (with a `.json` extension) to read. Only the fields you set are written, so the files stay short and readable. The [overview](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/#serialization-and-deserialization>) has a larger example file, with multi-phase time plans and per-position z-stacks.

## Next steps

Once you have a sequence, you'll probably want to run it:

- [The Acquisition Engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>) runs an `MDASequence` (or any iterable of `MDAEvent`) on a Micro-Manager-controlled microscope, and [Saving Data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>) shows how to write the images to OME-Zarr or OME-TIFF.
- The [`MDASequence`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/index.md>), [`MDAEvent`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/event/index.md>) and [axes](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/index.md>) reference pages describe every field.

# Qt Integration

`pymmcore-plus` is designed to integrate with Qt GUIs. (For complete Qt applications built on it, see [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>), and the widgets in [pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>).) It accomplishes this in two ways:

1. `CMMCorePlus.run_mda` runs in a thread in order to not block the event loop.
2. The [`events`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>) objects (`core.events` and `core.mda.events`) use Qt signals instead of signals from the [psygnal](<https://github.com/pyapp-kit/psygnal>) library when a Qt application is running. A Qt signal emitted in another thread is delivered in the main thread (to callbacks connected from the main thread), which keeps things from crashing when your callbacks update the GUI.

The examples on this page require qtpy, superqt and a Qt backend installed in the environment (all of which come with `pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]"`):

```bash
pip install qtpy superqt PyQt6  # or PySide6
```

## Create the QApplication first

Whether `CMMCorePlus` uses Qt signals or psygnal is decided once, when the core is created. It uses Qt signals if a `QApplication` exists at that moment, and psygnal otherwise. So **create the `QApplication` before the `CMMCorePlus`** (and that includes the first call to `CMMCorePlus.instance()`, which is what creates the global core):

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

app = QApplication([])
core = CMMCorePlus.instance()

print(type(core.events).__name__)  # QCoreSignaler
```

If the core comes first, `core.events` is a psygnal `CMMCoreSignaler`, and the callbacks connected to `core.mda.events` (`frameReady`, `sequenceFinished`, etc...) run in the acquisition thread. Qt widgets may only be touched from the main thread, so updating the GUI from one of those callbacks can crash the application, or make it misbehave in less obvious ways. (The events guide has more on [which thread runs your callbacks](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/#threads>).)

You can also choose the backend with the `PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND` environment variable (`qt`, `psygnal` or `auto`; see [Environment variables](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/env_var/index.md>)). Importing `pymmcore_widgets` sets it to `qt` (unless you've set it yourself), so in a GUI built from the widgets the order matters less. But creating the application first is a good habit.

## Avoiding blocking the Qt event loop

If you make a blocking call on the thread running the Qt event loop then your GUI will become unresponsive. The recommended way to avoid this is to use threads to call blocking methods like `snapImage` yourself, and let pymmcore-plus handle the threading when you use `run_mda`.

The simple application below consists of a counter that increments so long as the event loop is not blocked, and two buttons that call the `snapImage` method (with a 5 second exposure). One button calls it from a thread, and the counter continues; the other blocks, and the counter stops. Things to notice in the code below:

1. Create the `QApplication` before the core.
2. Use `CMMCorePlus.instance()` to create the core object. This allows another script (or widget) in the same process to use the same object.
3. Use a thread for blocking operations like `snapImage`.

```python
import sys

from qtpy.QtCore import QTimer
from qtpy.QtWidgets import (
    QApplication,
    QLabel,
    QMainWindow,
    QPushButton,
    QVBoxLayout,
    QWidget,
)
from superqt.utils import create_worker

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus


class MainWindow(QMainWindow):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()
        self.mmc.loadSystemConfiguration()
        self.mmc.setExposure(5000)  # 5 seconds

        self.counter = 0

        layout = QVBoxLayout()

        self.l = QLabel("Start")
        b_blocking = QPushButton("Snap blocking")
        b_threaded = QPushButton("Snap threaded")
        b_blocking.pressed.connect(self.snap_blocking)
        b_threaded.pressed.connect(self.snap_threaded)

        layout.addWidget(self.l)
        layout.addWidget(b_blocking)
        layout.addWidget(b_threaded)

        w = QWidget()
        w.setLayout(layout)
        self.setCentralWidget(w)
        self.show()

        self.timer = QTimer()
        self.timer.setInterval(1000)
        self.timer.timeout.connect(self._recurring_timer)
        self.timer.start()

    def _recurring_timer(self):
        self.counter += 1
        self.l.setText("Counter: %d" % self.counter)

    def snap_threaded(self):
        # alternatively you could use the python threading module
        # or directly use QThreads
        create_worker(
            self.mmc.snapImage,
            _start_thread=True,
        )

    def snap_blocking(self):
        self.mmc.snapImage()


app = QApplication(sys.argv)  # the app first...
window = MainWindow()  # ... then the core (created in MainWindow.__init__)
app.exec()
```

## Running an acquisition from a Qt application

`run_mda` starts the acquisition in another thread and returns immediately, so you can call it right before starting the event loop (or from a button). Because the `QApplication` exists before the core, the `frameReady` callback below runs in the main thread, where it would be safe to update a widget with the new image. The STOP button cancels the acquisition:

examples/qt\_integration.py

```python
"""
An example of integrating a MMCore object into an event loop.

This example requires qtpy and a Qt backend installed in the env:
```

pip install qtpy PyQt6 \# or PySide6

```text
"""

import numpy as np
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QPushButton
from useq import MDAEvent, MDASequence

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

# create the QApplication *before* the core, so that the core uses Qt signals
app = QApplication([])
mmcore = CMMCorePlus.instance()

# button for early stopping
stop = QPushButton("STOP")


def stop_clicked():
    mmcore.mda.cancel()
    app.quit()


stop.clicked.connect(stop_clicked)
stop.show()


@mmcore.mda.events.frameReady.connect
def on_frame(image: np.ndarray, event: MDAEvent):
    # with Qt signals, this runs in the main thread (not the acquisition thread),
    # so it's safe to update widgets from here
    print(
        f"received frame: {image.shape}, {image.dtype} "
        f"@ index {event.index}, z={event.z_pos}"
    )


@mmcore.events.propertyChanged.connect
def prop_changed(device, prop, value):
    print(f"{device}.{prop} changed to {value!r}")


# setup some callbacks
mmcore.events.systemConfigurationLoaded.connect(lambda: print("config loaded!"))
mmcore.mda.events.sequenceFinished.connect(app.quit)

# load config and start an experiment
mmcore.loadSystemConfiguration()

# see https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/useq-schema
x, y = mmcore.getXYPosition()
sequence = MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI", {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 50}],
    time_plan={"interval": 1.5, "loops": 5},
    # a relative z plan is relative to the stage position, so give it the current one
    stage_positions=[(x, y, mmcore.getZPosition())],
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    axis_order="tpcz",
)

mmcore.run_mda(sequence)  # runs in another thread, and returns immediately

# start the qt event loop
app.exec()
```

# Pycro-Manager-Style API

If you have been using Pycro-Manager and are familiar with its API, the following example may be useful to see what a Pycro-Manager-like API would look like implemented on the pymmcore-plus engine. It converts Pycro-Manager's event dicts to `useq.MDAEvent` objects, and most of its acquisition hooks to methods of a custom `MDAEngine` subclass (see [Custom Acquisition Engines](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/custom_engine/index.md>)).

> [!WARNING]
>
> This is not presented as a "suggestion", but rather as an educational example. If you are considering pymmcore-plus for a pure-python acquisition workflow, consider using the `pymmcore` and `pymmcore-plus` APIs directly.

pycro-api.py

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import inspect
from queue import Queue
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any, cast

from useq import MDAEvent

from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from pymmcore_plus.mda import MDAEngine

# These types represent what the pycro-manager API expects.
if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from collections import deque
    from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator, Sequence
    from typing import TypeAlias

    from numpy.typing import NDArray

    from pymmcore_plus.mda._protocol import PImagePayload

    Meta: TypeAlias = dict[str, Any]
    PycroEvent: TypeAlias = dict[str, Any]

    # Acquisition Hooks
    EventQueue = Queue[PycroEvent | None]
    EventHook = Callable[[PycroEvent], PycroEvent | None]
    EventQueueHook = Callable[[PycroEvent, EventQueue], PycroEvent | None]
    AcquisitionHook = EventHook | EventQueueHook

    # Processor Hooks
    ImgHookReturn = tuple[NDArray, Meta] | Sequence[tuple[NDArray, Meta]] | None
    ImgMetaHook = Callable[[NDArray, Meta], ImgHookReturn]
    ImgMetaQueueHook = Callable[[NDArray, Meta, EventQueue], ImgHookReturn]
    ProcessorHook = ImgMetaHook | ImgMetaQueueHook


class Acquisition:
    """Pycro-Manager -> pymmcore-plus adaptor.

    This doesn't re-implement file saving, but it gives you an example of how
    pycromanager hooks would be converted to pymmcore-plus.

    See `__main__` below for example usage.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        image_process_fn: ProcessorHook | None = None,
        event_generation_hook_fn: AcquisitionHook | None = None,
        pre_hardware_hook_fn: AcquisitionHook | None = None,
        post_hardware_hook_fn: AcquisitionHook | None = None,
        post_camera_hook_fn: AcquisitionHook | None = None,
    ):
        self._core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
        self._event_queue: EventQueue = Queue()
        self._event_generation_hook_fn = event_generation_hook_fn
        self._engine_cls = _build_engine(
            self._event_queue,
            pre_hardware_hook_fn,
            post_hardware_hook_fn,
            post_camera_hook_fn,
        )
        self._engine = self._engine_cls(self._core)
        self._core.mda.set_engine(self._engine)

        # see the "Event-Driven Acquisition" guide in the pymmcore-plus docs
        self._thread = self._core.run_mda(self._iter_events())

        # we can use `mda.events.frameReady` for the image_process hooks
        self._image_process_fn = image_process_fn
        if image_process_fn is not None:
            sig = inspect.signature(image_process_fn)
            if len(sig.parameters) == 2:
                self._core.mda.events.frameReady.connect(self._call_img_hook_2arg)
            elif len(sig.parameters) == 3:
                self._core.mda.events.frameReady.connect(self._call_img_hook_3arg)
            else:
                raise ValueError(f"Invalid image processing hook: {sig}")

    def acquire(self, event_or_events: PycroEvent | list[PycroEvent]) -> None:
        if isinstance(event_or_events, list):
            for event in event_or_events:
                self._event_queue.put(event)
        else:
            self._event_queue.put(event_or_events)

    def abort(self, exception: BaseException | None = None) -> None:
        self._core.mda.cancel()
        cast("deque", self._event_queue.queue).clear()

    def await_completion(self) -> None:
        self._thread.join()

    def mark_finished(self) -> None:
        self._event_queue.put(None)

    def _iter_events(self) -> Iterator[MDAEvent]:
        """Convert pycro-manager events from the queue into MDAEvents."""
        for pycro_event in iter(self._event_queue.get, None):
            hook = self._event_generation_hook_fn
            event = _call_acq_hook(hook, pycro_event, self._event_queue)
            if event is not None:
                yield _pycro_to_mda_event(event)

    def _call_img_hook_2arg(self, img: NDArray, event: MDAEvent) -> None:
        """Call a 2-argument image processing hook."""
        hook = cast("ImgMetaHook", self._image_process_fn)
        hook(img, {})  # todo: meta

    def _call_img_hook_3arg(self, img: NDArray, event: MDAEvent) -> None:
        """Call a 3-argument image processing hook."""
        hook = cast("ImgMetaQueueHook", self._image_process_fn)
        hook(img, {}, self._event_queue)  # todo: meta

    def __enter__(self) -> Acquisition:
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *args: Any) -> None:
        self.mark_finished()
        self.await_completion()


# note, this could be improved:
# we don't need to check signature every time...
def _call_acq_hook(
    hook: AcquisitionHook | None, event: PycroEvent, queue: EventQueue
) -> PycroEvent | None:
    if hook is None:
        return event

    sig = inspect.signature(hook)
    if len(sig.parameters) == 1:
        return cast("EventHook", hook)(event)
    elif len(sig.parameters) == 2:
        return cast("EventQueueHook", hook)(event, queue)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid signature for acquisition hook: {sig}")


PYCRO_KEY = "pycro_event"  # where we store the pycro event in the mda event
SKIP = "pycro_skip"  # if we should skip this event


def _build_engine(
    event_queue: EventQueue,
    pre_hardware_hook_fn: AcquisitionHook | None = None,
    post_hardware_hook_fn: AcquisitionHook | None = None,
    post_camera_hook_fn: AcquisitionHook | None = None,
) -> type[MDAEngine]:
    """Convert pycromanager hooks to a pymmcore-plus style MDAEngine subclass."""

    class PycroEngine(MDAEngine):
        def setup_event(self, event: MDAEvent) -> None:
            pyc_event = event.metadata[PYCRO_KEY]
            if pre_hardware_hook_fn is not None:
                pyc_event = _call_acq_hook(pre_hardware_hook_fn, pyc_event, event_queue)
                if pyc_event is None:
                    event.metadata[SKIP] = True
                    return
                event = _pycro_to_mda_event(pyc_event)

            super().setup_event(event)
            pyc_event = _call_acq_hook(post_hardware_hook_fn, pyc_event, event_queue)
            if pyc_event is None:
                event.metadata[SKIP] = True

        def exec_event(self, event: MDAEvent) -> Iterable[PImagePayload | None]:
            if event.metadata.get(SKIP):
                return ()

            result = super().exec_event(event)
            _call_acq_hook(post_camera_hook_fn, event.metadata[PYCRO_KEY], event_queue)
            return result

    return PycroEngine


def _pycro_to_mda_event(pycro_event: PycroEvent) -> MDAEvent:
    # This is rough estimation... ideally, useq-schema would be used directly,
    # and the need to convert pycro-manager events to MDAEvents would be eliminated.

    # TODO: convert row/col to useq grid plan
    index = {
        k[0]: v
        for k, v in pycro_event["axes"].items()
        if k in ["z", "time", "position"]
        # TODO: convert channel str to index integer
    }
    if cfg := pycro_event.get("config_group", []):
        channel = {"group": cfg[0], "config": cfg[1]}
    else:
        channel = None

    return MDAEvent(
        index=index,
        channel=channel,
        x_pos=pycro_event.get("x"),
        y_pos=pycro_event.get("y"),
        z_pos=pycro_event.get("z"),
        exposure=pycro_event.get("exposure"),
        keep_shutter_open=pycro_event.get("keep_shutter_open", False),
        min_start_time=pycro_event.get("min_start_time"),
        properties=[tuple(prop) for prop in pycro_event.get("properties", [])],
        metadata={PYCRO_KEY: pycro_event},  # store original event
    )


# Example usage:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from pycromanager import multi_d_acquisition_events

    core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
    core.loadSystemConfiguration()

    with Acquisition() as acq:
        # the pymmcore-plus equivalent here is to use MDASequence
        # (see "The Acquisition Engine" guide in the pymmcore-plus docs)
        events = multi_d_acquisition_events(
            num_time_points=4,
            time_interval_s=2,
            channel_group="Channel",
            channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
            z_start=0,
            z_end=6,
            z_step=0.4,
            order="tcz",
        )
        acq.acquire(events)
```

# Troubleshooting

## Micro-Manager directory not found

```sh
pymmcore-plus - ERROR - (_discovery.py:256) Could not find a compatible Micro-Manager installation for the device interface required by pymmcore 75.

Discovered installations:

Please run 'mmcore install'.
```

... usually followed, when you call `loadSystemConfiguration()`, by:

```sh
FileNotFoundError: Path does not exist: MMConfig_demo.cfg
```

If you tried to create a `pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus` instance and got an error similar to the one above, it means that pymmcore-plus was unable to find a Micro-Manager installation on your system whose device interface version matches your version of `pymmcore`. Please run `mmcore install` to install the latest compatible version of Micro-Manager. You can run `mmcore list` to see which installations were found (and which of them are incompatible).

See the [installation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/#installing-micro-manager-device-adapters>) section for more details.

## Incompatible device interface version

```sh
OSError: Line 7: Device,DHub,DemoCamera,DHub
Failed to load device adapter "DemoCamera" from "/Users/user/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm/Micro-Manager-74.20260129/libmmgr_dal_DemoCamera" [ Incompatible device interface version (MMCore requires 75; device adapter has 74) ]
```

If you create a `pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus` instance and you get an error similar to the one above when trying to load a Micro-Manager configuration file, the device adapters that pymmcore-plus is using were built for a different device interface version than your `pymmcore`. This usually means that `MICROMANAGER_PATH` (or the `mm_path` you passed to `CMMCorePlus`) points to an older (or newer) installation. Either point it at a compatible installation, or **update** your Micro-Manager device adapters (for example by running: `mmcore install`).

See [understanding device interface versions](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/#understanding-device-interface-versions>) for more details.

## Slow performance

If you are experiencing slow performance with pymmcore-plus, you can profile your code to identify bottlenecks. See the [profiling](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/profiling/index.md>) section for more details. If you identify a specific issue, or have a question regarding the interpretation of the profiling results, please [open an issue](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/issues/new>) and attach the profiling results if possible.

## Something else?

Turning up the [log level](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/logging/index.md>) (`PYMM_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`) often shows what pymmcore-plus was doing when things went wrong, and `mmcore logs` shows the log file. If you're still stuck, please [open an issue](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/issues/new>) and include the output of `mmcore info`.

# Troubleshooting Qt and Widgets

For problems with the core itself (finding Micro-Manager, loading device adapters), see [Troubleshooting](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/troubleshooting/index.md>) for pymmcore-plus.

## No Qt bindings

```sh
qtpy.QtBindingsNotFoundError: No Qt bindings could be found
```

If you get an error similar to the one above, it means that you did not install one of the necessary [PyQt](<https://riverbankcomputing.com/software/pyqt/>) or [PySide](<https://www.qt.io/qt-for-python>) libraries. Install `pymmcore-widgets` with an extra that brings one along:

```sh
pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]"  # or "pymmcore-widgets[PySide6]"
```

See [Installing a Qt backend](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/#installing-a-qt-backend>) for how to choose.

## "no matches found" when installing

```sh
zsh: no matches found: pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]
```

zsh (the default shell on macOS) treats the square brackets as a file pattern. Put quotes around the package name: `pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]"`.

## Must construct a QApplication

```text
QWidget: Must construct a QApplication before a QWidget
```

... followed by Python crashing. Every Qt program needs a `QApplication`, and it must exist before you create any widget. Create it first thing (and create it *before* the `CMMCorePlus`, too, for the reasons explained in [Qt integration](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/integration-with-qt/#create-the-qapplication-first>)):

```python
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

app = QApplication([])
# ... now create the core and the widgets
app.exec()
```

## The widgets don't follow my script

If you change something from your own code (`core.setExposure(50)`, say) and a widget doesn't update, the widget is probably connected to a different core. Widgets use the global `CMMCorePlus.instance()` unless you pass `mmcore=`, so a core you created with `CMMCorePlus()` is a separate object, with its own devices and its own events. Either use `CMMCorePlus.instance()` in your script, or pass your core to each widget: `ExposureWidget(mmcore=my_core)`.

Also check that the widget uses a core at all (the sequence editors, like `ChannelTable` and `ZPlanWidget`, don't). See [Choosing a core](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/#choosing-a-core>).

## The GUI freezes

Anything that blocks the main thread (the one running `app.exec()`) freezes the whole GUI until it returns: a long `core.snapImage()`, a slow stage move, a `time.sleep()` in a callback, etc... Run long operations in a thread instead. `CMMCorePlus.run_mda` already does this for you. See [Qt integration](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/integration-with-qt/index.md>) for an example.

Please [open an issue](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets/issues>) if you run into something that isn't covered here.

# Performance Profiling

This page covers a few tools for finding out where the time goes when you use pymmcore-plus. Every device behaves differently, so slowdowns depend a lot on your hardware and on what you're doing with it: measure on your own setup.

If you just want a quick look at how long common core and device calls take with your hardware, `mmcore bench` runs a short benchmark (with the demo configuration, or your own with `--config my.cfg`) and prints a table of timings.

## Profiling with py-spy

There are many tools available for profiling Python code. We recommend starting with [`py-spy`](<https://github.com/benfred/py-spy>). You can add it to your environment with `pip install py-spy`. For complete usage tips, see the [`py-spy` readme](<https://github.com/benfred/py-spy?tab=readme-ov-file#usage>), but here is a quick example of how to use it with pymmcore-plus:

### Example with python script

Create a Python script that uses pymmcore-plus to perform some operations, such as instantiating a CMMCorePlus object, loading a configuration, and performing some task such as running a multi-dimensional acquisition. Save this script somewhere (we'll call it `example.py`) and profile it with `py-spy`:

*Note: on macOS, py-spy requires sudo access*

```sh
sudo py-spy record -o profile.json -f speedscope -r 1000 -- python example.py
```

- the `-o profile.json` flag specifies the output file name
- the `-f speedscope` flag specifies the output format. Here, we use the `speedscope` format, which can be viewed in the [Speedscope](<https://www.speedscope.app/>) web viewer.
- the `-r 1000` flag specifies the sampling rate (in Hz). The default is 100 Hz, so if you want more detailed profiling, you can increase this number as we've done here.
- the `--` separates the `py-spy` arguments from the Python script to be profiled

### Example using `mmcore run`

If you are profiling a standard MDASequence acquisition, you can use the `mmcore run` command line tool to run the acquisition and profile it with `py-spy`. First, create a json/yaml file representing the MDASequence acquisition you want to run:

```python
from useq import MDASequence

seq = MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI", {"config": "FITC", "exposure": 1}],
    time_plan={"interval": 2, "loops": 5},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    axis_order="tpcz",
)
seq_json = seq.model_dump_json(exclude_unset=True)

with open("mda_seq.json", "w") as f:
    f.write(seq_json)
```

Then, run the acquisition with `mmcore run` and profile it with py-spy:

```sh
sudo py-spy record -o profile.json -f speedscope -r 1000 -- mmcore run mda_seq.json --config your_mm_config.cfg
```

- the `-o`, `-f`, `-r`, and `--` flags are the same as in the previous example
- the `mmcore run` command runs the acquisition specified in the json file (it doesn't save any data)
- the `--config` flag specifies the path to the MMCore configuration file defining your microscope.

### Example attaching to a running process

If you have a running Python process that you want to profile, you can attach `py-spy` to it using the `-p` flag:

```sh
sudo py-spy record -o profile.json -f speedscope -r 1000 -p <pid>
```

## Analyzing the profile

Once you have a profile, you can view it in the Speedscope web viewer.

Open [https://www.speedscope.app/](<https://www.speedscope.app/>) and drag the profile file into the window.

See the [Speedscope documentation](<https://github.com/jlfwong/speedscope#usage>) for more information. The "Sandwich" view is particularly useful for identifying slow functions and hot paths in your code:

Feel free to open an issue with your `profile.json` file if you need help interpreting the results.

# useq-schema

`useq-schema` (imported as `useq`) is an implementation-agnostic schema for describing a sequence of events during a multi-dimensional imaging acquisition: the time points, stage positions, channels, z-planes, etc... that you want to acquire. It describes *what* to do, and leaves it to an acquisition engine (such as the one in [pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>)) to actually do it.

The goal of useq-schema is to provide a **specification** (and some python utilities) for generating event objects that can be consumed by microscope acquisition engines. A *hope* is that this will encourage inter-operability between various efforts to drive automated image acquisition.

The schema *tries* to remain agnostic to the specific acquisition engine (though it was designed based on the capabilities of [Micro-Manager](<https://micro-manager.org>)). We welcome feedback from interested parties regarding limitations and/or potential extensions to the schema! Similarly, while the "ideal" schema will support arbitrary dimensions (i.e. more than the conventional position, time, channel, z, ...), it is also hard to avoid hard-coding some assumptions about dimensionality in certain places. Any and all feedback (even minor stuff, such as parameter naming, etc...) is welcome! Please [open an issue](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/useq-schema/issues/new>).

## A quick example

```python
from useq import MDASequence

mda_seq = MDASequence(
    stage_positions=[(100, 100, 30), (200, 150, 35)],
    channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
    time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 20},
    z_plan={"range": 4, "step": 0.5},
    axis_order="tpcz",
)
```

The `MDASequence` object is iterable, yielding `MDAEvent` objects in the order specified by the `axis_order` attribute:

```python
>>> mda_seq.sizes
{'t': 20, 'p': 2, 'c': 2, 'z': 9}
>>> events = list(mda_seq)
>>> len(events)
720
>>> events[1]
MDAEvent(index={'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1}, channel=Channel(config='DAPI'), min_start_time=0.0, x_pos=100.0, y_pos=100.0, z_pos=28.5)
```

[Building Sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>) walks through the common cases (time series, z-stacks, grids, skipping channels, etc...).

## Core schema

### `MDAEvent`

The primary "event" object is `useq.MDAEvent`. This describes a single event that a microscope should perform, including preparation of the hardware, and execution of the event (such as an image acquisition).

- For [Micro-Manager](<https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager>), this object is most similar (though not identical) to the events generated by [`generate-acq-sequence`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager/blob/2b0f51a2f916112d39c6135ad35a112065f8d58d/acqEngine/src/main/clj/org/micromanager/sequence_generator.clj#L410>) in the clojure acquisition engine that drives Micro-Manager's multi-dimensional acquisitions.
- For [Pycro-Manager](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pycro-manager>), this object is similar to an individual [acquisition event `dict`](<https://pycro-manager.readthedocs.io/en/latest/apis.html#acquisition-event-specification>) generated by [`multi_d_acquisition_events`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pycro-manager/blob/63cf209a8907fd23932ee9f8016cb6a2b61b45aa/pycromanager/acquire.py#L605>), (and, `useq.pycromanager` provides a `to_pycromanager` function that returns a dict following the pycro-manager event spec)

### `MDASequence`

`useq.MDASequence` represents a **sequence** of events, as might be generated by the multidimensional acquisition GUI in most microscope software. The Python `MDASequence` object is itself [iterable](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/#how-sequences-are-iterated>), and yields `useq.MDAEvent` objects.

- For [Micro-Manager](<https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager>), this object is most similar to [`org.micromanager.acquisition.SequenceSettings`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager/blob/2b0f51a2f916112d39c6135ad35a112065f8d58d/mmstudio/src/main/java/org/micromanager/acquisition/SequenceSettings.java#L39>), (generated by clicking the `Acquire!` button in the [Multi-D Acquisition GUI](<https://micro-manager.org/Version_2.0_Users_Guide#multi-dimensional-acquisition>))
- For [Pycro-Manager](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pycro-manager>), this object is similar to the [`multi_d_acquisition_events`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pycro-manager/blob/63cf209a8907fd23932ee9f8016cb6a2b61b45aa/pycromanager/acquire.py#L605>) convenience function, (and `useq.pycromanager` provides a `to_pycromanager` function that returns a list of pycro-manager event dicts)

## Executing an MDASequence

This library is just a schema, and does not provide any built-in functionality for executing an `MDASequence`. However, [pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>) implements an acquisition engine that can execute an `MDASequence` object (or any iterable of `MDAEvent` objects) with [Micro-Manager](<https://micro-manager.org>) (via the [`pymmcore`](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>) python wrapper around the C++ MMCore). The `MDAWidget` in pymmcore-widgets, [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) and [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>) all build a `useq.MDASequence` from user input and hand it to pymmcore-plus to run.

Built an engine that runs an `MDASequence` (or know of a similar schema in other software)? [Open an issue](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/useq-schema/issues/new>) and we'll list it here.

## Serialization and deserialization

`MDASequence` and `MDAEvent` objects are designed to be serialized and deserialized, allowing you to define an entire multi-dimensional acquisition in a human-readable YAML (or JSON) file, and then load that file into your acquisition engine.

For example, the following file defines an experiment with:

- 3 channels (`Cy5`, `FITC`, and `DAPI`), specifying exposure times in ms for `Cy5` and `FITC`, and acquiring `DAPI` (without a z-stack) only every third timepoint
- a two-phase time-lapse: 3 frames, 3 seconds apart, followed by a frame every 10 seconds for 40 minutes
- a Z-stack at each timepoint, with a range of 4 microns and a step size of 0.5 micron
- two stage positions, specifying a unique Z-stack for the second position

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Example**
>
> my\_experiment.yaml
>
> ```YAML
> axis_order: tpcz
> channels:
>   - config: Cy5
>     exposure: 50.0
>   - config: FITC
>     exposure: 100.0
>   - config: DAPI
>     acquire_every: 3
>     do_stack: false
> time_plan:
>   phases:
>     - interval: 0:00:03
>       loops: 3
>     - duration: 0:40:00
>       interval: 0:00:10
> z_plan:
>   range: 4.0
>   step: 0.5
> stage_positions:
>   - x: 10.0
>     y: 20.0
>     z: 50.0
>   - name: Cell 1
>     x: 110.0
>     y: 220.0
>     z: 50.0
>     sequence:
>       z_plan:
>         above: 10.0
>         below: 0.0
>         step: 1.0
> metadata:
>   some info: about my experiment
> ```
>
> my\_experiment.json
>
> ```JSON
> {
>   "axis_order": "tpcz",
>   "channels": [
>     {
>       "config": "Cy5",
>       "exposure": 50.0
>     },
>     {
>       "config": "FITC",
>       "exposure": 100.0
>     },
>     {
>       "config": "DAPI",
>       "acquire_every": 3,
>       "do_stack": false
>     }
>   ],
>   "time_plan": {
>     "phases": [
>       {
>         "interval": "0:00:03",
>         "loops": 3
>       },
>       {
>         "duration": "0:40:00",
>         "interval": "0:00:10"
>       }
>     ]
>   },
>   "z_plan": {
>     "range": 4.0,
>     "step": 0.5
>   },
>   "stage_positions": [
>     {
>       "x": 10.0,
>       "y": 20.0,
>       "z": 50.0
>     },
>     {
>       "name": "Cell 1",
>       "x": 110.0,
>       "y": 220.0,
>       "z": 50.0,
>       "sequence": {
>         "z_plan": {
>           "above": 10.0,
>           "below": 0.0,
>           "step": 1.0
>         }
>       }
>     }
>   ],
>   "metadata": {
>     "some info": "about my experiment"
>   }
> }
> ```

Either file can be loaded with:

```python
import useq

seq = useq.MDASequence.from_file("my_experiment.yaml")
```

... and `seq.yaml()` or `seq.model_dump_json(exclude_unset=True)` go the other way (see [saving and loading sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/#saving-and-loading-sequences>)).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Unknown keys are ignored**
>
> Keys that aren't part of the schema are silently dropped when a file is loaded, so a misspelled or misplaced key (for example a `z_plan` placed directly on a stage position, rather than inside its `sequence`) won't raise an error. It's worth checking the loaded sequence (`list(seq)`, or `seq.sizes`) before running it.

## What about `useq.v2`?

`useq.v2` is a preview of the next version of the API (with user-defined axes, among other things). `useq.MDASequence`, as described on these pages, is unchanged, and nothing needs to migrate yet. See [useq-schema v2 (preview)](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/v2-migration/index.md>) if you're curious.

## Next steps

- [Building Sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>): common experiments, step by step.
- The [`MDASequence`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/index.md>), [`MDAEvent`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/event/index.md>), [axes](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/axes/index.md>) and [autofocus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/hardware_autofocus/index.md>) reference pages.
- [The Acquisition Engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>), to run a sequence on a microscope.

# useq-schema v2 (Preview)

> [!WARNING]
>
> **This is a preview**
>
> `useq.v2` is a preview of the next version of the useq-schema API, and it may still change. `useq.MDASequence`, as described in the rest of these docs, is unchanged, and *nothing needs to migrate yet*.
>
> pymmcore-plus can already run a `useq.v2.MDASequence`, but (for now) it treats it like any other iterable of events. The engine doesn't see the sequence itself, and [saved data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/#lists-and-generators-are-saved-as-a-flat-stack>) is written as one flat stack of frames.

In `useq.MDASequence`, the axes are fixed: time, positions, grid, channels and z (`"tpgcz"`), and the logic for combining them lives inside useq. In `useq.v2`, a sequence is a tuple of *axes*, and any object that follows the `v2.AxisIterable` interface can be one (it has an `axis_key`, yields values, and says what each value contributes to an event). The familiar plans (time plans, z plans, grids, channels, stage positions) are all v2 axes, so the same experiments can still be described, but you can also add your own axes, decide per axis which combinations to skip, give a single position its own plans, and post-process the stream of events with *transforms*.

The examples below all run against the current preview.

## The old arguments still work

`v2.MDASequence` accepts the same keyword arguments as `useq.MDASequence`, and converts them into `axes`:

```python
from useq import v2

seq = v2.MDASequence(
    time_plan={"interval": 1.0, "loops": 2},
    stage_positions=[(10, 20, 5)],
    channels=["DAPI", "FITC"],
    z_plan={"range": 2, "step": 1},
)
print([str(axis.axis_key) for axis in seq.axes])
# ['t', 'p', 'c', 'z']

# ... which is the same as:
seq2 = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.TIntervalLoops(interval=1.0, loops=2),
        v2.StagePositions(values=[v2.Position(x=10, y=20, z=5)]),
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=[v2.Channel(config="DAPI"), v2.Channel(config="FITC")]),
        v2.ZRangeAround(range=2, step=1),
    ),
)
assert list(seq) == list(seq2)
```

An existing `useq.MDASequence` can be converted with `v2.MDASequence.model_validate(old_sequence)`. The events are the same as the ones `useq.MDASequence` yields (except that v2 events don't carry a reference to their `sequence`), with these exceptions in the current preview:

- The `Channel` options `acquire_every`, `do_stack` and `z_offset` are *not* applied yet, so every channel is acquired at every time point and z position.
- Giving a position its own sub-sequence with `Position(sequence=...)` emits a `DeprecationWarning`; see [below](<#different-plans-for-one-position>) for the v2 way.

## Custom axes

An axis yields values, and its `contribute_to_mda_event` method says what each value adds to the event. For example, here's an axis that steps a laser power (as a device property):

```python
from collections.abc import Mapping

from useq import v2


class LaserPowerAxis(v2.SimpleValueAxis[float]):
    axis_key: str = "laser"

    def contribute_to_mda_event(self, value: float, index: Mapping[str, int]) -> dict:
        return {"properties": [("Laser", "Power", value)]}  # (1)!


seq = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI", "FITC"]),
        LaserPowerAxis(values=[10, 50]),
    ),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event)
```

1. Whatever this returns is passed to `MDAEvent(...)`. (For type checkers, the return type is `MDAEvent.Kwargs`, a `TypedDict` that only exists when type checking.)

```text
index={'c': 0, 'laser': 0} channel=Channel(config='DAPI') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=10.0)]
index={'c': 0, 'laser': 1} channel=Channel(config='DAPI') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=50.0)]
index={'c': 1, 'laser': 0} channel=Channel(config='FITC') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=10.0)]
index={'c': 1, 'laser': 1} channel=Channel(config='FITC') properties=[PropertyTuple(device_name='Laser', property_name='Power', property_value=50.0)]
```

`v2.SimpleValueAxis` iterates over a list of `values`. For anything else, subclass `v2.AxisIterable` and implement `__iter__` (see [Sequences that never end](<#sequences-that-never-end>)).

## Skipping combinations

Any axis can veto a combination of values by overriding `should_skip`. It receives a dict that maps each axis key to an `(index, value, axis)` tuple. Here the second channel gets a single plane rather than a z-stack:

```python
from useq import v2


class SparseZ(v2.ZRangeAround):
    """Only take the full z-stack in the first channel."""

    def should_skip(self, prefix: dict) -> bool:
        c_index = prefix["c"][0]
        z_index = prefix["z"][0]
        return c_index > 0 and z_index != 1


seq = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI", "FITC"]),
        SparseZ(range=2, step=1),  # (1)!
    ),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event.index, event.channel.config, event.z_pos)
```

1. There's no stage position here, so (just as in v1) this relative z plan is centered on z = 0, not on the current focus.

```text
{'c': 0, 'z': 0} DAPI -1.0
{'c': 0, 'z': 1} DAPI 0.0
{'c': 0, 'z': 2} DAPI 1.0
{'c': 1, 'z': 1} FITC 0.0
```

## Different plans for one position

A value yielded by an axis may itself be a sequence, whose `value` stands in for the plain value, and whose axes replace (or add to) the parent's axes for that branch. Here, the second position gets a bigger z-stack:

```python
from useq import v2

cell_1 = v2.MDASequence(
    value=v2.Position(x=100, y=100, z=10),
    axes=(v2.ZRangeAround(range=4, step=2),),
)

seq = v2.MDASequence(
    axes=(
        v2.StagePositions(values=[v2.Position(x=0, y=0, z=10), cell_1]),
        v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI"]),
        v2.ZRangeAround(range=1, step=1),
    ),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event.index, event.x_pos, event.z_pos)
```

```text
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} 0.0 9.5
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} 0.0 10.5
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} 100.0 8.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} 100.0 10.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} 100.0 12.0
```

## Transforms

Transforms see each event after it has been built, and may change it, drop it, or add more events, which makes it possible to insert events that don't belong to any axis. A transform is a callable that returns (or yields) events. It also gets the previous event, and a function that builds the next one, for look-ahead:

```python
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable

from useq import v2


class SnapBrightfieldAfterStack:
    """After each z-stack, add a single brightfield image."""

    def __call__(
        self,
        event: v2.MDAEvent,
        *,
        prev_event: v2.MDAEvent | None,
        make_next_event: Callable[[], v2.MDAEvent | None],
    ) -> Iterable[v2.MDAEvent]:
        yield event
        next_event = make_next_event()
        if next_event is None or next_event.index.get("z", 0) == 0:
            yield event.model_copy(
                update={"channel": v2.EventChannel(config="BF"), "z_pos": None}
            )


seq = v2.MDASequence(
    channels=["DAPI"],
    stage_positions=[(0, 0, 10), (100, 100, 10)],
    z_plan={"range": 2, "step": 1},
    transforms=(SnapBrightfieldAfterStack(),),
)
for event in seq:
    print(event.index, event.channel.config, event.z_pos)
```

```text
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} DAPI 9.0
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} DAPI 10.0
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} DAPI 11.0
{'p': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} BF None
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 0} DAPI 9.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 1} DAPI 10.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} DAPI 11.0
{'p': 1, 'c': 0, 'z': 2} BF None
```

Some of v1's built-in behavior is implemented as transforms, which v2 adds for you: `ResetEventTimerTransform` (when there is a time plan), and `KeepShutterOpenTransform` and `AutoFocusTransform` (when you set `keep_shutter_open_across` or `autofocus_plan`).

> [!WARNING]
>
> Passing `transforms=` *replaces* the default transforms. If your sequence has a time plan, add `v2.ResetEventTimerTransform()` to your own tuple, or the first event will no longer reset the event timer.

## Sequences that never end

v2 axes don't need a length, so a sequence can go on forever (or until the acquisition is cancelled):

```python
import itertools
from collections.abc import Iterator, Mapping

from useq import v2


class Forever(v2.AxisIterable[int]):
    """A time axis with no end."""

    axis_key: str = "t"

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[int]:
        yield from itertools.count()

    def contribute_to_mda_event(self, value: int, index: Mapping[str, int]) -> dict:
        return {"min_start_time": value * 5.0}


seq = v2.MDASequence(axes=(Forever(), v2.ChannelsPlan(values=["DAPI", "FITC"])))
print(seq.is_finite())  # False
for event in itertools.islice(seq, 5):
    print(event.index, event.channel.config, event.min_start_time)
```

```text
{'t': 0, 'c': 0} DAPI 0.0
{'t': 0, 'c': 1} FITC 0.0
{'t': 1, 'c': 0} DAPI 5.0
{'t': 1, 'c': 1} FITC 5.0
{'t': 2, 'c': 0} DAPI 10.0
```

## Other kinds of events

`v2.MDASequence` builds `MDAEvent` objects, but the class it is built on, `v2.MultiAxisSequence`, can build anything. Pass it an `event_builder`, which is called with the axes index (and the chain of enclosing sequences) for each combination:

```python
from useq import v2


class DictBuilder:
    def __call__(self, axes_index: dict, context: tuple) -> dict:
        return {key: value for key, (index, value, axis) in axes_index.items()}


seq = v2.MultiAxisSequence(
    axes=(
        v2.SimpleValueAxis(axis_key="a", values=[1, 2]),
        v2.SimpleValueAxis(axis_key="b", values=["x", "y"]),
    ),
    event_builder=DictBuilder(),
)
print(list(seq.iter_events()))
# [{'a': 1, 'b': 'x'}, {'a': 1, 'b': 'y'}, {'a': 2, 'b': 'x'}, {'a': 2, 'b': 'y'}]
```

## v1 and v2 side by side

|  | `useq.MDASequence` | `useq.v2.MDASequence` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| axes | `time_plan`, `stage_positions`, `grid_plan`, `channels`, `z_plan` | `axes=(...)`, any `AxisIterable` (the v1 keywords are converted) |
| plan for one position | `Position(sequence=MDASequence(...))` | `MDASequence(value=Position(...), axes=(...))`, as an item in `StagePositions` |
| skipping | `Channel(acquire_every=..., do_stack=...)` | `should_skip()` on any axis (the `Channel` options aren't applied yet) |
| sizes | `seq.sizes`, `seq.shape` | `[len(axis) for axis in seq.axes]` and `seq.is_finite()` (`sizes` and `shape` still work, with a `FutureWarning`) |
| finding a plan | `seq.time_plan`, `seq.z_plan`, ... | the same properties, which return the axis with that key (or `None`) |
| z plan values | `float` | `Position` (with only `z` set) |
| extra events | build the list of events yourself | transforms |
| length | always finite | may be infinite |
| files | `seq.yaml()`, `MDASequence.from_file()` | no `yaml()` or `from_file()` yet |

# Building a Custom GUI

The widgets in `pymmcore-widgets` are ordinary `QWidget`s that control a `CMMCorePlus`, so you can arrange them with Qt layouts like any other widget. [Your first GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-gui/index.md>) puts a few of them in a window. This page covers the things you'll want to know once you start building something bigger: which Qt to install, how widgets find their core, and a larger example.

## Installing a Qt backend

`pymmcore-widgets` does *not* install Qt for you, so you choose the Qt backend with an extra:

```sh
pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PyQt6]"
# or
pip install "pymmcore-widgets[PySide6]"
```

(Keep the quotes. In zsh, the default shell on macOS, the square brackets otherwise cause a "no matches found" error.) You'll also need Python 3.11 or newer, and the Micro-Manager device adapters (see [Installation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/install/index.md>)).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **PyQt6 or PySide6?**
>
> Qt is the C++ toolkit the widgets are drawn with, and PyQt6 and PySide6 are two sets of Python bindings for it. The widgets work with (and are tested on) both, on macOS and Windows. The main difference is the license. PyQt6 is GPL (or commercial), and PySide6 is LGPL. That matters if you distribute your GUI, for example as a bundled application. If you don't have a reason to choose, PyQt6 is a fine default (it's what [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) uses).
>
> We no longer test PyQt5 or PySide2 (and PySide2 can't be installed on Python 3.11 or newer).

The widgets import Qt through [qtpy](<https://github.com/spyder-ide/qtpy>), which is installed with `pymmcore-widgets`. qtpy provides one API (`from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication`) on top of whichever binding is installed, and the examples on this site use it too. If you write your own code against qtpy as well, it will run with either backend. (If both are installed in the same environment, qtpy picks PyQt6; set the environment variable `QT_API=pyside6` to use PySide6.)

## Basic usage

For a basic use of any of the widgets, we need to:

1. create a Qt application (`QApplication`);
2. create a Micro-Manager core instance so that all the widgets will control the same core;
3. load a configuration file;
4. create and show the widget(s) we want.

The order of the first two steps matters. Create the `QApplication` before the core (see [Qt integration](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/integration-with-qt/index.md>) for why).

In this example, we replace step 3 with the ConfigurationWidget, which lets us load any Micro-Manager configuration file. We also add the GroupPresetTableWidget, which shows the configuration groups and presets stored in the configuration file:

basic\_usage.py

```python
# import the necessary packages
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from pymmcore_widgets import ConfigurationWidget, GroupPresetTableWidget

# create a QApplication
app = QApplication([])

# create a CMMCorePlus instance.
mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()

# create a ConfigurationWidget
cfg_widget = ConfigurationWidget()

# create a GroupPresetTableWidget
gp_widget = GroupPresetTableWidget()

# show the created widgets
cfg_widget.show()
gp_widget.show()

app.exec()
```

The code above will create a Qt application with the `ConfigurationWidget` and the `GroupPresetTableWidget`:

## Choosing a core

By default, most widgets use the global singleton core, `CMMCorePlus.instance()`, and create it if it doesn't exist yet. This means that all the widgets in your GUI control the same core without you connecting anything, and so does any other code that calls `CMMCorePlus.instance()`. (So in the example above, the `mmc = CMMCorePlus.instance()` line isn't strictly necessary. Without it, the `ConfigurationWidget` would create the core.)

If you need a specific core instead, create it first and pass it to each widget as the `mmcore` argument, for example `GroupPresetTableWidget(mmcore=my_core)`. A few widgets are different:

- The sequence editors (`MDASequenceWidget`, `ChannelTable`, `PositionTable`, `TimePlanWidget`, `ZPlanWidget` and `GridPlanWidget`) don't use a core at all. They edit `useq` objects. Read the result with `value()`, set it with `setValue()`, and connect to `valueChanged`. `MDAWidget` is the sequence editor that *is* connected to a core (and can run the acquisition).
- `ConfigWizard` calls the argument `core`, not `mmcore`.
- `ConfigGroupsEditor` and `ConfigGroupsTree` are built from a core with `create_from_core(core)`, and don't follow it afterwards.
- `InstallWidget` installs device adapters and doesn't need a core.

## Custom GUI

The widgets are ordinary `QWidget`s, so building a custom GUI with them is mostly a matter of Qt layouts. If you're new to Qt, the [Qt for Python tutorials](<https://doc.qt.io/qtforpython-6/tutorials/index.html>) are a good place to start. Here, we only give a simple example of a custom GUI built from some of the `pymmcore-widgets`.

We create a [Qt application](<https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qapplication.html>) with a general-purpose [QWidget](<https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qwidget.html>) that incorporates a variety of `pymmcore-widgets`: ConfigurationWidget, ChannelGroupWidget, ChannelWidget, DefaultCameraExposureWidget, ImagePreview, SnapButton, and LiveButton.

This simple GUI can be used to load a Micro-Manager configuration file, snap an image or stream images from the camera, with the flexibility to select a channel and adjust the exposure time:

custom\_gui.py

```python
# Import the necessary packages
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QGridLayout, QWidget

from pymmcore_widgets import (
    ChannelGroupWidget,
    ChannelWidget,
    ConfigurationWidget,
    DefaultCameraExposureWidget,
    ImagePreview,
    LiveButton,
    SnapButton,
)


# Create a QWidget class named MyWidget
class MyWidget(QWidget):
    """An example QWidget that uses some of the widgets in pymmcore_widgets."""

    def __init__(self, parent: QWidget | None = None):
        super().__init__(parent=parent)

        # This is not strictly necessary but we can create a Micro-Manager core
        # instance so that all the widgets can control the same core. If you don't
        # create a core instance, the first widget to be instantiated will create
        # a new core instance.
        CMMCorePlus.instance()

        # Create the wanted pymmcore_widgets
        cfg = ConfigurationWidget()
        ch_group_combo = ChannelGroupWidget()
        ch_combo = ChannelWidget()
        exp = DefaultCameraExposureWidget()
        preview = ImagePreview()
        snap = SnapButton()
        live = LiveButton()

        # Create the layout for MyWidget
        # In Qt, a `layout` (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/layout.html) is used to add
        # widgets to a `QWidget`. For this example, we'll employ a
        # `QGridLayout` (https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qgridlayout.html) to organize the
        # widgets in a grid-like arrangement.
        layout = QGridLayout(self)

        # Add the wanted pymmcore_widgets to the layout.
        # The first two arguments of 'addWidget' specify the grid position
        # in terms of rows and columns. The third and fourth arguments
        # define the span of the widget across multiple rows and columns.
        layout.addWidget(cfg, 0, 0, 1, 3)
        layout.addWidget(ch_group_combo, 1, 0)
        layout.addWidget(ch_combo, 1, 1)
        layout.addWidget(exp, 1, 2)
        layout.addWidget(preview, 2, 0, 1, 3)
        layout.addWidget(snap, 3, 1)
        layout.addWidget(live, 3, 2)


# Create a QApplication and show MyWidget
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

    app = QApplication([])
    widget = MyWidget()
    widget.show()
    app.exec()
```

Running it (and loading a configuration) looks like this:

## Next steps
