If you'd rather start from a ready-made application, see [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) (which you can also extend with your own widgets) or [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>).

# Widget Gallery

The top-level widgets in `pymmcore-widgets`, grouped by what they do, roughly in the order you'd reach for them when building a GUI. Click a widget for a runnable example and its API (the screenshots are generated from those examples).

Most of these widgets control a `CMMCorePlus` (by default the global `CMMCorePlus.instance()`, or the one you pass as `mmcore=`). They follow the core's [events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>), so they stay in sync with each other and with your own code. The [sequence editors](<#sequence-editors>) are the exception: they don't use a core at all. (See [Building a custom GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/#choosing-a-core>) for the details.)

## Camera and images

Snap and live buttons, an image preview, and the camera's exposure and ROI.

- [**`SnapButton`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/SnapButton/index.md>)

  Button that snaps an image with the current camera.
- [**`LiveButton`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/LiveButton/index.md>)

  Button that starts and stops live mode.
- [**`ImagePreview`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ImagePreview/index.md>)

  A Widget that displays the latest image from the core.
- [**`ExposureWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ExposureWidget/index.md>)

  Spin box that shows and sets the exposure time (in ms) of a camera.
- [**`DefaultCameraExposureWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/DefaultCameraExposureWidget/index.md>)

  A Widget to get/set exposure on the default camera.
- [**`CameraRoiWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/CameraRoiWidget/index.md>)

  A Widget to control the camera device ROI.

## Channels, objectives and presets

These widgets show (and change) the current state of the microscope: the channel, the objective, the preset of any configuration group, and the shutters.

- [**`ChannelWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ChannelWidget/index.md>)

  Combo box that shows and sets the current channel.
- [**`ChannelGroupWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ChannelGroupWidget/index.md>)

  Combo box that chooses which configuration group is the channel group.
- [**`ObjectivesWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ObjectivesWidget/index.md>)

  Combo box that shows and sets the current objective.
- [**`PresetsWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/PresetsWidget/index.md>)

  Combo box that shows and sets the current preset of one configuration group.
- [**`GroupPresetTableWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/GroupPresetTableWidget/index.md>)

  Table of all configuration groups, to view and set their presets.
- [**`ShuttersWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ShuttersWidget/index.md>)

  Button that opens and closes a shutter, with an optional autoshutter checkbox.

## Stages

Move an XY or Z stage, or explore the sample in a zoomable view of the stage, where snapped images appear at the position they were taken.

- [**`StageWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/StageWidget/index.md>)

  Arrow buttons to move an XY stage or a Z (focus) stage.
- [**`StageExplorer`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/StageExplorer/index.md>)

  Zoomable view of the stage, where snapped images appear at their positions.

## Devices and properties

View and change the properties of any of the loaded devices.

- [**`PropertyBrowser`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/PropertyBrowser/index.md>)

  A Widget to browse and change properties of all devices.
- [**`PropertiesWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/PropertiesWidget/index.md>)

  Controls for a filtered set of device properties (a PropertyWidget each).
- [**`PropertyWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/PropertyWidget/index.md>)

  Widget to display and control a single device property.

## Acquisition

Define a multi-dimensional acquisition (a `useq.MDASequence`) and run it on the core. `MDAWidget` is the `MDASequenceWidget` below, connected to a core. It offers the core's channels, can add the current stage position, and has buttons to run, pause and cancel the acquisition.

- [**`MDAWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/MDAWidget/index.md>)

  Main MDA Widget connected to a `pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus` instance.
- [**`HCSWizard`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/HCSWizard/index.md>)

  A wizard to set up a high-content screening (HCS) experiment.

## Sequence editors

> [!NOTE]
>
> **No core needed**
>
> These widgets edit `useq` objects and don't touch the microscope. Read the result with `value()`, set it with `setValue()`, and connect to `valueChanged` to hear about changes. Use them to describe an experiment in your own GUI; to run one, pass the sequence to `CMMCorePlus.run_mda` (or use the `MDAWidget` above).

- [**`MDASequenceWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/MDASequenceWidget/index.md>)

  A widget that provides a GUI to construct and edit a `useq.MDASequence`.
- [**`ChannelTable`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ChannelTable/index.md>)

  Table to edit a list of channels (`useq.Channel`).
- [**`TimePlanWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/TimePlanWidget/index.md>)

  Table to edit a time plan (`useq.AnyTimePlan`), one row per phase.
- [**`ZPlanWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ZPlanWidget/index.md>)

  Widget to edit a z plan (`useq.AnyZPlan`).
- [**`PositionTable`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/PositionTable/index.md>)

  Table to edit a list of stage positions (`useq.Position`).
- [**`GridPlanWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/GridPlanWidget/index.md>)

  Widget to edit a grid plan.

## Configuration and setup

Load, create and edit a configuration file (the `ConfigWizard` is Micro-Manager's Hardware Configuration Wizard), set pixel sizes, install device adapters, and watch the core's log.

- [**`ConfigurationWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ConfigurationWidget/index.md>)

  A Widget to select and load a Micro-Manager system configuration.
- [**`ConfigWizard`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ConfigWizard/index.md>)

  Hardware Configuration Wizard for Micro-Manager.
- [**`ConfigGroupsEditor`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ConfigGroupsEditor/index.md>)

  Editor for configuration groups and their presets.
- [**`ConfigGroupsTree`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ConfigGroupsTree/index.md>)

  A tree widget that displays configuration groups.
- [**`PixelConfigurationWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/PixelConfigurationWidget/index.md>)

  A Widget to define the pixel size configurations.
- [**`ObjectivesPixelConfigurationWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/ObjectivesPixelConfigurationWidget/index.md>)

  A Widget to define the pixel size configurations using the objective device.
- [**`InstallWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/InstallWidget/index.md>)

  Widget to install Micro-Manager's device adapters (like `mmcore install`).
- [**`CoreLogWidget`**](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/CoreLogWidget/index.md>)

  Live view of the core's log file.

# pymmcore-gui

**pymmcore-gui** is a desktop application for controlling microscopes with the Micro-Manager core, written in Python. It's built from the other packages on this site (plus [ndv](<https://github.com/pyapp-kit/ndv>) for viewing images), and the goal is to provide a pure-Python replacement for Micro-Manager's Java GUI (MMStudio).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Name pending**
>
> *pymmcore-gui* is a working title. The application is usable today, but expect rough edges and frequent changes.

## Who it's for

pymmcore-gui is for people who want to *use* a microscope from a Python application the way they'd use MMStudio: load a configuration, look at the live image, set up a multi-dimensional acquisition and run it, without writing code. It's also a place to start if you're a developer who'd rather add a few panels to an existing application than build a GUI from scratch with [pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/index.md>). You can [add your own widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/usage/#adding-your-own-widget>), and [script the running GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/usage/#the-console>) from its built-in console.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **pymmcore-gui or napari-micromanager?**
>
> [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>) came first. It's a [napari](<https://napari.org>) plugin built from the same widgets, in which images become napari layers. It's still maintained, but new development is going into pymmcore-gui, which uses ndv instead of napari (for performance, and to keep the dependencies down). If your analysis already lives in napari, napari-micromanager may suit you better; otherwise, start with pymmcore-gui.

## What's inside

| Component | Role in the GUI |
| --- | --- |
| [pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/index.md>) | Device control and the acquisition engine (`CMMCorePlus`, `MDAEngine`). |
| [useq-schema](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/index.md>) | Describes the experiments you run: time-lapses, z-stacks, channels, well plates, grids, ... |
| [pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) | The panels: camera and stage control, property browser, acquisition setup, ... |
| [ndv](<https://github.com/pyapp-kit/ndv>) | Fast, lightweight n-dimensional viewer for live and acquired images. |

## Features

- Device control and configuration (including the Hardware Configuration Wizard)
- Multi-dimensional acquisitions: time, z, channels, positions, grids, well plates
- Real-time image preview and acquisition visualization (2D and 3D)
- Customizable, dockable layouts
- An integrated IPython console with access to the running core
- Double-clickable application bundles for Windows and macOS

## Next steps

To try it out, [install pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/install/index.md>) (as a Python package or a bundled app), then see [Using pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/usage/index.md>) for launching it, its command-line options, and scripting it from Python. The [API reference](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/api/pymmcore_gui/index.md>) documents the parts you can build on.

# Installing pymmcore-gui

There are two ways to get pymmcore-gui: as a Python package, or as a bundled, double-clickable application.

You'll need Python 3.11 or newer, and `git` (pip uses it to fetch the code).

```sh
# install the latest version from GitHub
pip install git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui

# install Micro-Manager device adapters
mmcore install

# run the app (with the demo devices)
mmgui run --demo-config
```

Or run it without installing anything permanently, using [uv](<https://docs.astral.sh/uv/>):

```sh
uvx --from git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui mmgui
```

pymmcore-gui isn't released on PyPI yet. (There *is* a `pymmcore-gui` package there, but it's an outdated pre-release, so please install from GitHub.)

pymmcore-gui requires a specific version of PyQt6, so install it in its own environment rather than next to another Qt application (or a PySide6 project).

> [!TIP]
>
> The GitHub version may change at any time, so pin a specific commit if you add it to your own dependencies: `pymmcore-gui @ git+https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui@<commit>`

Pre-built bundles include the Python runtime and all dependencies. Download and extract the archive, then run the application.

| Platform | Latest nightly build |
| :---: | :--- |
| Windows | [pymmgui-Windows.zip](<https://nightly.link/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui/workflows/bundle/main/pymmgui-Windows.zip>) |
| macOS | [pymmgui-macOS.zip](<https://nightly.link/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui/workflows/bundle/main/pymmgui-macOS.zip>) |

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Unsigned app**
>
> Until the bundles are signed, your OS will warn you about running an app from an unidentified developer; you will need to accept that warning.

## Micro-Manager device adapters

Neither option includes the Micro-Manager device adapters (the drivers for your hardware). Install them in one of these ways:

- Use the **Devices \> Install Devices...** menu in the GUI.
- Run `mmcore install` (or `uvx --from "pymmcore-plus[cli]" mmcore install`).
- Install a [Micro-Manager nightly build](<https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager_Nightly_Builds>).

See [Installing Micro-Manager device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/#installing-micro-manager-device-adapters>) for details.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **License**
>
> The bundled application includes PyQt6 (GPL-3.0), so the bundle is distributed as a combined work under the GPL-3.0. pymmcore-gui itself is BSD-3-Clause.

# Using pymmcore-gui

## Launching the app

Double-click the bundled application, or run `mmgui` from a terminal in the environment where you installed pymmcore-gui.

On first launch, no configuration is loaded, so there isn't much to control yet. To try the GUI without hardware, load Micro-Manager's demo devices with **Devices \> Load Demo Configuration**, or start the app with them:

```sh
mmgui run --demo-config
```

Load your own configuration from **Devices \> Load System Configuration...**, or create one with the Hardware Configuration Wizard (**Devices \> Hardware Config Wizard...**). On later launches, the GUI offers to reload the last configuration you used.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Error reports**
>
> The first time you launch it, the app asks whether you'd like to send error reports to the developers (through [Sentry](<https://sentry.io>)). This is opt-in: nothing is sent unless you agree, and the [privacy policy](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-gui/blob/main/PRIVACY.md>) lists what's included. Your answer is saved in the app's settings (`mmgui settings --reset` clears it). Starting the app with `mmgui run --no-telemetry` skips the question and doesn't send anything.

### Command-line options

`mmgui` is short for `mmgui run`, which starts the app. It takes these options:

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `-c FILE`, `--config FILE` | Load this Micro-Manager configuration file. |
| `--demo-config` | Load Micro-Manager's demo configuration. |
| `--no-telemetry` | Don't ask about (or send) error reports. |

For example, `mmgui run -c path/to/my_scope.cfg`. (Spell out `run` when you pass options. Plain `mmgui -c FILE` works, but `mmgui --demo-config` does not.)

The app keeps its settings (window layout, last configuration, your answer about error reports) in a settings file. `mmgui settings --edit` opens that file, `mmgui settings --reveal` shows it in your file browser, and `mmgui settings --reset` restores the defaults. `mmgui --version` prints the versions of pymmcore-gui, pymmcore-plus and pymmcore.

## The console

The **Console** (in the **Window** menu, and the `>_` button in the toolbar) is an IPython console running in the app itself. It predefines a few names, so you can script the running GUI:

- `mmc` (also `core` and `mmcore`): the `CMMCorePlus` the GUI is using;
- `mda`: its acquisition runner (`mmc.mda`);
- `window`: the main window;
- `np`, `useq`, and the top-level names from `pymmcore_plus` and `useq` (`MDASequence`, ...).

For example, `mmc.setExposure(50)` updates the exposure everywhere in the GUI.

## Launching from Python

Start the GUI from a script or an interactive session with `create_mmgui`:

```python
from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui

create_mmgui()
```

This call blocks until the window is closed (it runs the Qt event loop).

### Customizing before launch

Pass `exec_app=False` to get the main window back *before* the Qt event loop starts, customize it, then start the event loop yourself. (You don't need to create a `QApplication`, because `create_mmgui` makes one for you.)

```python
from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

window = create_mmgui(exec_app=False)

# customize the window, or script the core it uses:
mmcore = window.mmcore

QApplication.instance().exec()
```

### Using your own core

By default, the GUI uses the global `CMMCorePlus.instance()`, creating it if needed, so any script can reach the same core the GUI is driving. If you already have a `CMMCorePlus` instance with a configuration loaded, pass it in, along with `mm_config=False`:

```python
from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

my_core = CMMCorePlus()
my_core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # or your own configuration file

create_mmgui(mmcore=my_core, mm_config=False)
```

Without `mm_config=False`, the GUI goes through its usual startup logic, and may load (or offer to load) the last configuration you used on top of the one you set up.

### Adding your own widget

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Experimental**
>
> Clearer paths for customizing the interface are on the to-do list, so this may change.

The panels in the **Window** menu are registered as `WidgetActionInfo` objects, and you can register your own. Give it a unique `key`, the `text` to show in the menu, and a function that takes the main window (the parent) and returns your widget. Register it *before* calling `create_mmgui`, and it shows up in the **Window** menu, and opens as a dockable panel:

```python
from pymmcore_gui import create_mmgui
from pymmcore_gui.actions import WidgetActionInfo
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QLabel


def make_notes(parent):
    return QLabel("Remember to turn off the laser!", parent)


WidgetActionInfo(key="mylab.notes", text="Lab Notes", create_widget=make_notes)

window = create_mmgui(exec_app=False)
window.get_widget("mylab.notes")  # (optional) open it right away
QApplication.instance().exec()
```

Widgets from [pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) work too. The `parent` passed to your function is the main window, so you can hand them the GUI's core: `ExposureWidget(parent=parent, mmcore=parent.mmcore)`.

# Installing and Launching napari-micromanager

## Installation

### Installing napari-micromanager

```sh
pip install "napari-micromanager[PyQt6]"
# or, for the PySide6 Qt backend: pip install "napari-micromanager[PySide6]"
```

(The quotes keep zsh, the default shell on macOS, from complaining about the square brackets.) If you've already installed napari with a Qt backend in this environment (e.g. `pip install "napari[all]"`), plain `pip install napari-micromanager` is enough.

You will then also need to grab the Micro-Manager device adapters:

```sh
mmcore install
```

See [Installing Micro-Manager device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/#installing-micro-manager-device-adapters>) for details on the `mmcore` helper command.

## Usage

```sh
napari-micromanager
```

This will open a new napari window with the micromanager plugin enabled. To load a configuration file right away, pass it with `-c`:

```sh
napari-micromanager -c path/to/config.cfg
napari-micromanager -c MMConfig_demo.cfg  # Micro-Manager's demo devices
```

Otherwise, select a MM Config file at the top left of the window, then click load. (You can also add the plugin to a napari window that's already open, from the **Plugins** menu, or start napari with it: `napari -w napari-micromanager`.)

The plugin adds a row of toolbars along the top of the napari window: the configuration file, the channel group and channel, the objective, the shutters, Snap and Live, and the exposure time. The buttons at the end of the row open more panels, docked in the napari window: the device property browser, configuration groups and presets, illumination, stage control, camera ROI, pixel size, and **MDA** for multi-dimensional acquisitions. Snapped and live images go to a napari layer called "preview", and each acquisition gets layers of its own, so you can use any napari tool or plugin on them. A **MinMax** panel shows the minimum and maximum pixel values of the layers. Then ... much of the rest is hopefully self explanatory 😄.

Underlying napari-micromanager is the `pymmcore-plus` package, which is a python wrapper around `pymmcore` and the C++ CMMCore library (*not* pycro-manager and not the Java-based MMStudio). See the [User Guide](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/index.md>) for more on `pymmcore-plus`; the widgets in the GUI are all powered by [`pymmcore-widgets`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>).

# napari-micromanager

`napari-micromanager` is a [napari](<https://napari.org>) plugin that turns napari into a microscope control application, powered by [pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/index.md>) and [pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/index.md>). Images you snap or acquire show up as napari layers, right next to whatever analysis you do in napari.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Development has moved to pymmcore-gui**
>
> `napari-micromanager` continues to be maintained, but current development is focused on [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>), a napari-independent application (using [ndv](<https://github.com/pyapp-kit/ndv>) for viewing), for reasons of performance and fewer dependencies. If you don't need napari, start with pymmcore-gui.

- [Installing and launching](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/getting_started/index.md>) the plugin.
- [Scripting](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/scripting/index.md>): drive napari-micromanager from Python.

# Scripting napari-micromanager

`napari-micromanager` creates and owns its own `CMMCorePlus`. (It deliberately does *not* use the global `CMMCorePlus.instance()`, so a core you configured with `CMMCorePlus.instance()` is not the one the plugin drives.) Once you have a reference to the plugin's core, anything you can do with [pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/index.md>) can be combined with the GUI. There are a few ways to get it:

- `main_window.core`, where `main_window` is the plugin's `MainWindow` (see the script below);
- `napari_micromanager.get_core()`, which finds the plugin in the current napari viewer;
- in napari's console, the variable `mmcore` (see below).

## Launching napari from a script

For complex scripting you will likely want to launch napari from a script or a Jupyter notebook:

examples/launch\_from\_script.py

```python
import napari

v = napari.Viewer()
dw, main_window = v.window.add_plugin_dock_widget("napari-micromanager")

# the CMMCorePlus instance that napari-micromanager is driving
mmc = main_window.core

# do any complicated scripting you want here
...

# start napari
napari.run()
```

## Using a core you created

To have the plugin drive a core that you created and configured yourself, pass it as `mmcore` when you create the `MainWindow`, and add that to the viewer:

```python
import napari
from napari_micromanager import MainWindow
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()  # or your own configuration file

viewer = napari.Viewer()
main_window = MainWindow(viewer, mmcore=core)
viewer.window.add_dock_widget(main_window, name="MicroManager", area="top")

napari.run()
```

The plugin then leaves the core's lifecycle to you. When the window closes, it doesn't cancel a running acquisition or unload the devices, as it does for a core it created itself.

## Using the integrated napari console

After launching napari and starting the `napari-micromanager` plugin, open the napari console (the `>_` button at the bottom left of the window). It already defines `mmcore`, the core the plugin is driving, along with `MDASequence` and `MDAEvent` from [useq](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/index.md>), so you can run an acquisition from there:

```python
mmcore.run_mda(MDASequence(time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 5}))
```

# API reference

# API Reference

These pages are generated from the docstrings of each package. Each object is documented once, under the shortest path you can import it from (e.g. `pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus`, not `pymmcore_plus.core.CMMCorePlus`). Other modules that re-export it just link there.

- **[pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/index.md>)**

  ---

  `CMMCorePlus` (all of the core's methods, marking what pymmcore-plus adds or changes), the acquisition engine, device objects, constants, metadata, and the [`mmcore` command line tool](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/cli/index.md>).
- **[useq-schema](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/index.md>)**

  ---

  `MDASequence`, `MDAEvent`, and the plans for each axis (time, z, positions, grids, autofocus).
- **[pymmcore-widgets](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/index.md>)**

  ---

  One page for each widget, with a screenshot and an example. (The [widget gallery](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) is a quicker way to browse them.)
- **[pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/api/pymmcore_gui/index.md>)**

  ---

  The application's entry points (`create_mmgui`) and the actions and widgets you can use to extend it.

napari-micromanager has no public Python API of its own, but you can drive it from a script (see [Scripting napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/scripting/index.md>)).

Release notes for each package are on GitHub: [pymmcore-plus](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/releases>), [useq-schema](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/useq-schema/releases>), [pymmcore-widgets](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets/releases>), [napari-micromanager](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/napari-micromanager/releases>).

> [!TIP]
>
> **Linking to these docs from your own project**
>
> Each package publishes an object inventory for [mkdocstrings](<https://mkdocstrings.github.io/>) and [intersphinx](<https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/extensions/intersphinx.html>), e.g. `https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/objects.inv` (or `https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/objects.inv` for everything).

# pymmcore-plus

`pymmcore-plus` aims to extend [pymmcore](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore>) (Python bindings for the C++ [Micro-Manager core](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mmCoreAndDevices/>)) with a number of features designed to facilitate working with Micro-Manager in pure Python/C environments. The main object in this library, `CMMCorePlus`, aims to be a drop-in replacement for `pymmcore.CMMCore`, while adding a number of additional features including:

- A multi-dimensional [acquisition engine](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>) implemented in pure Python. (The existing acquisition engines in Micro-Manager are written in Java and Clojure.)
- More flexible [event](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>) connections and callback handling.
- Extended convenience APIs for working with the core (which would be hard or impossible to implement in the `pymmcore` SWIG wrapper).
- More pythonic APIs for various pymmcore objects (e.g. `Device`, `Configuration`) and [constants](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/constants/index.md>).

## Where to start

If you're new here, start with [Installation](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/install/index.md>) (which includes getting the [Micro-Manager device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/index.md>)), then [First steps](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-steps/index.md>) and [Your first acquisition](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-acquisition/index.md>). The User Guide goes into more depth on [devices and properties](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/devices/index.md>), [configuration groups](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/configuration/index.md>), [events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>), [running acquisitions](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/mda_engine/index.md>) and [saving data](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/saving_data/index.md>).

## Reference

- `CMMCorePlus`: every method of the core, with what `pymmcore-plus` adds or overrides marked.
- `pymmcore_plus.mda`: the acquisition runner (`MDARunner`) and engine (`MDAEngine`).
- [Events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/reference/events/index.md>): the signals emitted by `core.events` and `core.mda.events`.
- Metadata schema: the metadata dicts that come with each acquired frame.
- [Constants](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/constants/index.md>): the enums that replace pymmcore's integer constants.
- [Command line (`mmcore`)](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/cli/index.md>) and [environment variables](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/env_var/index.md>).

# pymmcore-widgets

[pymmcore-widgets](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets>) is a library of Qt widgets for [pymmcore-plus](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/index.md>), meant for building your own microscope GUI in Python. There are widgets for most of the things you do at the microscope (channels, exposure, stages, device properties, configuration groups, snapping and live mode, multi-dimensional acquisitions) and for setting it up (the Hardware Configuration Wizard, pixel sizes, installing device adapters). Most of them control a `CMMCorePlus` and follow its [events](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>), so they stay in sync with each other and with your own code. They are also the building blocks of [pymmcore-gui](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-gui/index.md>) and [napari-micromanager](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/napari-micromanager/index.md>).

A few widgets in one window (the code is the [StageExplorer example](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/StageExplorer/#example>)).

## Where to start

- [Your first GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/getting-started/first-gui/index.md>) puts a few of them together in a window.
- The [widget gallery](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) shows each widget with a screenshot, and links to its page with a runnable example and the API.
- [Building a custom GUI](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/getting_started/index.md>) covers choosing a Qt backend, how widgets find their core, and a larger example.
- [Qt integration](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/examples/integration-with-qt/index.md>) explains how pymmcore-plus and Qt work together (and how to keep your GUI responsive).

## API reference

Import widgets from the top-level package:

```python
from pymmcore_widgets import MDAWidget, PropertyBrowser, StageWidget
```

Each of these has its own page (listed under `pymmcore_widgets` in the sidebar, and in the [gallery](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>)). A few more specialized widgets live in submodules: the sequence editors' building blocks in [`pymmcore_widgets.useq_widgets`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/api/pymmcore_widgets/useq_widgets/index.md>) (for example `WellPlateWidget` and `PointsPlanWidget`), and `StackViewer` in `pymmcore_widgets.experimental`.

```python
get_widget(key: str, create: bool = ...) -> QWidget
```

```python
get_widget(key: str, create: bool = True) -> QWidget
```

Get (or create) widget for `key` ensuring that it is linked to its QAction.

If the widget has been "closed" (hidden), it will be re-shown.

Note that all widgets created this way are singletons, so calling this method multiple times will return the same widget instance.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `WidgetAction` | The widget to get. | *required* |
| `create` | `bool` | Whether to create the widget if it doesn't exist yet, by default True. | `True` |

Raises:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `KeyError` | If the widget doesn't exist and `create` is False. |

#### get\_dock\_widget

```python
get_dock_widget(key: str) -> CDockWidget
```

Get the QDockWidget for `key`.

Note, you can also get the QDockWidget by calling `get_widget(key)`, and then calling `widget.parent()`. The parent will *either* be an instance of `QDockWidget` (if it's actually a docked widget), or `MicroManagerGUI`, if it's not docked. You *should* use `isisinstance` in this case to check.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `WidgetAction` | The key for the *inner* widget owned by the requested QDockWidget. | *required* |

Raises:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `KeyError` | If the widget doesn't exist. |

#### closeEvent

```python
closeEvent(a0: QCloseEvent) -> None
```

#### restore\_state

```python
restore_state(*, show: bool = False) -> None
```

Restore the state of the window from settings (or load default state).

show is added as a convenience here because it may be a common use case to restore the state in a single shot timer and (only) then show the window. This avoids the window flashing on the screen before it is properly positioned.

## Functions

### create\_mmgui

```python
create_mmgui(
    *,
    mm_config: Path | str | None | Literal[False] = None,
    mmcore: CMMCorePlus | None = None,
    install_sys_excepthook: bool = True,
    install_sentry: bool = True,
    exec_app: bool = True,
) -> MicroManagerGUI
```

Initialize the pymmcore-gui application and Main Window.

This is the primary way to start pymmcore-gui. (It is also called by `__main__.main()` when running from the command line.)

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mm_config` | `str \| None \| False` | The path to the Micro-Manager configuration file to load. - If `False`, no configuration will be loaded. - If a non-empty string, that configuration will be loaded. - If None (or the empty string), auto-deciding logic will be used based on the stored user settings (based on the settings values for `Settings.last_config` and `Settings.auto_load_last_config`). | `None` |
| `mmcore` | `CMMCorePlus \| None` | The CMMCorePlus instance to use. If `None` (default), the global `CMMCorePlus.instance()` will be used if it exists, or a new (global) instance will be created (which you may access later with `CMMCorePlus.instance()`). Note: you may wish to also pass `mm_config = False` to prevent loading a system configuration, if you have already loaded one in your instance. | `None` |
| `install_sys_excepthook` | `bool` | If True (the default), installs a custom excepthook that does not raise sys.exit(). This is necessary to prevent the application from closing when an unhandled exception is raised in the main thread. | `True` |
| `install_sentry` | `bool` | If True (the default), the user will be given an option to send error reports to the developers, unless they have previously opted in/out. If False, no prompt will be shown, and no error reports will be sent. | `True` |
| `exec_app` | `bool` | If True (the default), the QApplication event loop will be started. If False, the event loop will not be started, and the caller is responsible for starting it with `QApplication.instance().exec()`. | `True` |

# CMMCorePlus

```python
CMMCorePlus(mm_path: str | None = None, adapter_paths: Sequence[str] = ())
```

Bases: `CMMCore`

Wrapper for CMMCore with extended functionality.

`CMMCorePlus` is a subclass of `pymmcore.CMMCore` with additional functionality, and some overrides for the sake of convenience or fixed behavior. It aims to be a drop-in replacement. Most methods behave as they do in `CMMCore`, but many return enums or `Configuration` objects instead of plain integers and SWIG objects, and many setters emit `events` even when the device adapter doesn't. Additions include an acquisition engine (`run_mda`) and object-oriented views onto devices, properties and config groups (e.g. `getDeviceObject`). (`registerCallback` is disallowed; use `events` instead.)

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mm_path` | `str \| None` | Path to the Micro-Manager installation. If `None` (default), will use the return value of `pymmcore_plus.find_micromanager`. | `None` |
| `adapter_paths` | `Sequence[str]` | Paths to search for device adapters, by default () | `()` |

Use the filters to show only what `pymmcore-plus` adds or overrides (each override says why it was changed). Deprecated methods are hidden unless you tick "show deprecated".

| [`stopSequenceAcquisition`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.stopSequenceAcquisition>)(cameraLabel) | ➕ | [Images &amp; buffer](<#cmmcoreplus-images-buffer>) | Stops streaming camera sequence acquisition.<br>*Why override?* To emit a `sequenceAcquisitionStopped` event. |
| [`stopSLMSequence`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.stopSLMSequence>)(slmLabel) |  | [SLMs](<#cmmcoreplus-slms>) | Stops the SLM sequence if previously started |
| [`stopStageSequence`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.stopStageSequence>)(stageLabel) |  | [Hardware sequencing](<#cmmcoreplus-hardware-sequencing>) | Stops an ongoing sequence of triggered events in a stage. |
| [`stopXYStageSequence`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.stopXYStageSequence>)(xyStageLabel) |  | [Hardware sequencing](<#cmmcoreplus-hardware-sequencing>) | Stops an ongoing sequence of triggered events in an XY stage. |
| [`supportsDeviceDetection`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.supportsDeviceDetection>)(deviceLabel) |  | [Devices](<#cmmcoreplus-devices>) | Return whether or not the device supports automatic device detection (i.e. |
| [`systemBusy`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.systemBusy>)() |  | [Devices](<#cmmcoreplus-devices>) | Checks the busy status of the entire system. |
| [`systemConfigurationFile`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.systemConfigurationFile>)() | ✨ | [System state &amp; config files](<#cmmcoreplus-system-state-config-files>) | Return the path to the last loaded system configuration file, or `None`. |
| [`unloadAllDevices`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.unloadAllDevices>)() | ➕ | [Devices](<#cmmcoreplus-devices>) | Unload all devices from the core and reset all configuration data.<br>*Why override?* To add logging. |
| [`unloadDevice`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.unloadDevice>)(label) |  | [Devices](<#cmmcoreplus-devices>) | Unloads the device from the core and adjusts all configuration data. |
| [`unloadLibrary`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.unloadLibrary>)(moduleName) |  | [Devices](<#cmmcoreplus-devices>) | Forcefully unload a library. |
| [`unsetDeviceTimeout`](<#pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus.unsetDeviceTimeout>)(label) |  | [Devices](<#cmmcoreplus-devices>) | Removes any per-device timeout, restoring the default. |

## General

### describe

```python
describe(
    sort: str | None = None,
    show_config_groups: bool = False,
    show_available: bool = False,
) -> None
```

Print information table with the current configuration.

Intended to provide a quick overview of the microscope configuration during interactive terminal usage.

### getAPIVersionInfo

```python
getAPIVersionInfo() -> str
```

Returns the module and device interface versions.

### getMMCoreVersionMajor




```python
getMMDeviceDeviceInterfaceVersion() -> int
```

### getMMDeviceModuleInterfaceVersion

```python
getMMDeviceModuleInterfaceVersion() -> int
```

### getVersionInfo

```python
getVersionInfo() -> str
```

Displays core version.

### instance

```python
instance() -> CMMCorePlus
```

Return the global singleton instance of `CMMCorePlus`.

In many cases, a single instance of `CMMCorePlus` is all that will be created in a given session. This class method provides a convenient way to access that instance.

> [!TIP]
>
> Creating/accessing a `CMMCorePlus` object using `CMMCorePlus.instance()` is a convenient way to access the same core instance from multiple places in your code. All widgets in [`pymmcore-widgets`](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets>) also use `CMMCorePlus.instance()` by default, so any widgets you use will automatically connect to the same core instance without any additional configuration.
>
> Attempts *are* made to make it thread-safe. But please open an issue if you find any problems.

### noop

```python
noop() -> None
```

A static method that does nothing.

### reset

```python
reset() -> None
```

Unloads all devices from the core, clears all configuration data and property blocks.

### sleep

```python
sleep(intervalMs: float) -> None
```

Waits (blocks the calling thread) for specified time in milliseconds.

### state

```python
state(
    *, cached: bool = True, include_time: bool = False, **_kwargs: Any
) -> SummaryMetaV1
```

Return info on the current state of the core.

## Acquisition engine &amp; events

### events

```python
events: PCoreSignaler
```

Signaler for core events.

✨ *This attribute is new in `CMMCorePlus`.*

This attribute allows connecting callbacks to various events that occur within the core. See `pymmcore_plus.core.events.PCoreSignaler` documentation for details of the available signals, and how to connect to them.

### mda

```python
mda: MDARunner
```

Return the `MDARunner` for this `CMMCorePlus` instance.

✨ *This attribute is new in `CMMCorePlus`.*

### register\_mda\_engine

```python
register_mda_engine(engine: PMDAEngine) -> None
```

Set the MDA Engine to be used on `run_mda`.

This will unregister the previous engine and emit an `mdaEngineRegistered` signal. The current Engine must not be running an MDA in order to register a new engine.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `engine` | `PMDAEngine` | Any object conforming to the PMDAEngine protocol. | *required* |

### registerCallback

```python
registerCallback(*_: Never) -> Never
```

*registerCallback is disallowed in pymmcore-plus!*

If you want to connect callbacks to events, use the `CMMCorePlus.events` property instead.

### run\_mda

```python
run_mda(
    events: Iterable[MDAEvent],
    *,
    output: SingleOutput | Sequence[SingleOutput] | None = None,
    block: bool = False,
    dimension_overrides: dict[str, DimensionOverride] | None = None,
) -> Thread
```

Run a sequence of useq.MDAEvent on a new thread.

The currently registered MDAEngine (`core.mda.engine`) will be responsible for executing the acquisition.

After starting the sequence you can pause or cancel the mda with the mda object's `set_paused` and `cancel` methods.

Parameters:

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Thread` | The thread the sequence is running on. Use `thread.join()` to block until done, or `thread.is_alive()` to check if the sequence is complete. |

## System state &amp; config files

### getSystemState

```python
getSystemState(*, native: bool = False) -> Configuration | Configuration
```

Return the entire system state.

**Why Override?** The `pymmcore_plus.Configuration` object returned when `native=False` (the default) provides a nicer `Mapping` interface. Pass `native=True` to get the original `pymmcore.Configuration` object.

### getSystemStateCache

```python
getSystemStateCache(*, native: Literal[True]) -> Configuration
```

```python
getSystemStateCache(*, native: Literal[False] = False) -> Configuration
```

```python
getSystemStateCache(*, native: bool = False) -> Configuration | Configuration
```

Return the entire system state from cache.

**Why Override?** The `pymmcore_plus.Configuration` object returned when `native=False` (the default) provides a nicer `Mapping` interface. Pass `native=True` to get the original `pymmcore.Configuration` object.

### loadSystemConfiguration

```python
loadSystemConfiguration(fileName: str | Path = 'MMConfig_demo.cfg') -> None
```

Load a system config file conforming to the MM `.cfg` format.

[https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager\_Configuration\_Guide\#configuration-file-syntax](<https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager_Configuration_Guide#configuration-file-syntax>)

For relative paths, the current working directory is first checked, then the then device adapter path is checked.

**Why Override?** This method overrides the default implementation to A) allow loading the `MMConfig_demo.cfg` file by default, B) to provide more flexible path declarations and C) better error messages when the file cannot be found.

### loadSystemState

```python
loadSystemState(fileName: str) -> None
```

Loads the system configuration from the text file conforming to the MM specific format.

### saveSystemConfiguration

```python
saveSystemConfiguration(filename: str) -> None
```

Saves the current system configuration to a text file.

**Why Override?** To also save pixel size configurations.

### saveSystemState

```python
saveSystemState(fileName: str) -> None
```

Saves the current system state to a text file of the MM specific format.

### setContext

```python
setContext(**kwargs: Unpack[SetContextKwargs]) -> Iterator[None]
```

Set core properties in a context restoring the initial values on exit.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `**kwargs` | `Any` | Keyword arguments may be any `Name` for which `get<Name>` and `set<Name>` methods exist (where the first letter in `<Name>` may be either lower or upper case). For example, `setContext(exposure=10)` will call `setExposure(10)` when entering the context and `setExposure(<initial>)` when exiting the context. If the property is not found, a warning is logged and the property is skipped. If the value is a tuple, it is unpacked and passed to the `set<Name>` method (but lists are not unpacked). | `{}` |

Examples:

```python
core = CMMCorePlus.instance()

with core.setContext(autoShutter=False):
    assert not core.getAutoShutter()
    # do other stuff
    ...

# autoShutter is restored to its original value when the context exits
assert core.getAutoShutter()
```

### setSystemState

```python
setSystemState(conf: Configuration) -> None
```

Sets all properties contained in the Configuration object.

```python
systemConfigurationFile() -> str | None
```

Return the path to the last loaded system configuration file, or `None`.

```python
updateSystemStateCache() -> None
```

Updates the state of the entire hardware.

### waitForSystem

```python
waitForSystem() -> None
```

Blocks until all devices in the system become ready (not-busy).

## Devices

### detectDevice

```python
detectDevice(deviceLabel: str) -> DeviceDetectionStatus
```

Tries to communicate to a device through a given serial port.

Used to automate discovery of correct serial port. Also configures the serial port correctly.

**Why Override?** The returned `pymmcore_plus.DeviceDetectionStatus` enum is more interpretable than the raw `int` returned by `pymmcore`

### deviceBusy


### deviceTypeBusy

```python

```

Checks the busy status for all devices of the specific type.

### getAdapterObject

```python
getAdapterObject(library_name: str) -> DeviceAdapter
```

Return an `Adapter` object bound to library\_name on this core.

`Adapter` objects are a convenient object oriented way to interact with device adapters. They allow you to call any method on `CMMCore` that normally requires a `library_name` as the first argument as an argument-free method on the `Adapter` object.


### getCurrentDeviceOfType

```python
getCurrentDeviceOfType(
    device_type: DeviceTypesWithCurrent,
) -> DeviceLabel | Literal[""]
```

Return the current device of type `device_type`.

Only the following device types have a "current" device: - CameraDevice - ShutterDevice - StageDevice - XYStageDevice - AutoFocusDevice - SLMDevice - GalvoDevice - ImageProcessorDevice

Calling this method with any other device type will raise a `ValueError`.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `device_type` | `DeviceType` | The type of device to get the current device for. See `DeviceType` for a list of device types. | *required* |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `str` | The label of the current device of type `device_type`. If no device of that type is currently set, an empty string is returned. |

Raises:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `ValueError` | If the core does not have the concept of a "current" device of the provided `device_type`. |

```python
getDeviceObject(
    device_label: str, device_type: type[_DT] | DeviceType = Any
) -> _DT | Device
```

Return a `Device` object bound to device\_label on this core.

`Device` objects are a convenient object oriented way to interact with devices. They allow you to call any method on `CMMCore` that normally requires a `deviceLabel` as the first argument as an argument-free method on the `Device` object.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `device_label` | `str` | Device label to get a device object for. | *required* |

Examples:

```pycon
>>> core = CMMCorePlus()
>>> cam = core.getDeviceObject("DemoCamera")
>>> cam.isLoaded()
False
>>> cam.load("DemoCamera", "DCam")
>>> cam.isLoaded()
True
>>> cam.initialize()
```

get the device schema

```pycon
>>> cam.schema()
{
    'title': 'DCam',
    'description': 'Demo camera',
    'type': 'object',
    'properties': {
        'HubID': {'type': 'string', 'readOnly': True, 'default': ''},
        'MaximumExposureMs': {'type': 'number', 'preInit': True},
        'TransposeCorrection': {'type': 'boolean'},
        'TransposeMirrorX': {'type': 'boolean'},
        'TransposeMirrorY': {'type': 'boolean'},
        'TransposeXY': {'type': 'boolean'}
    }
}
```

### getDeviceSchema

```python
getDeviceSchema(device_label: str) -> DeviceSchema
```

Return JSON-schema describing device `device_label` and its properties.

✨ *This method is new in `CMMCorePlus`. It provides a convenient way to get all of the information about a device in a single call.*

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `DeviceSchema` | JSON-schema describing device `device_label` and its properties. |

Examples:

```pycon
>>> core = CMMCorePlus()
>>> core.loadDevice("DemoCamera", "DemoCamera", "DCam")
>>> core.getDeviceSchema("DemoCamera")
{
    'title': 'DCam',
    'description': 'Demo camera',
    'type': 'object',
    'properties': {
        'HubID': {'type': 'string', 'readOnly': True, 'default': ''},
        'MaximumExposureMs': {'type': 'number', 'preInit': True},
        'TransposeCorrection': {'type': 'boolean'},
        'TransposeMirrorX': {'type': 'boolean'},
        'TransposeMirrorY': {'type': 'boolean'},
        'TransposeXY': {'type': 'boolean'}
    }
}
```

### setDeviceAdapterSearchPaths

```python
setDeviceAdapterSearchPaths(paths: Sequence[str]) -> None
```

Set the device adapter search paths.

**Why Override?** In cases where MM device adapters use dynamically loaded libraries, the device adapter search paths must also be added to the `PATH` environment variable (e.g. [https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore/issues/28](<https://github.com/micro-manager/pymmcore/issues/28>)). This method overrides the default implementation to ensure that the `PATH` environment variable is updated when the device adapter search paths are changed.

### getPropertyObject

```python
getPropertyObject(device_label: str, property_name: str) -> DeviceProperty
```

Return a DeviceProperty object bound to a device/property on this core.

`DeviceProperty` objects are a convenient object oriented way to interact with a specific device properties. They allow you to call any method on `CMMCore` that normally requires a `deviceLabel` and `propertyName` as the first two arguments as an argument-free method on the `DeviceProperty` object.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `device_label` | `str` | Device label to get a property object for. | *required* |
| `property_name` | `str` | Property name to get a property object for. | *required* |

Examples:

```pycon
>>> core = CMMCorePlus()
>>> core.loadDevice("DemoCamera", "DemoCamera", "DCam")
>>> core.initializeDevice("DemoCamera")
>>> core.setCameraDevice("DemoCamera")
>>> exposure = core.getPropertyObject("DemoCamera", "Exposure")
>>> exposure.type()
<PropertyType.Float: 2>
>>> exposure.upperLimit()
10000.0
```

get/set property values easily:

```pycon
>>> exposure.value
10.0
>>> exposure.value = 5.0
>>> exposure.value
5.0
>>> core.getExposure()  # changes reflected in core
5.0
```

### getPropertyType

```python
getPropertyType(label: str, propName: str) -> PropertyType
```

Return the intrinsic property type for a given device and property.

**Why Override?** The returned `pymmcore_plus.PropertyType` enum is more interpretable than the raw `int` returned by `pymmcore`

### iterProperties

```python
iterProperties(
    property_type: int | Iterable[int] | None = ...,
    property_name_pattern: str | Pattern | None = ...,
    *,
    device_type: int | Iterable[int] | None = ...,
    device_label: str | Pattern | None = ...,
    has_limits: bool | None = None,
    is_read_only: bool | None = None,
    is_sequenceable: bool | None = None,
    as_object: Literal[False],
) -> Iterator[tuple[str, str]]
```

```python
iterProperties(
    property_type: int | Iterable[int] | None = ...,
    property_name_pattern: str | Pattern | None = ...,
    *,
    device_type: int | Iterable[int] | None = ...,
    device_label: str | Pattern | None = ...,
    has_limits: bool | None = None,
    is_read_only: bool | None = None,
    is_sequenceable: bool | None = None,
    as_object: Literal[True] = ...,
) -> Iterator[DeviceProperty]
```

```python
iterProperties(
    property_type: int | Iterable[int] | None = None,
    property_name_pattern: str | Pattern | None = None,
    *,
    device_type: int | Iterable[int] | None = None,
    device_label: str | Pattern | None = None,
    has_limits: bool | None = None,
    is_read_only: bool | None = None,
    is_sequenceable: bool | None = None,
    as_object: bool = True,
) -> Iterator[DeviceProperty] | Iterator[tuple[str, str]]
```

Iterate over currently loaded (device\_label, property\_name) pairs.

It offers a convenient way to iterate over loaded devices, optionally filtering by `DeviceType` and/or device label. It can also yields `DeviceProperty` objects if `as_object` is `True` (the default).

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `property_type` | `int \| Sequence[int] \| None` | PropertyType (or types) to filter by, by default all property types will be yielded. | `None` |
| `property_name_pattern` | `str \| Pattern \| None` | Property name to filter by, by default all property names will be yielded. May be a compiled regular expression or a string, in which case it will be compiled with `re.IGNORECASE`. | `None` |
| `device_type` | `DeviceType \| None` | DeviceType to filter by, by default all device types will be yielded. | `None` |
| `device_label` | `str \| None` | Device label to filter by, by default all device labels will be yielded. | `None` |
| `has_limits` | `bool \| None` | If provided, only properties with `hasPropertyLimits` matching this value will be yielded. | `None` |
| `is_read_only` | `bool \| None` | If provided, only properties with `isPropertyReadOnly` matching this value will be yielded. | `None` |
| `is_sequenceable` | `bool \| None` | If provided only properties with `isPropertySequenceable` matching this value will be yielded. | `None` |
| `as_object` | `bool` | If `True`, `DeviceProperty` objects will be yielded instead of `(device_label, property_name)` tuples. By default True | `True` |

Yields:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `DeviceProperty \| tuple[str, str]` | `DeviceProperty` objects (if `as_object==True`) or 2-tuples of (device\_name, property\_name) |

### setProperty

```python
setProperty(
    label: str, propName: str, propValue: bool | float | int | str
) -> None
```

Set property named `propName` on device `label` to `propValue`.

**Why Override?** In `MMCore`, the calling of the `onPropertyChanged` callback is left to the underlying device adapter, which means it is not always called. This method overrides the default implementation to ensure that `events.propertyChanged` is *always* emitted when `setProperty` has been called and the property Value has actually changed.

### updateCoreProperties

```python
updateCoreProperties() -> None
```

Updates CoreProperties (currently all Core properties are devices types) with the loaded hardware.

## Config groups &amp; presets

### channelGroup\_pattern

```python
channelGroup_pattern: Pattern
```

The regex pattern used to identify channel groups.

It is the regex used by `getOrGuessChannelGroup` to find a config group likely to be a channel group in `getAvailableConfigGroups` if `getChannelGroup` returns `None`.

By default:

```text
re.compile("(chan{1,2}(el)?|filt(er)?)s?", re.IGNORECASE)
```

### defineConfig

```python
    propName: str | None = None,
    value: str | None = None,
) -> None
```

Defines a configuration.

**Why Override?** To emit a `configDefined` event. Also, if `groupName` is not a defined group, then `defineConfigGroup(groupName)` is called.

### getConfigGroupObject

```python
getConfigGroupObject(
    group_name: str, allow_missing: bool = False
```

Return a `ConfigGroup` object bound to group\_name on this core.

`ConfigGroup` objects are a convenient object oriented way to interact with configuration groups (i.e. groups of [Configuration Presets](<https://micro-manager.org/Micro-Manager_Configuration_Guide#configuration-presets>) in Micro-Manager). They allow you to call any method on `CMMCore` that normally requires a `groupName` as the first argument as an argument-free method on the `ConfigGroup` object.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `group_name` | `str` | Configuration group name to get a config group object for. | *required* |
| `allow_missing` | `bool` | If `False` and the `ConfigGroup` does not exist, a `KeyError` will be raised. By default False. | `False` |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `ConfigGroup` | `ConfigGroup` object bound to `group_name` on this core. |

### getOrGuessChannelGroup

```python
getOrGuessChannelGroup() -> list[str]
```

Get the channelGroup or find a likely set of candidates.

If the group is not defined via `.getChannelGroup` then likely candidates will be found by searching for config groups with names that match this object's `channelGroup_pattern` property. This is a settable property with a default value of:

```text
reg = re.compile("(chan{1,2}(el)?|filt(er)?)s?", re.IGNORECASE)
```

### getROI

```python
getROI() -> Rectangle
```

```python
getROI(label: DeviceLabel | str) -> Rectangle
```

```python
getROI() -> Rectangle
```

Return the current hardware region of interest for a camera.

If multiple ROIs are set, this method instead returns a rectangle that describes the image that the camera will generate. The coordinates are in units of binned pixels. That is, conceptually, binning is applied before the ROI.

Returns \[0,0,0,0\] if no camera is selected.

### fixImage

```python

```

Fix img shape/dtype based on `self.getNumberOfComponents()`.

convert images with n\_components \> 1 to a shape (w, h, num\_components) and dtype `img.dtype.itemsize//ncomp`

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `img` | `ndarray` | input image | *required* |
| `ncomponents` | `int` | number of components in the image, by default `self.getNumberOfComponents()` | `None` |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `ndarray` | output image (possibly new shape and dtype) |

### getLastImageAndMD

```python
getLastImageAndMD(
    channel: int, slice: int, *, fix: bool = True
) -> tuple[ndarray, Metadata]
```

```python
getLastImageAndMD(*, fix: bool = True) -> tuple[ndarray, Metadata]
```

```python
getLastImageAndMD(
    channel: int | None = None, slice: int | None = None, *, fix: bool = True
) -> tuple[ndarray, Metadata]
```

Return last image from the circular buffer along with metadata.

This is a convenience method that is very similar to `getLastImageMD`, except that it doesn't require instantiating a `MetaData` object first. It returns a tuple containing the image and a `pymmcore_plus.Metadata` object.

It also adds a `fix` parameter, which reshapes multi-component images (like RGB images) to (w, h, n\_components) using `fixImage` by default.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `channel` | `int` | Channel index, by default None | `None` |
| `slice` | `int` | Slice index, by default None | `None` |
| `fix` | `bool` | If `True` (the default), then images with n\_components \> 1 (like RGB images) will be reshaped to (w, h, n\_components) using `fixImage`. | `True` |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `tuple[ndarray, Metadata]` | Image and metadata |

### guessObjectiveDevices

```python
guessObjectiveDevices() -> list[str]
```

Find any loaded devices that are likely to be an Objective/Nosepiece.

Likely matches are loaded StateDevices with names that match this object's `objective_device_pattern` property. This is a settable property with a default value of::

```text
re.compile("(.+)?(nosepiece|obj(ective)?)(turret)?s?", re.IGNORECASE)
```

### objective\_device\_pattern

```python
objective_device_pattern: Pattern
```

Pattern used to guess objective device labels.

It is the regex used by `guessObjectiveDevices` to find any devices that are likely to be objective devices.

By default:

```text
re.compile("(.+)?(nosepiece|obj(ective)?)(turret)?s?", re.IGNORECASE)
```

### setState

```python
setState(stateDeviceLabel: str, state: int) -> None
```

Set state (by position) on `stateDeviceLabel`, with reliable event emission.

**Why Override?** In `MMCore`, the calling of the `onPropertyChanged` callback is left to the underlying device adapter, which means it is not always called. This method overrides the default implementation to ensure that `events.propertyChanged` is *always* emitted when `setProperty` has been called and the property Value has actually changed.

### setStateLabel

```python
setStateLabel(stateDeviceLabel: str, stateLabel: str) -> None
```

Set state (by label) on `stateDeviceLabel`, with reliable event emission.

**Why Override?** In `MMCore`, the calling of the `onPropertyChanged` callback is left to the underlying device adapter, which means it is not always called. This method overrides the default implementation to ensure that `events.propertyChanged` is *always* emitted when `setProperty` has been called and the property Value has actually changed.

### setAutoFocusDevice

```python

```

### setAutoFocusOffset

```python
setAutoFocusOffset(offset: float) -> None
```

Applies offset the one-shot focusing device.

In micro-manager, there is some variability in the way that autofocus devices are implemented. Some have a separate offset device, while others can directly set the offset of an associated device. As a result, calling `setAutoFocusOffset`, may or may not do anything depending on the current autofocus device.

This method attempts to detect known autofocus devices that have a separate offset device, and for those it also sets the position of the offset device.

### getPixelSizedxdz

```python
getPixelSizedxdz() -> float
```

```python
getPixelSizedxdz(cached: bool) -> float
```

```python
getPixelSizedxdz(resolutionID: PixelSizeConfigName | str) -> float
```

```python
getPixelSizedxdz() -> float
```

Returns the angle between the camera's x axis and the axis (direction) of the z drive.

This angle is dimensionless (i.e. the ratio of the translation in x caused by a translation in z, i.e. dx / dz). This angle can be different for different z drives (if there are multiple Z drives in the system, please add the Core-Focus device to the pixel size configuration). See: [https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager/issues/1984](<https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager/issues/1984>)

### getPixelSizedydz


```python

```

```python
getPixelSizedydz() -> float
```

Returns the angle between the camera's y axis and the axis (direction) of the z drive.

This angle is dimensionless (i.e. the ratio of the translation in x caused by a translation in z, i.e. dy / dz). This angle can be different for different z drives (if there are multiple Z drives in the system, please add the Core-Focus device to the pixel size configuration). See: [https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager/issues/1984](<https://github.com/micro-manager/micro-manager/issues/1984>)

## Hardware sequencing

### canSequenceEvents

```python
canSequenceEvents(e1: MDAEvent, e2: MDAEvent, cur_length: int = -1) -> bool
```

Check whether two `useq.MDAEvent` are sequenceable by this core instance.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Deprecated**
>
> `canSequenceEvents` is deprecated. To see how this core will combine a list of events into `SequencedEvent` objects, use `iter_sequenced_events`: `list(iter_sequenced_events(core, [e1, e2]))`.

Micro-Manager calls hardware triggering "sequencing". Two events can be sequenced if *all* device properties that are changing between the first and second event support sequencing.

If `cur_length` is provided, it is used to determine if the sequence is "full" (i.e. the sequence is already at the maximum length) as determined by the `...SequenceMaxLength()` method corresponding to the device property.

See: [https://micro-manager.org/Hardware-based\_Synchronization\_in\_Micro-Manager](<https://micro-manager.org/Hardware-based_Synchronization_in_Micro-Manager>)

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e1` | `MDAEvent` | The first event. | *required* |
| `e2` | `MDAEvent` | The second event. | *required* |
| `cur_length` | `int` | The current length of the sequence. Used when checking `.get<...>SequenceMaxLength` for a given property. If the current length is greater than the max length, the events cannot be sequenced. By default -1, which means the current length is not checked. | `-1` |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `bool` | True if the events can be sequenced, False otherwise. |

Examples:

> [!NOTE]
>
> The results here will depend on the current state of the core and devices.

```python
>>> from useq import MDAEvent
>>> core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
>>> core.loadSystemConfiguration()
>>> core.canSequenceEvents(MDAEvent(), MDAEvent())
True
>>> core.canSequenceEvents(MDAEvent(x_pos=1), MDAEvent(x_pos=2))
False
>>> core.canSequenceEvents(
...     MDAEvent(channel={'config': 'DAPI'}),
...     MDAEvent(channel={'config': 'FITC'})
... )
False
```

## Logging &amp; errors

### debugLogEnabled

```python
debugLogEnabled() -> bool
```

Indicates if logging of debug messages is enabled

### enableDebugLog

```python
enableDebugLog(enable: bool) -> None
```

Enable or disable logging of debug messages.

### enableFeature

```python
enableFeature(name: FeatureFlag | str, enable: bool) -> None
```

Enable or disable the given Core feature.

Core features control whether experimental functionality (which is subject to breaking changes) is exposed, or whether stricter API usage is enforced.

Currently switchable features:

- "StrictInitializationChecks" (default: disabled) When enabled, an exception is thrown when an operation requiring an initialized device is attempted on a device that is not successfully initialized. When disabled, no exception is thrown and a warning is logged (and the operation may potentially cause incorrect behavior or a crash).
- "ParallelDeviceInitialization" (default: enabled) When enabled, serial ports are initialized in serial order, and all other devices are in parallel, using multiple threads, one per device module. Early testing shows this to be reliable, but switch this off when issues are encountered during device initialization.

### enableStderrLog

```python
enableStderrLog(enable: bool) -> None
```

### setSLMImage

```python
setSLMImage(slmLabel: DeviceLabel | str, pixels: NDArray[uint8]) -> None
```

```python
setSLMImage(slmLabel: DeviceLabel | str, pixels: Any) -> None
```

```python
setSLMImage(slmLabel: DeviceLabel | str, pixels: NDArray[uint8]) -> None
```

Write an image to the SLM .

When passing a numpy array, `pixels` must be one of the following:

- a 2D numpy array \[h,w\] of uint8s, representing a grayscale image to write to the SLM.
- a 3D numpy array \[h,w,3\] of uint8s with 3 color channels \[R,G,B\], representing an imgRGB32 image to write to the SLM.

In both cases, the dimensions of the array should match the width and height of the SLM.

> [!WARNING]
>
> SLM might convert grayscale to binary internally.

Sets the volume of fluid in the pump in uL.

Note it does not withdraw upto this amount. It is merely to inform MM of the volume in a prefilled pump.

### volumetricPumpHome

```python
volumetricPumpHome(pumpLabel: str) -> None
```

Homes the volumetric pump.

### volumetricPumpRequiresHoming

```python
volumetricPumpRequiresHoming(pumpLabel: str) -> bool
```

Return True if the volumetric pump requires homing.

### volumetricPumpStop

```python
volumetricPumpStop(pumpLabel: str) -> None
```

Stops the volumetric pump.

#### devicePropertyChanged

```python
devicePropertyChanged(
    device: str, property: str | None = None
) -> _PropertySignal
```

Return object to connect/disconnect to device/property-specific changes.

Note that the callback provided to `.connect()` must take *two* parameters (property\_name, new\_value) if only `device` is provided, and *one* parameter (new\_value) of both `device` and `property` are provided.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `device` | `str` | A device label | *required* |
| `property` | `Optional[str]` | Optional property label. If not provided, all property changes on `device` will trigger an event emission. by default None | `None` |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `_PropertySignal` | Object with `connect` and `disconnect` methods that attach a callback to the change event of a specific property or device. |

Examples:

```pycon
>>> core.events.devicePropertyChanged("Camera", "Gain").connect(callback)
>>> core.events.devicePropertyChanged("Camera").connect(callback)
```

## Re-exports

These can also be imported from this module, but each is documented under its shortest import path (linked below).

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `CMMCoreSignaler` | Signals that will be emitted from CMMCorePlus objects (psygnal backend). |
| `PCoreSignaler` | Declares the protocol for all signals that will be emitted from CMMCorePlus. |

# pymmcore\_plus.core

`CMMCorePlus` and its supporting classes.

This includes the object-oriented views onto devices, properties and config groups, the enums that replace pymmcore's integer constants, and hardware sequencing helpers.

**Submodules**

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `events` | Signals emitted by `CMMCorePlus.events`. |

**Classes**

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `AutoFocusDevice` |  |
| `CameraDevice` |  |
| `CoreDevice` |  |
| `GalvoDevice` |  |
| `GenericDevice` |  |
| `HubDevice` |  |
| `ImageProcessorDevice` |  |
| `MagnifierDevice` |  |
| `SLMDevice` |  |
| `SequencedEvent` | Subclass of MDAEvent that represents a sequence of triggered events. |
| `SerialDevice` |  |
| `ShutterDevice` |  |
| `SignalIODevice` |  |
| `StageDevice` |  |
| `StateDevice` |  |
| `XYStageDevice` |  |

**Functions**

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `iter_sequenced_events` | Iterate over a sequence of MDAEvents, yielding SequencedEvents when possible. |

## Functions

### iter\_sequenced\_events

```python
iter_sequenced_events(
    core: CMMCorePlus, events: Iterable[MDAEvent]
) -> Iterator[MDAEvent | SequencedEvent]
```

Iterate over a sequence of MDAEvents, yielding SequencedEvents when possible.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `core` | `CMMCorePlus` | The core object to use for determining sequenceable properties. | *required* |
| `events` | `Iterable[MDAEvent]` | The events to iterate over. | *required* |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Iterator[MDAEvent \| SequencedEvent]` | A new iterator that will combine multiple MDAEvents into a single SequencedEvent when possible, based on the sequenceable properties of the core object. Note that `SequencedEvent` itself is a subclass of `MDAEvent`, but it's up to the engine to check `isinstance(event, SequencedEvent)` in order to handle SequencedEvents differently. |

# pymmcore\_plus.experimental

Experimental features. The APIs here may change in future releases.

**Submodules**

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `simulate` | Simulated microscope sample for testing and development. |
| `unicore` | Pure-Python device adapters, used alongside C++ devices with `UniMMCore`. |

# pymmcore\_plus.experimental.simulate

Simulated microscope sample for testing and development.

This module provides tools for creating virtual microscope samples that integrate with CMMCorePlus. When a sample is installed on a core, image acquisition returns rendered images based on the sample objects and current microscope state (stage position, exposure, pixel size, etc.).

Examples:

Create a sample with some objects and use it with a core:

```pycon
>>> from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus
>>> from pymmcore_plus.experimental.simulate import (
...     Sample,
...     Point,
...     Line,
...     Rectangle,
...     RenderConfig,
... )
>>>
>>> # Create core and load config
>>> core = CMMCorePlus.instance()
>>> core.loadSystemConfiguration()
>>>
>>> # Define sample objects (coordinates in microns)
>>> sample = Sample(
...     [
...         Point(0, 0, intensity=200, radius=5),
...         Point(50, 50, intensity=150, radius=3),
...         Line((0, 0), (100, 100), intensity=100),
...         Rectangle((20, 20), width=30, height=20, intensity=180, fill=True),
...     ]
... )
>>>
>>> # Use as context manager
>>> with sample.patch(core):
...     core.snapImage()
...     img = core.getImage()  # Returns rendered simulation
...     print(img.shape, img.dtype)
```

Custom render configuration:

```pycon
>>> config = RenderConfig(
...     noise_std=5.0,  # More noise
...     defocus_scale=0.2,  # More blur with Z
...     shot_noise=False,  # Disable shot noise
...     bit_depth=16,  # 16-bit output
... )
>>> sample = Sample([Point(0, 0)], config=config)
```

Manual install/uninstall:

```pycon
>>> sample.install(core)
>>> # ... do stuff ...
>>> sample.uninstall()
```

### Bitmap

```python
Bitmap(
    top_left: tuple[float, float],
    data: ndarray | Image | str,
    bitmap_scale: float = 1.0,
)
```

Bases: `SampleObject`

A bitmap image placed in the sample.

The bitmap is placed at a fixed position and scale in world coordinates. Each pixel of the bitmap corresponds to one world unit.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `top_left` | `tuple[float, float]` | Top-left corner (x, y) in world units. | *required* |
| `data` | `ndarray \| Image \| str` | Image data as numpy array, PIL Image, or path to image file. | *required* |
| `bitmap_scale` | `float` | World units per bitmap pixel. Default 1.0 (1 pixel = 1 world unit). | `1.0` |

```python
    center: tuple[float, float],
    radius: float,
    n_sides: int,
    rotation: float = 0,
    intensity: int = 255,
    fill: bool = False,
    width: int = 1,
    _vertices: list[tuple[float, float]] = list(),
)
```

Bases: `SampleObject`

A regular polygon inscribed in a circle.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `center` | `tuple[float, float]` | Center (x, y) in world units. | *required* |
| `radius` | `float` | Radius of bounding circle in world units. | *required* |
| `n_sides` | `int` | Number of sides. | *required* |
| `rotation` | `float` | Rotation angle in degrees. Default 0. | `0` |
| `intensity` | `int` | Brightness value (0-255). Default 255. | `255` |
| `fill` | `bool` | If True, fill the polygon. Default False. | `False` |
| `width` | `int` | Outline width in pixels (only used if fill=False). Default 1. | `1` |

### SampleObject

Bases: `ABC`

Base class for drawable sample objects.

All coordinates are in world-space (typically microns). Objects are rendered by calling `draw()` with a transform function that converts world coordinates to pixel coordinates.

Subclasses must implement: - `draw()`: Render the object onto a PIL ImageDraw context - `get_bounds()`: Return the bounding box in world coordinates - `intensity`: Property returning the object's intensity value

#### intensity

```python
intensity: int
```

#### draw

```python
draw(draw_context: ImageDraw, transform: TransformFn, scale: float) -> None
```

Draw this object onto the given context.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `draw_context` | `ImageDraw` | PIL ImageDraw context to draw on. | *required* |
| `transform` | `TransformFn` | Function to convert (world\_x, world\_y) to (pixel\_x, pixel\_y). | *required* |
| `scale` | `float` | Pixels per world unit (e.g., pixels per micron). | *required* |

#### get\_bounds

```python
get_bounds() -> Bounds
```

Return bounding box in world coordinates.

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Bounds` | Tuple of (left, top, right, bottom) in world units. |

```python
draw_cv2(img: ndarray, transform: TransformFn, scale: float) -> None
```

| Name | Type | Description | Default |

| `transform` | `TransformFn` | Function to convert (world\_x, world\_y) to (pixel\_x, pixel\_y). | *required* |
| `scale` | `float` | Pixels per world unit. | *required* |
