## Well plates

## useq.WellPlatePlan

Bases: `UseqModel`, `Sequence[Position]`

A plan for acquiring images from a multi-well plate.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `plate` | `WellPlate` | The well-plate definition. Minimally including rows, columns, and well spacing. If expressed as a string, it is assumed to be a key in `useq.registered_well_plate_keys`. |
| `a1_center_xy` | `tuple[float, float]` | The stage coordinates in µm of the center of well A1 (top-left corner). |
| `rotation` | `float \| None` | The rotation angle in degrees (anti-clockwise) of the plate. If None, no rotation is applied. If expressed as a string, it is assumed to be an angle with units (e.g., "5°", "4 rad", "4.5deg"). If expressed as an arraylike, it is assumed to be a 2x2 rotation matrix `[[cos, -sin], [sin, cos]]`, or a 4-tuple `(cos, -sin, sin, cos)`. |
| `selected_wells` | `tuple[tuple[int, ...], tuple[int, ...]] \| None` | Any \<=2-dimensional index expression for selecting wells. for example: - None -\> No wells are selected. - slice(0) -\> (also) select no wells. - slice(None) -\> Selects all wells. - 0 -\> Selects the first row. - \[0, 1, 2\] -\> Selects the first three rows. - slice(1, 5) -\> selects wells from row 1 to row 4. - (2, slice(1, 4)) -\> select wells in the second row and only columns 1 to 3. - (\[1, 2\], \[3, 4\]) -\> select wells in (row, column): (1, 3) and (2, 4) |
| `well_points_plan` | `GridRowsColumns \| GridWidthHeight \| RandomPoints \| RelativePosition` | A plan for acquiring images within each well. This can be a single position (for a single image per well), a GridRowsColumns (for a grid of images), or RandomPoints (for random points within each well). |

## useq.WellPlate

Bases: `FrozenModel`

A multi-well plate definition.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rows` | `int` | The number of rows in the plate. Must be \> 0. |
| `columns` | `int` | The number of columns in the plate. Must be \> 0. |
| `well_spacing` | `tuple[float, float]` | The center-to-center distance in mm (pitch) between wells in the x and y directions. If a single value is provided, it is used for both x and y. |
| `well_size` | `tuple[float, float]` | The size in mm of each well in the x and y directions. If the well is squared or rectangular, this is the width and height of the well. If the well is circular, this is the diameter. If a single value is provided, it is used for both x and y. |
| `circular_wells` | `bool` | Whether wells are circular (True) or squared/rectangular (False). |
| `name` | `str` | A name for the plate. |

## useq.register\_well\_plates

```python
register_well_plates(
    plates: Mapping[str, PlateOrKwargs], /, **kwargs: PlateOrKwargs
) -> None
```

```python
register_well_plates(
    plates: Iterable[tuple[str, PlateOrKwargs]], /, **kwargs: PlateOrKwargs
) -> None
```

```python
register_well_plates(**kwargs: PlateOrKwargs) -> None
```

```python
register_well_plates(
    plates: Mapping[str, PlateOrKwargs]
    | Iterable[tuple[str, PlateOrKwargs]] = (),
    /,
    **kwargs: PlateOrKwargs,
) -> None
```

Register well-plate definitions to allow lookup by key.

Added keys will override existing keys if they already exist.

Values may either be WellPlate instances, or dictionaries with the following keys: - rows: Required\[int\] - columns: Required\[int\] - well\_spacing: Required\[tuple\[float, float\]\] - well\_size: tuple\[float, float\] | None - circular\_wells: bool - name: str

Examples:

```pycon
>>> import useq
>>> useq.register_well_plates(
...     {
...         "custom-square-plate": {
...             "rows": 8, "columns": 8, "well_spacing": 9.3, "well_size": 7.1
...         },
...         "silly-plate": {"rows": 1, "columns": 1, "well_spacing": 100}
...     }
... )
```

## useq.registered\_well\_plate\_keys

```python
registered_well_plate_keys() -> set[str]
```

Return a set of all registered well-plate keys.

These keys may be used as an argument to `WellPlatePlan.plate` to select a plate definition.

# Event

An `MDAEvent` describes one thing for the microscope to do (usually: acquire an image), and the hardware state to do it in. Fields that are left as `None` mean "use the current setting". Iterating over an [`MDASequence`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/index.md>) yields events, but you can also create them yourself.

## useq.MDAEvent

Bases: `UseqModel`

Define a single event in a `MDASequence`.

Usually, this object will be generated by iterating over a `MDASequence` (see `useq.MDASequence.iter_events`).

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `index` | `ReadOnlyDict` | Index of this event in the sequence. This is a mapping of axis name to index. For example: `{'t': 4, 'c': 0, 'z': 5}`. |
| `channel` | `Channel \| None` | Channel to use for this event. If `None`, implies use current channel. By default, `None`. `Channel` is a simple pydantic object with two attributes: `config` and `group`. `config` is the name of the configuration to use for this channel, (e.g. `"488nm"`, `"DAPI"`, `"FITC"`). `group` is the name of the group to which this channel belongs. By default, `"Channel"`. |
| `exposure` | `float \| None` | Exposure time in milliseconds. If not provided, implies use current exposure time. By default, `None`. |
| `min_start_time` | `float \| None` | Minimum start time of this event, in seconds. If provided, the engine will pause until this time has elapsed before starting this event. Times are relative to the start of the sequence, or the last event with `reset_event_timer` set to `True`. |
| `pos_name` | `str \| None` | The name assigned to the position. By default, `None`. |
| `x_pos` | `float \| None` | X position in microns. If not provided, implies use current position. By default, `None`. |
| `y_pos` | `float \| None` | Y position in microns. If not provided, implies use current position. By default, `None`. |
| `z_pos` | `float \| None` | Z position in microns. If not provided, implies use current position. By default, `None`. |
| `slm_image` | `SLMImage \| None` | Image data to display on an SLM device. `SLMImage` is a simple pydantic object with two attributes: `data` and `device`. `data` is the image data (anything that can be cast to a numpy array), `device` is the name of the SLM device to use. If not provided, the "default" SLM device should be used. By default, `None`. |
| `sequence` | `MDASequence \| None` | A reference to the `useq.MDASequence` this event belongs to. This is a read-only attribute. By default, `None`. |
| `properties` | `list[PropertyTuple] \| None` | List of `useq.PropertyTuple` to set before starting this event. Where each item in the list is a 3-member named tuple of `(device_name, property_name, property_value)`. This is inspired by micro-manager's Device Adapter API, but could be used to set arbitrary properties in any backend that supports the concept of devices that have properties with values. By default, `None`. |
| `roi` | `CameraROI \| None` | Camera region of interest. Accepts a `CameraROI` object or a bare tuple of `(offset_x, offset_y, width, height)` which will be automatically converted. By default, `None`. |
| `metadata` | `dict[str, Any]` | Optional metadata to be associated with this event. This is the place for any user-defined data (for example, parameters that a custom acquisition engine needs). |
| `action` | `HardwareAutofocus \| AcquireImage \| CustomAction` | The action to perform for this event. By default, `useq.AcquireImage`. Example of another action is `useq.HardwareAutofocus` which could be used to perform a hardware autofocus. For backwards compatibility, an `action` of `None` implies `AcquireImage`. You may use `CustomAction` to indicate any custom action, with the `data` attribute containing any data required to perform the custom action. |
| `keep_shutter_open` | `bool` | If `True`, the illumination shutter should be left open after the event has been executed, otherwise it should be closed. By default, `False`. This is useful when the sequence of events being executed use the same illumination scheme (such as a z-stack in a single channel), and closing and opening the shutter between events would be slow. |
| `reset_event_timer` | `bool` | If `True`, the engine should reset the event timer to the time of this event, and future `min_start_time` values will be relative to this event. By default, `False`. |

## useq.EventChannel

Bases: `UseqModel`

Channel in a MDA event.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `config` | `str` | Name of the configuration to use for this channel, (e.g. `"488nm"`, `"DAPI"`, `"FITC"`). |
| `group` | `str` | Optional name of the group to which this channel belongs. By default, `"Channel"`. |

## useq.PropertyTuple

Bases: `NamedTuple`

Three-tuple capturing a device, property, and value.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `device_name` | `str` | Name of a device. |
| `property_name` | `str` | Name of a property recognized by the device. |
| `property_value` | `Any` | Value for the property. |

## Event Actions

## useq.Action

Bases: `FrozenModel`

Base class for a `useq.MDAEvent` action.

An `Action` specifies what task should be performed during a `useq.MDAEvent`. An `Action` can be for example used to acquire an image (`useq.AcquireImage`) or to perform a hardware autofocus (`useq.HardwareAutofocus`). An action of `None` implies `AcquireImage`.

You may use `CustomAction` to indicate any custom action, with the `data` attribute containing any data required to perform the custom action.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `str` | Type of the action that should be performed at the `useq.MDAEvent`. |

## useq.AcquireImage

Bases: `Action`

`useq.Action` to acquire an image.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `Literal['acquire_image']` | This action can be used to acquire an image. |

## useq.HardwareAutofocus

Bases: `Action`

`useq.Action` to perform a hardware autofocus.

See also `useq.AutoFocusPlan`.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `Literal['hardware_autofocus']` | This action can be used to trigger hardware autofocus. |
| `autofocus_device_name` | `str \| None` | The name of the autofocus offset motor device (if applicable). If `None`, acquisition engines may attempt to set the offset however they see fit (such as using a current or default autofocus device.) |
| `autofocus_motor_offset` | `float \| None` | Before autofocus is performed, the autofocus motor should be moved to this offset, if applicable. (Not all autofocus devices have an offset motor.) If None, the autofocus motor should not be moved. |
| `max_retries` | `int` | The number of retries if autofocus fails. By default, 3. |

## useq.CustomAction

Bases: `Action`

`useq.Action` to perform a custom action.

This is a generic user action that can be used to represent anything that is not covered by the other action types, such as a microfluidic event, or a photostimulation, etc...

The `data` attribute is a dictionary that can contain any data that is needed to perform the custom action. It *must* be serializable to JSON by `pydantic`.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `Literal['custom']` | This action can be used to perform a custom action. |
| `name` | `str` | A name for the custom action (not to be confused with the `type` attribute, which must always be `"custom"`). |
| `data` | `dict` | Custom data associated with the action. |

# Hardware Autofocus Plan

Ways to describe a hardware-based autofocus plan. An `autofocus_plan` on an [`MDASequence`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/schema/sequence/index.md>) inserts events with a `HardwareAutofocus` action into the sequence (for example, every time the stage position changes).

## useq.AutoFocusPlan

Bases: `FrozenModel`

Base class for hardware autofocus plans.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `autofocus_device_name` | `str \| None` | Optional name of the offset motor device. If `None`, acquisition engines may attempt to set the offset however they see fit (such as using a current or default autofocus device.) |
| `autofocus_motor_offset` | `float \| None` | Before autofocus is performed, the autofocus motor should be moved to this offset, if applicable. (Not all autofocus devices have an offset motor.) If None, the autofocus motor should not be moved. |

### as\_action

```python
as_action() -> HardwareAutofocus
```

Return a `useq.HardwareAutofocus` for this autofocus plan.

### event

```python
event(event: MDAEvent) -> MDAEvent | None
```

Return an autofocus `useq.MDAEvent` if autofocus should be performed.

The z position of the new `useq.MDAEvent` is also updated if a relative zplan is provided since autofocus should be performed on the home z stack position.

### should\_autofocus

```python
should_autofocus(event: MDAEvent) -> bool
```

Method that must be implemented by a subclass.

Should return True if autofocus should be performed (see `useq.AxesBasedAF`).

## useq.AxesBasedAF

Bases: `AutoFocusPlan`

Autofocus plan that performs autofocus when any of the specified axes change.

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `axes` | `tuple[str, ...]` | Tuple of axis label to use for hardware autofocus. At every event in which *any* axis in this tuple changes, autofocus will be performed. For example, if `axes` is `('p',)` then autofocus will be performed every time the `p` axis changes (in other words: every time the position is changed). |
| `autofocus_device_name` | `str \| None` | Optional name of the offset motor device. If `None`, acquisition engines may attempt to set the offset however they see fit (such as using a current or default autofocus device.) |
| `autofocus_motor_offset` | `float \| None` | Before autofocus is performed, the autofocus motor should be moved to this offset, if applicable. (Not all autofocus devices have an offset motor.) If None, the autofocus motor should not be moved. |

### should\_autofocus

```python
should_autofocus(event: MDAEvent) -> bool
```

Return `True` if autofocus should be performed at this event.

Will return `True` if any of the axes specified in `axes` have changed from the previous event.

# Sequence

An `MDASequence` describes a whole experiment: a plan for each axis (time, stage positions, grid, channels and z), and the order in which to iterate them. See [Building Sequences](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/useq-schema/guides/sequences/index.md>) for examples.

## useq.MDASequence

Bases: `UseqModel`

A sequence of MDA (Multi-Dimensional Acquisition) events.

This is the core object in the `useq` library, and is used to define a sequence of events to be run on a microscope. The object may be constructed manually, or loaded from a file (JSON or YAML) with `MDASequence.from_file`.

Iterating over the sequence yields `useq.MDAEvent` objects (see Examples).

Attributes:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `metadata` | `dict[str, Any]` | A dictionary of user metadata to be stored with the sequence. |
| `axis_order` | `tuple[str, ...]` | The order in which the axes are iterated, slowest first. May be given as a string (e.g. `"tpcz"`). Each axis may appear once, and axes that are left out are not iterated (even if they have a plan). The default is `"tpgcz"`. |
| `stage_positions` | `WellPlatePlan \| tuple[AbsolutePosition, ...]` | The stage positions to visit (each with `x`, `y`, `z`, `name`, and `sequence`, all of which are optional), or a `WellPlatePlan`. |
| `grid_plan` | `GridFromEdges \| GridFromPolygon \| GridRowsColumns \| GridWidthHeight \| RandomPoints \| RelativePosition \| None` | The grid plan to follow at each position, or `None`. |
| `channels` | `tuple[Channel, ...]` | The channels to acquire. See `Channel`. |
| `time_plan` | `MultiPhaseTimePlan \| TIntervalDuration \| TIntervalLoops \| TDurationLoops \| None` | The time plan to follow. One of `TIntervalDuration`, `TIntervalLoops`, `TDurationLoops`, `MultiPhaseTimePlan`, or `None` |
| `z_plan` | `ZTopBottom \| ZAboveBelow \| ZRangeAround \| ZAbsolutePositions \| ZRelativePositions \| None` | The z plan to follow. One of `ZTopBottom`, `ZRangeAround`, `ZAboveBelow`, `ZRelativePositions`, `ZAbsolutePositions`, or `None`. Relative plans (`ZRangeAround`, `ZAboveBelow`, `ZRelativePositions`) are added to the `z` of each stage position; if a position has no `z` (or there are no positions), they are relative to `z=0`, *not* to the current focus. |
| `uid` | `UUID` | A read-only unique identifier (uuid version 4) for the sequence. This will be generated, do not set. |
| `autofocus_plan` | `AxesBasedAF \| None` | The hardware autofocus plan to follow. One of `AxesBasedAF` or `None`. |
| `setup` | `MDAEvent \| None` | An optional setup event for the sequence. This event is **not** yielded during iteration; it is intended to be handled separately by the engine. It can be used to set hardware state (e.g. device properties, ROI) before the main acquisition events. By default, `None`. |
| `keep_shutter_open_across` | `tuple[str, ...]` | A tuple of axes `str` across which the illumination shutter should be kept open. Resulting events will have `keep_shutter_open` set to `True` if and only if ALL axes whose indices are changing are in this tuple. For example, if `keep_shutter_open_across=('z',)`, then the shutter would be kept open between events axes {'t': 0, 'z': 0} and {'t': 0, 'z': 1}, but not between {'t': 0, 'z': 0} and {'t': 1, 'z': 0}. |

Examples:

Create a MDASequence

```pycon
>>> from useq import MDASequence
>>> seq = MDASequence(
...     axis_order="tpgcz",
...     time_plan={"interval": 0.1, "loops": 2},
...     stage_positions=[(1, 1, 1)],
...     grid_plan={"rows": 2, "columns": 2},
...     z_plan={"range": 3, "step": 1},
...     channels=[{"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 1}],
... )
```

Look at the sequence to visualize its structure (only fields that were set are shown, and long outputs here are wrapped for readability)

```pycon
>>> seq
MDASequence(
    stage_positions=(AbsolutePosition(x=1.0, y=1.0, z=1.0),),
    grid_plan=GridRowsColumns(rows=2, columns=2),
    channels=(Channel(config='DAPI', exposure=1.0),),
    time_plan=TIntervalLoops(
        interval=datetime.timedelta(microseconds=100000), loops=2
    ),
    z_plan=ZRangeAround(range=3.0, step=1.0),
)
```

Iterate over the events in the sequence

```pycon
>>> events = list(seq)
>>> len(events)
32
>>> events[:2]
[
    MDAEvent(
        index={'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'g': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 0},
        channel=Channel(config='DAPI'),
        exposure=1.0,
        min_start_time=0.0,
        x_pos=0.5,
        y_pos=1.5,
        z_pos=-0.5,
        reset_event_timer=True,
    ),
    MDAEvent(
        index={'t': 0, 'p': 0, 'g': 0, 'c': 0, 'z': 1},
        channel=Channel(config='DAPI'),
        exposure=1.0,
        min_start_time=0.0,
        x_pos=0.5,
        y_pos=1.5,
        z_pos=0.5,
    ),
]
```

Print the sequence as yaml

```pycon
>>> print(seq.yaml())
axis_order:
- t
- p
- g
- c
- z
channels:
- config: DAPI
  exposure: 1.0
grid_plan:
  columns: 2
  rows: 2
stage_positions:
- x: 1.0
  y: 1.0
  z: 1.0
time_plan:
  interval: 0.1
  loops: 2
z_plan:
  range: 3.0
  step: 1.0
```

Create a sequence with a setup event

```pycon
>>> from useq import MDASequence, MDAEvent
>>> seq = MDASequence(
...     setup=MDAEvent(
...         properties=[("Camera", "Binning", "2")],
...         roi=(0, 0, 512, 512),
...     ),
...     channels=["GFP"],
...     time_plan={"interval": 1, "loops": 5},
... )
```

The setup event is accessible via `seq.setup` but is not yielded during iteration (it should be handled separately by implementing engines):

```pycon
>>> seq.setup.action.name
'setup'
>>> seq.setup.roi
CameraROI(offset_x=0, offset_y=0, width=512, height=512)
```

Print setup sequence as yaml

```pycon
>>> print(seq.yaml())
channels:
- config: GFP
setup:
  action:
    name: setup
  properties:
  - - Camera
    - Binning
    - '2'
  roi:
    height: 512
    offset_x: 0
    offset_y: 0
    width: 512
time_plan:
  interval: 1.0
  loops: 5
```

### estimate\_duration

```python
estimate_duration() -> TimeEstimate
```

Estimate duration and other timing issues of an MDASequence.

Notable mis-estimations may include:

- when the time interval is shorter than the time it takes to acquire the data and any of the channels have `acquire_every` \> 1
- when channel exposure times are omitted. In this case, we assume 1ms exposure.

Returns:

<table>       <thead>         <tr>           <th>Type</th>           <th>Description</th>         </tr>       </thead>       <tbody>           <tr class="doc-section-item">             <td>                   <code><autoref backlink-anchor="useq.MDASequence.estimate_duration" backlink-type="returned-by" hover="" identifier="useq._utils.TimeEstimate" optional="">TimeEstimate</autoref></code>             </td>             <td>               <div class="doc-md-description">                 <p>A named 3-tuple with the following fields:</p> <ul> <li><code>total_duration</code> (<code>float</code>): Estimated total duration of the experiment,   in seconds.</li> <li><code>per_t_duration</code> (<code>float</code>): Estimated duration of a single timepoint, in   seconds.</li> <li><code>time_interval_exceeded</code> (<code>bool</code>): Whether the time interval between   timepoints is shorter than the time it takes to acquire the data.</li> </ul>                </div>             </td>           </tr>       </tbody>     </table>

## How sequences are iterated

Iterating an `MDASequence` yields `MDAEvent` objects. The logic lives in `iter_sequence`, an implementation detail (it isn't part of the schema itself) that is shown here for reference:

### iter\_sequence

```python
iter_sequence(sequence)
```

Iterate over all events in the MDA sequence.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This method will usually be used via `useq.MDASequence.iter_events`, or by simply iterating over the sequence.

This does the job of iterating over all the frames in the MDA sequence, handling the logic of merging all z plans in channels and stage positions defined in the plans for each axis.

This is the most "logic heavy" part of `useq-schema` (the rest of which is almost entirely declarative). This iterator is useful for consuming `MDASequence` objects in a python runtime, but it isn't considered a "core" part of the schema.

The `sequence.setup` event is not yielded during iteration. It is intended to be handled separately by an engine.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sequence` | `MDASequence` | The sequence to iterate over. | *required* |

Yields:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `MDAEvent` | Each event in the MDA sequence. |

# Events

There are two objects that emit events in `pymmcore-plus`. The `CMMCorePlus` object emits the `PCoreSignaler` signals at `core.events` when the state of the microscope changes, and the `MDARunner` emits the `PMDASignaler` signals at `core.mda.events` as an acquisition sequence progresses.

See [Events and Callbacks](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/index.md>) for how to connect callbacks, choosing the Qt or psygnal backend, and which thread your callbacks run on.

## PCoreSignaler

Bases: `Protocol`

Declares the protocol for all signals that will be emitted from CMMCorePlus.

The main instance of this interface is available on the `CMMCorePlus` object at the `events` attribute. Each signal on `events` is an object that has a `connect` and a `disconnect` method that you can use to connect/disconnect your own callback functions. `connect` and `disconnect` accept a single argument, which is a callable that will be called when the signal is emitted. The callable should accept no more positional arguments than the signal emits (noted for each signal below), but may accept fewer.

> [!NOTE]
>
> These events are a superset of those emitted by [MMEventCallback](<https://micro-manager.org/apidoc/mmcorej/latest/mmcorej/MMEventCallback.html>) in the MMCore C++ library. The "on" prefix has been removed from the names here and the first letter lower cased.
>
> **Important**
>
> In the core C++ library (and in `pymmcore`), the emission of many of these events is left to the discretion of the device adapter. In `pymmcore_plus`, we attempt to emit these events in a more consistent manner (e.g. by checking a particular value before and after calling into the C++ library). So, the emission of these events is not guaranteed to be 1:1 with the C++ library; however, it should be easier to follow the state of the core when using `pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus`.

Examples:

To connect to the `onExposureChanged` event emitted by MMCore, you would connect to the `exposureChanged` signal on this class:

```python
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()


def on_exposure_changed(device: str, new_exposure: float):
    print(f"Exposure changed for {device} to {new_exposure}")


core.events.exposureChanged.connect(on_exposure_changed)
```

Events may also be connected as a decorator:

```python
@core.events.exposureChanged.connect
def on_exposure_changed(device: str, new_exposure: float): ...
```

---

### devicePropertyChanged

```python
devicePropertyChanged(
    device: str, property: str | None = None
) -> PSignalInstance
```

Return object to connect/disconnect to device/property-specific changes.

Note that the callback provided to `.connect()` must take *two* parameters (property\_name, new\_value) if only `device` is provided, and *one* parameter (new\_value) of both `device` and `property` are provided.

Parameters:

| Name | Type | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `device` | `str` | A device label | *required* |
| `property` | `Optional[str]` | Optional property label. If not provided, all property changes on `device` will trigger an event emission. by default None | `None` |

Returns:

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `_PropertySignal` | Object with `connect` and `disconnect` methods that attach a callback to the change event of a specific property or device. |

Examples:

```pycon
>>> core.events.devicePropertyChanged("Camera", "Gain").connect(callback)
>>> core.events.devicePropertyChanged("Camera").connect(callback)
```

## PMDASignaler

Bases: `Protocol`

Declares the protocol for all signals that will be emitted from `pymmcore_plus.mda.MDARunner`.

### sequenceStarted

```python
sequenceStarted: PSignal
```

Emits `(sequence: MDASequence, metadata: dict)` when an acquisition sequence is started.

For the default `MDAEngine`, the metadata `dict` will be of type `SummaryMetaV1`.

### sequencePauseToggled

```python
sequencePauseToggled: PSignal
```

Emits `(paused: bool)` when an acquisition sequence is paused or unpaused.

### sequenceCanceled

```python
sequenceCanceled: PSignal
```

Emits `(sequence: MDASequence)` when an acquisition sequence is canceled.

### sequenceFinished

```python
sequenceFinished: PSignal
```

Emits `(sequence: MDASequence)` when an acquisition sequence is finished.

### frameReady

```python
frameReady: PSignal
```

Emits `(img: np.ndarray, event: MDAEvent, metadata: dict)` after an image is acquired during an acquisition sequence.

For the default `MDAEngine`, the metadata `dict` will be of type `FrameMetaV1`.

### awaitingEvent

```python
awaitingEvent: PSignal
```

Emits `(event: MDAEvent, remaining_sec: float)` when the runner is waiting to start an event.

Note: Not all events in a sequence will emit this signal. This will only be emitted if the wait time is non-zero.

### eventStarted

```python
eventStarted: PSignal
```

Emits `(event: MDAEvent)` immediately before event setup and execution.

# CLI Reference

This page provides documentation for the `mmcore` command line tool, which is installed along with `pymmcore-plus`.

The CLI can be used to interact with the `pymmcore_plus` package from the command line, including the installation, removal, and selection of Micro-Manager device adapters, showing log files, and running a test acquisition (`mmcore run`, which doesn't save anything). (The default `--dest` folder for `install` and `build-dev` depends on your platform; see [Micro-Manager device adapters](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/#installing-micro-manager-device-adapters>).)

## `mmcore`

mmcore: pymmcore-plus command line.

For additional help on a specific command: type `mmcore COMMAND --help`

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Options**:

- `--version`: Show version and exit.
- `--install-completion`: Install completion for the current shell.
- `--show-completion`: Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore clean`

Remove all Micro-Manager installs downloaded by pymmcore-plus.

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore clean [OPTIONS] [glob]
```

**Arguments**:

- `glob`: glob pattern to clean \[default: \*\]

**Options**:

- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore list`

Show all discovered Micro-Manager installations.

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore list [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**:

- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore mmstudio`

Run the Java Micro-Manager GUI.

This command will attempt to locate and execute an ImageJ application found in the active Micro-Manager directory.

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore mmstudio [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**:

- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore install`

Install Micro-Manager device adapters from [https://download.micro-manager.org](<https://download.micro-manager.org>).

On Windows and Intel macOS, this downloads a nightly build of Micro-Manager. Micro-Manager doesn't publish nightly builds for Linux or Apple Silicon, so on those platforms only the test adapters (DemoCamera, Utilities, etc...) are installed, from [https://github.com/micro-manager/mm-test-adapters](<https://github.com/micro-manager/mm-test-adapters>).

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore install [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**:

- `-d, --dest <directory>`: Installation directory. \[default: \<user data dir\>/pymmcore-plus/mm\]
- `-r, --release <str>`: Release date. e.g. 20210201 \[default: latest-compatible\]
- `--plain-output`: Do not use rich output. Useful for scripting.
- `--test-adapters`: Install only test adapters (e.g. DemoCamera and others for testing).
- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore run`

Run a Micro-Manager acquisition from a useq-schema MDASequence file.

Nothing is saved to disk (this is mostly useful for testing and profiling).

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore run [OPTIONS] [useq]
```

**Arguments**:

- `useq`: Path to useq-schema file.

**Options**:

- `-c, --config <file>`: Path to Micro-Manager system configuration file.
- `--z-go-up / --no-z-go-up`: Acquire from bottom to top.
- `--z-top <float>`: Top of z-stack.
- `--z-bottom <float>`: Bottom of z-stack.
- `--z-range <float>`: Symmetric range of z-stack around position.
- `--z-above <float>`: Asymmetric range of z-stack above position.
- `--z-below <float>`: Asymmetric range of z-stack below position.
- `--z-step <float>`: Step size of z-stack.
- `-zr <float>`: Relative z-positions to acquire (may use multiple times).
- `-za <float>`: Absolute z-positions to acquire (may use multiple times).
- `--t-interval <float>`: Interval between timepoints.
- `--t-duration <float>`: Duration of time lapse.
- `--t-loops <float>`: Number of time points to acquire.
- `--dry-run / --no-dry-run`: Do not run the acquisition. \[default: no-dry-run\]
- `--axis-order <str>`: Order of axes to acquire (e.g. 'TPCZ').
- `--channel <str>`: Channel to acquire. Argument is a string of the following form:

  - name: "DAPI"
  - name;exposure: "DAPI;0.5"
  - useq-schema JSON: '{"config": "DAPI", "exposure": 0.5, "z\_offset": 0.5}'
- `--channel-group <str>`: Name of Micro-Manager configuration group for channels. \[default: Channel\]
- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore build-dev`

Build Micro-Manager device adapters from the git repo.

Currently only supports macos and linux.

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore build-dev [OPTIONS] [devices]...
```

**Arguments**:

- `devices...`: Device adapters to build. Defaults to \['DemoCamera', 'Utilities', 'SequenceTester'\]

**Options**:

- `-d, --dest <directory>`: Installation directory. \[default: \<user data dir\>/pymmcore-plus/mm\]
- `-y`: Overwrite existing if git sha is already built. If not specified, will prompt.
- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore logs`

Display recent output from pymmcore-plus log.

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore logs [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**:

- `-n, --num <int>`: Number of lines to display.
- `-t, --tail`: Continually stream logs.
- `-c, --clear`: Delete all log files.
- `--reveal`: Reveal log file in Explorer/Finder.
- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore info`

Display information about the Micro-Manager and pymmcore install.

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore info [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**:

- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore use`

Change the currently used Micro-Manager version/path.

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore use [OPTIONS] {pattern}
```

**Arguments**:

- `pattern`: Path to an existing directory, or pattern to match against installations found by `mmcore list` \[required\]

**Options**:

- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

### `mmcore bench`

Run a benchmark of Core and Devices loaded with `config` (or Demo).

**Usage**:

```console
$ mmcore bench [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**:

- `-c, --config <file>`: Path to Micro-Manager system configuration file.
- `-n, --number <int>`: Number of iterations for each test. \[default: 10\]
- `--help`: Show this message and exit.

# Environment Variables

The following environment variables may be used to configure pymmcore-plus globally.

*Unless noted otherwise, boolean variables can be set to `1`, `0`, `True`, or `False` (case insensitive).*

| Variable | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`PYMM_DEBUG_LOG`** | Call `enableDebugLog(True)` when creating a `CMMCorePlus`. |  |
| **`PYMM_STDERR_LOG`** | Call `enableStderrLog(True)` when creating a `CMMCorePlus`. |  |
| **`PYMM_BUFFER_SIZE_MB`** | Circular buffer memory footprint in MB. | MMCore's default (250 MB) |
| **`PYMM_STRICT_INIT_CHECKS`** | Enable/disable strict initialization checks | Enabled |
| **`PYMM_PARALLEL_INIT`** | Enable/disable parallel device initialization | Enabled |
| **`PYMM_LOG_LEVEL`** | pymmcore-plus [logging](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/logging/index.md>) level for the console. | `'WARNING'` |
| **`PYMM_LOG_FILE`** | Logfile location. Set to `0`, `false`, `no` or `none` to disable logging to a file. | `pymmcore-plus.log` in the pymmcore-plus [log directory](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/logging/#customizing-logging>) |
| **`PYMM_LOG_RICH`** | Use [rich](<https://rich.readthedocs.io/>) for stderr logging (`1`, `true` or `yes`). Adds some formatting overhead ([\#449](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus/issues/449>)). | `"0"` (disabled) |
| **`MICROMANAGER_PATH`** | Override location of Micro-Manager directory (with device adapters) | Found automatically (see the [search order](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/install/#setting-the-active-installation>)) |
| **`PYMM_SIGNALS_BACKEND`** | The event backend to use. Must be one of `'qt'`, `'psygnal'`, or `'auto'` | `auto` (Qt if a `QApplication` exists when `CMMCorePlus` is created, otherwise psygnal) |
| **`PYMM_DISABLE_IPYTHON_COMPLETIONS`** | Set to `1` to disable [Tab autocompletion for IPython](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/ipython_completion/index.md>) | `"0"` (enabled) |
| **`UNICORE_SEQUENCE_BUFFER_MB`** | Size of the sequence buffer used by [`UniMMCore`](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-plus/guides/unicore/index.md>) for Python cameras, in MB. | 1024 MB (250 MB on CI) |

# Contributing

# How These Docs Work

This site is put together from the `docs/` folders (and docstrings) of several repositories, so that all of the packages share one navigation and search, and can link to each other. It's built with [zensical](<https://zensical.org>) by [pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus.github.io](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus.github.io>) (the *hub*).

```
graph LR
  subgraph members [Member repositories]
    plus[pymmcore-plus<br/>docs/ + src/]
    useq[useq-schema<br/>docs/ + src/]
    widgets[pymmcore-widgets<br/>docs/ + src/]
    more[...]
  end
  hub[hub: compose.py] --> build[build/docs + zensical.toml] --> site[pymmcore-plus.github.io]
  plus --> hub
  useq --> hub
  widgets --> hub
  more --> hub
```

## Who owns what

**Each member repository** owns:

- `docs/`: its pages, written as they would be for a stand-alone site. The folder is published at `/<repo-name>/`, so `pymmcore-plus/docs/guides/events.md` becomes `/pymmcore-plus/guides/events/`.
- `docs/**/.nav.yml`: [awesome-nav](<https://lukasgeiter.github.io/mkdocs-awesome-nav/>) files ordering the package's own section.
- `zensical.toml`: what is specific to the package: mkdocstrings `paths`, griffe `extensions`, and the `api-autonav` settings for its API reference.
- `docs/_gen.py` (optional): a script that generates content before the build, writing into git-ignored files (for example the `CMMCorePlus` method table or the widget screenshots).

**The hub** owns the theme, global settings, the landing page, *Getting Started* (plus a few pages that don't belong to any one package, like [Using your own microscope](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/guide/own-microscope/index.md>)), and the top-level navigation (`docs/.nav.yml`), which places member pages into the site-wide *User Guide*.

## Previewing locally

```sh
git clone https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus.github.io
cd pymmcore-plus.github.io
just serve          # clones members into .repos/ and serves http://localhost:8000
```

To edit a member's docs or code and see the result live, put a git worktree of your own clone in `.repos/` instead (`tools/repos.py --worktrees ~/path/to/clones`, or `git worktree add`). Use `--only pymmcore-plus,useq-schema` for a faster preview of just some packages, and `--no-gen` to skip the generation scripts.

`just check` builds with `--strict`, which fails on any warning (broken links, unresolved cross-references, docstring problems).

## The API reference

API pages are generated from each member's `api-autonav` settings, with two rules on top:

1. **Each object is documented once, at its highest-level public name.** `pymmcore_plus.Device` is documented on the `pymmcore_plus` page; the `pymmcore_plus.core` page lists it under *Re-exports* with a link. Cross-references to any public path (`[x][pymmcore_plus.core.Device]`) still resolve.
2. **Hand-written pages claim objects.** If a page in `docs/` renders an object with a `identifier` block, that page is where the object is documented, and the generated pages link to it. A hand-written page at a module's generated path (for example `docs/api/pymmcore_plus/metadata/index.md`) replaces the generated page.

## Writing tips

- Link to API objects with [autorefs](<https://mkdocstrings.github.io/autorefs/>): ``[`CMMCorePlus`][pymmcore_plus.CMMCorePlus]`` works from any page in any repository.
- Link to pages in other packages with relative paths (`../useq-schema/schema/axes.md`); they are checked when the site is built.
- Snippets (`--8<-- "examples/foo.py"`) are resolved relative to the member's repository root.
- If you want a heading to be linked from other repositories, give it an explicit, namespaced id: `## Installing {#widgets-install}`.

## How changes get published

- **Pull requests** to a member repository build the whole site with the PR's changes (failing only on warnings in that member's pages), and upload the result as an artifact you can download and browse.
- **Merges** to `main` trigger a rebuild and deploy of the full site. The site is also rebuilt nightly.

## Development setup

We use [uv](<https://docs.astral.sh/uv/>) in all of the repositories (but any virtual environment manager should work), and [prek](<https://github.com/j178/prek>) (or pre-commit) for linting:

```sh
git clone <your fork>
cd <repo>
uv sync
uv run prek install  # or: uv run pre-commit install
uv run pytest
```

Most of the tests need Micro-Manager's demo device adapters, so run `uv run mmcore install` once if you haven't already.

## Improving the docs

Most pages have an edit button (top right) that opens the source file in the right repository. (Pages in the API reference are generated from docstrings, so edit those in the package's `src/` folder.) Each package's docs live in its own `docs/` folder, so a pull request that changes code can update the documentation at the same time. To preview the full site locally, see [How these docs work](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/contributing/docs/index.md>).

# Contributing to pymmcore-plus

All development for this library happens in the [pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus>) repo on GitHub. The general setup (cloning, `uv sync`, `prek`, running the tests) is the same as for the other packages, and is described on the main [Contributing](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/contributing/index.md>) page. This page has a few notes that are specific to pymmcore-plus.

## Without uv

If you're using a different virtual environment manager (like conda) instead of uv, you can install the package and its development dependencies with:

```bash
pip install -e . --group dev
```

> This requires a newer version of `pip` (\>= 25.1) to work.

## Device adapters for the tests

Most of the tests use Micro-Manager's demo devices, so you'll need a compatible set of device adapters:

```bash
uv run mmcore install
```

On Linux and Apple Silicon this installs just the test adapters (which is all the tests need). Alternatively, `pip install mm-test-adapters` puts them in your environment, where `pymmcore-plus` will find them (this can be handy on CI). You can confirm that everything works by running:

```py
from pymmcore_plus import CMMCorePlus

core = CMMCorePlus()
core.loadSystemConfiguration()
core.snap()
```

If you want to test against device adapters built from the current `mmCoreAndDevices` source (on macOS or Linux), run `uv run mmcore build-dev`. This will download the micro-manager repo, build it, and drop the DemoCamera, Utilities and SequenceTester devices into the pymmcore-plus user data folder (by default `~/Library/Application Support/pymmcore-plus/mm` on macOS), which is on the default search path. (On macOS you must have [homebrew](<https://brew.sh>) installed.)

## Contributing documentation

These docs live in the `docs/` folder of this repository (and in docstrings), but the site itself is built by [pymmcore-plus.github.io](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-plus.github.io>), which combines the docs of all the pymmcore-plus packages. See [How these docs work](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/contributing/docs/index.md>) to preview your changes locally. The `CMMCorePlus` method table and the CLI reference are generated by `docs/_gen.py`.

# Contributing to pymmcore-widgets

Thanks for thinking of a way to help improve this library!

Remember that contributions come in all shapes and sizes beyond writing bug fixes. Contributing to documentation, opening new issues for bugs, asking for clarification on things you find unclear or requesting new features, are all super valuable contributions.

You can do any of the above by opening a new [issue](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets/issues>) or by submitting a [pull request](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets/pulls>) on the [GitHub repository](<https://github.com/pymmcore-plus/pymmcore-widgets>) for this project. The [contributing guide](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/contributing/index.md>) has the parts that are the same for every package (and the ways to reach us); this page has the parts that are specific to the widgets.

## Development setup

We use [uv](<https://docs.astral.sh/uv/>). `uv sync` installs the package with its `dev` dependency group, which includes PyQt6:

```sh
git clone <your-fork>
cd pymmcore-widgets
uv sync
uv run mmcore install  # the demo device adapters, used by most tests
```

## Running the tests

```sh
uv run pytest
```

Some of the tests show real windows. To run them without any windows (on a machine without a display, or just to keep your screen quiet), use Qt's offscreen platform:

```sh
QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen uv run pytest
```

(On Windows PowerShell: `$env:QT_QPA_PLATFORM = "offscreen"` first.) CI runs the tests on macOS and Windows, with both PyQt6 and PySide6.

## Widget pages and screenshots

Each widget's documentation page, its screenshots and its card in the [widget gallery](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/pymmcore-widgets/widgets/index.md>) are generated by `docs/_gen.py`:

- `docs/widget_list.json` lists the widgets, by gallery section.
- `examples/<snake_case_name>.py` is the example for each one (e.g. `examples/mda_widget.py` for `MDAWidget`). `_gen.py` runs it offscreen, grabs the window it shows (in light and dark mode), and puts the code on the widget's page.
- The widget's docstring becomes the rest of the page, and its first line is the description on the gallery card.

So, to add a widget to the docs, export it from `pymmcore_widgets`, add it to `widget_list.json`, and write an example that shows it with the demo configuration. `_gen.py` warns about exported widgets that are missing from the list. You can run it yourself to check that the example works:

```sh
uv run python docs/_gen.py          # only redoes screenshots whose example changed
uv run python docs/_gen.py --force  # redo them all
```

The output (`docs/api/`, `docs/_generated/`, `docs/images/generated/`) is not committed. The docs themselves are built as part of the unified pymmcore-plus site: see [How These Docs Work](<https://pymmcore-plus.github.io/contributing/docs/index.md>) to preview them.
